teile.einleitung: An **argumentative essay** is a text in which you think a question through carefully and weigh up the arguments. At the end comes your own opinion, backed up with reasons.
wichtigste: The **linear essay** looks at only one side of a question.
The **dialectical essay** weighs up the pros and cons.
A decision question such as “Should we ...?” leads to a dialectical essay.
In the **hourglass method**, all the counter-arguments come first, then your own.
In the **ping-pong method**, pros and cons take turns.
The conclusion contains a reasoned **position**.

abschnitte.text: The **linear** or building essay develops arguments in one direction, usually from the weakest to the strongest. It suits questions about causes, effects or solutions, such as “Why do young people read less?” The **dialectical** essay deals with a **decision question** that can be answered with yes or no: “Should school start later?” Then you weigh up the pros and cons.

An argument is made up of a **claim**, a **reason** and an **example**. In a building essay, the strongest argument goes at the **end of the main part**, because that way it is remembered best. With a **concession** you admit that the other side has a fair point: “It is true that ..., but ...” This comes across as fair and believable.

There are two ways to build a dialectical essay. In the **hourglass method**, the counter-arguments come first, from strongest to weakest, followed by your own, from weakest to strongest. This creates the shape of an hourglass. In the **ping-pong method**, also called the zip method, each argument is followed directly by a counter-argument.

The **introduction** leads into the topic and states the question. In the **conclusion** you weigh things up and reach a judgement, sometimes a compromise or a look ahead. New arguments do not belong there. In a **text-based** essay you examine the position of a given text. Weighing things up is also important in Switzerland: before every popular vote, voters read the arguments for and against.

gewusst: The word “dialectical” comes from Greek and has to do with the art of discussion.
If you know the counter-arguments well, you can usually defend your own opinion more convincingly.

teile.einleitung: “The Swiss Family Robinson” (in German “Der Schweizerische Robinson”) is a famous adventure novel from Bern. It tells the story of a family who build a new life on a lonely island after a shipwreck.
wichtigste: The Bern pastor **Johann David Wyss** made up the story for his sons.
His son **Johann Rudolf Wyss** published the book in 1812.
A pastor's family with four sons is stranded on an island after a shipwreck.
With hard work and knowledge the family builds a new home.
The book is one of the **Robinsonades** and was translated into many languages.

abschnitte.text: Johann David Wyss was a pastor in Bern. He told his four sons a long adventure story and wrote it down bit by bit. His son **Johann Rudolf Wyss**, a professor in Bern, revised the notes and published them as a book in **1812**. In this way a family story became a novel that children all over Europe were soon reading.

A ship is caught in a terrible storm and runs aground. The crew save themselves, but one family is left behind: father, mother and four sons. They reach an uninhabited island and fetch tools, supplies and animals from the wreck. Over time they build huts, lay out fields and even live in a big **tree house**. Again and again they discover new plants and animals.

The model was the novel **“Robinson Crusoe”** by Daniel Defoe from 1719. In it a man survives alone on an island. Stories that follow this pattern are called **Robinsonades**. In The Swiss Family Robinson, however, it is not one person but a whole family who are stranded. That is why it is also about sticking together.

Wyss wanted to entertain his children and teach them at the same time. In the book the father explains a lot about nature, animals, plants and crafts. The sons learn to solve problems by thinking and by not giving up. Faith and gratitude also play an important part, since the narrator is a pastor.

gewusst: In English the book is called “The Swiss Family Robinson”. It has been filmed several times, including by Disney.
In the novel the island is home to animals that in reality would never be found together in one place.

teile.einleitung: Denglisch is a word for the mixture of German (Deutsch) and English. It is mostly used disapprovingly when someone uses a great many or unnecessary English expressions. Opinions differ on whether English words enrich the German language or spoil it.
wichtigste: **Denglisch** is a **blend word** made from “Deutsch” and “Englisch”.
It is used to criticise unnecessary or frequent English expressions in German.
English words in German are called **anglicisms**.
Some words that seem English do not exist in English at all, such as “Handy”.
In Switzerland people also use the word “Natel” for it.

abschnitte.text: The word **Denglisch** is a **blend word**. This means it was packed together from two words: “Deutsch” (German) and “Englisch” (English). It is mostly used critically. It refers to sentences like “Wir müssen das Meeting downloaden und dann updaten” (We have to download the meeting and then update it). Not everyone understands sentences like this well.

English words that have been taken into German are called **anglicisms**. Examples are “Computer”, “Team” or “online”. Some words only sound English but are not used that way in English at all. They are called **pseudo-anglicisms**. The best-known example is “Handy”, the German word for a mobile phone: in English you say “mobile phone” or “cell phone”. In Switzerland many people also say “Natel”.

Denglisch is much debated. Some people think English words make the language more modern and suit technology and business well. Others think many anglicisms are unnecessary because there are good German words. They also fear that older people are left out. But languages have always taken in words from other languages; in the past German took many from French and Latin, for example.

gewusst: Similar mixtures exist in other languages too; in French they are called “Franglais”.
The word “Natel” was originally short for “Nationales Autotelefon” (national car telephone).

teile.einleitung: **Diglossia** means that a society uses two forms of a language for different purposes. German-speaking Switzerland, with dialect and standard German, is a well-known example.
wichtigste: In diglossia, each of two forms of a language has its own areas of use.
**Charles A. Ferguson** coined the term in its present meaning in 1959.
Ferguson distinguished the formal **H variety** from the everyday **L variety**.
His examples were Arabic, Modern Greek, Haitian and the German of Switzerland.
**Joshua Fishman** extended the concept to different languages in 1967.
In German-speaking Switzerland people speak of **medial diglossia**.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek and means something like “speaking two languages”. In linguistics it refers to a particular situation: a community uses two **varieties**, that is two forms of a language. Which form you choose depends on the situation. One is suited to formal occasions, the other to everyday life.

In 1959 the linguist **Charles A. Ferguson** described four examples in an essay: Arabic, Modern Greek, Haitian and the German of Switzerland. He called the respected, usually written form the **H variety** (from “high”) and the everyday form the **L variety** (from “low”). In 1967 **Joshua Fishman** applied the idea to two completely different languages as well. He also separated diglossia in society from bilingualism in individual people.

In German-speaking Switzerland people almost always speak **dialect** in everyday life, in all sections of society. Writing, however, is mostly in **standard German**, for example in newspapers, books and letters. So what matters is whether something is spoken or written. That is why it is called **medial diglossia**. Standard German is spoken at school and on many news programmes.

Since text messages and chats came along, many German-speaking Swiss people write in dialect in private. There is no fixed spelling for it; everyone writes the way they speak. For official texts standard German remains the rule. In the **National Council and the Council of States**, too, German-speaking Swiss members mostly speak standard German. This makes it easier for members from other language regions and for the interpreters to follow.

gewusst: The word diglossia existed before Ferguson, but he gave it its present scientific meaning.
In Arabic, Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects exist side by side in a similar way to dialect and standard German in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Words change their meaning over time. Something that was neutral many hundreds of years ago can sound disparaging today, and the other way round. This process is called semantic change.
wichtigste: **Semantic change** means that the meaning of a word changes over time.
In **pejoration** a word takes on a disparaging sound, for example the German “Weib” (woman).
In **amelioration** a word rises in status, for example “Marschall” (marshal).
In **broadening** a word comes to fit more things, for example “Sache” (thing).
In **narrowing** a word comes to fit fewer things, for example “Gift” (poison).
The old meaning often lives on in fixed expressions.

abschnitte.text: In Middle High German the word **“Weib”** simply meant a woman, quite neutrally. Today it sounds disparaging. This change is called **pejoration**, from the Latin “peior”, worse. The old meaning is still present in the German adjective “weiblich” (female, feminine).

A **“Marschall”** (marshal) was originally a groom, that is a servant who looked after the horses. Later it became a high military rank. When a word rises in status like this, it is called **amelioration**. This comes from the Latin “melior”, better.

The German word **“Sache”** originally meant only a legal dispute. Today it can mean almost anything (thing, matter). This is **broadening**. The old meaning lives on in expressions such as “in Sachen” (in the matter of). The other way round, **“Gift”** used to mean a gift in general, but today it only means a dangerous substance, poison. This is **narrowing**, and the old meaning is still found in “Mitgift” (dowry).

Sometimes a word gains a completely new meaning. A **mouse** is an animal, but also a device for the computer, because it looks similar. Such transfers are called **semantic transfer**. New meanings are still appearing all the time today, especially through technology and young people’s language. So anyone reading old texts must be careful: a word may have meant something different there from today.

gewusst: The English word “gift” still means a present today and shows the old meaning.
The German word “toll” used to mean “mad”; today it means something great.

teile.einleitung: In a shopping centre, at the station or at a festival, you can suddenly lose sight of your parents. That is frightening, but there are good rules. The best thing is to ask someone who works there for help.
wichtigste: Stay calm and do not wander around aimlessly.
Ask a person who works there for help, for example at the till.
Staff can have your parents called over the loudspeaker.
Never go away with a stranger, for example to their car.
It helps to know your parents’ mobile number by heart.
Before going shopping you can agree on a meeting point.

abschnitte.text: If you can no longer see your parents, first **stand still** and take a deep breath. Look around; perhaps they are very close by. Do not run here and there all over the building. Your parents are looking for you too, and if you both wander about, you can easily miss each other.

It is best to ask someone who **works** there. That might be a shop assistant at the **till**, someone at the information desk or a security guard. They know what to do and can call your parents over the **loudspeaker**. If you cannot see any staff, you can ask a mother or father with children.

Learn your parents’ **mobile number** by heart. Some children also carry a note with the number on it. Before an outing you can agree on a **meeting point**, for example at the entrance or at the information desk. If you know a meeting point, you find each other again more quickly.

**Never** go with a stranger, even if they seem friendly or say they will take you to your parents. Stay inside the **building** and in a place with lots of people. Never get into a stranger’s **car**. You always get help where you are.

gewusst: Many large shopping centres and festivals have a place where lost children can be collected.
At big events small children are sometimes given a wristband with their parents’ phone number.

teile.einleitung: A defect is a fault or damage in a rented flat, for example a dripping tap or a broken heating system. Swiss tenancy law sets out who has to repair what.
wichtigste: A defect is damage or a fault in the rented property.
The tenant must **report** defects to the landlord.
It is best to report a defect **in writing**.
The landlord must fix larger defects.
The tenant pays for small repairs, the **minor maintenance**, themselves.
If defects are serious, the rent can be reduced.

abschnitte.text: The landlord must hand over the flat in a condition in which people can live in it well. If something is broken or does not work, this is called a **defect**. It could be a dripping tap, a leak in the roof, **mould** on the wall or a heating system that does not get warm. Defects may already be there when you move in or appear later.

When you move in, you draw up a **handover report** together with the landlord or the management. It records what damage already exists. If you discover further defects after moving in, you report them quickly. This makes it clear that you did not cause the damage yourself. This is also important when you move out.

A tenant must **report** defects to the landlord, even if they cannot fix them themselves. It is best to do this **in writing**, for example with a letter or an email, and to include photos. A written report counts as **evidence** later. Anyone who does not report damage and it gets worse as a result can be held liable for it.

Small jobs such as replacing a shower hose or clearing a blocked drain are part of **minor maintenance**. The tenant pays for these. Larger defects must be fixed by the **landlord** at their own expense. This applies, for example, to a faulty heating system or a broken fridge that belongs to the flat.

If the landlord does not repair a defect, the tenant has rights. They can ask for a **reduction in the rent** for as long as the defect lasts. After setting a deadline in writing, they can also **deposit** the rent with an office named by the canton. But you must follow the rules exactly, ideally with advice, for example from the tenants’ association or the conciliation authority.

gewusst: What exactly counts as minor maintenance is not set out in a fixed list; it comes from court decisions and local custom.
Mould often forms when there is too little airing, but it can also be due to the way the building was built.

teile.einleitung: A roundabout is a round junction where everyone drives in the same direction around a central island. There are a great many roundabouts in Switzerland, and there are clear rules about who has right of way.
wichtigste: In a roundabout everyone drives anticlockwise around the central island.
Whoever is already in the roundabout has **right of way**.
Anyone who wants to enter waits until the gap is big enough.
When leaving the roundabout, you indicate right or give the hand signal.
Cyclists should ride in the middle of the lane in a roundabout.
Zebra crossings are often just before the roundabout.

abschnitte.text: A **roundabout**, officially called a **circular junction**, replaces a normal crossroads. In the middle is a round **island**, often with flowers or art. All vehicles drive round to the right, that is anticlockwise. Because nobody drives straight across the junction, fewer serious accidents happen, and traffic often flows better than with traffic lights.

In a roundabout there is a simple rule: whoever is **already in it** has right of way. Before the entrance there is a sign with three arrows in a circle and a triangle meaning **“Give way”**. Anyone who wants to enter slows down, looks to the left and waits until it is clear. Only then do they drive into the roundabout.

For cyclists a roundabout is a challenge. It is best to ride in the **middle of the lane** and not right at the edge. That way no car can overtake you in the roundabout and cut you off. Before the exit you look behind you and signal with your **right arm** that you are leaving. If the roundabout is big and busy, you can also get off and push your bike.

The **zebra crossings** are usually a little way before the roundabout. There, cars wait for pedestrians before entering the roundabout. People on foot also watch out for cars that are just leaving the roundabout. Eye contact with the driver helps you to cross the road safely.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the countries with especially many roundabouts; there are several thousand.
On many roundabout islands in Switzerland there are works of art that show what a municipality is known for.

teile.einleitung: Serafe is the company that collects the radio and television fee in Switzerland. This fee is also called the media fee. Since 2019 basically every household has paid it, whether or not it has any devices.
wichtigste: The media fee pays for radio and television in Switzerland.
Since 2019 it has been linked to the household, not to devices.
The company Serafe sends the bills to households.
Before that, the company Billag collected the fees.
People receiving supplementary benefits can apply to be exempted.
Larger companies also pay a fee.

abschnitte.text: The **media fee** is used to pay radio and television broadcasters. Most of it goes to the **SRG**, which includes, for example, SRF, RTS and RSI. Part goes to **private local radio stations** and regional television channels. This means there are programmes in all the **national languages** and in all regions.

In the past, only people who had a radio or a television paid. Today you can also receive programmes on a **mobile phone** or a computer. That is why, since **2019**, basically every **household** has paid the fee. It does not matter how many people live there. In 2024 the fee was 335 francs a year.

Anyone receiving **supplementary benefits** to the AVS or IV can apply to be exempted. Deafblind people and certain diplomats do not have to pay either. For **companies** there is a separate fee, which is collected by the Federal Tax Administration. Small firms are exempt from it.

In Switzerland there are repeated **votes** on the fees. In **2018** the “No Billag” initiative wanted to abolish the fees completely. The people clearly **rejected** it. Some think that media for everyone should be paid for together. Others think everyone should only pay for what they use.

gewusst: The name Serafe is short for the German “Schweizerische Erhebungsstelle für die Radio- und Fernsehabgabe”, the Swiss collection office for the radio and television fee.
In the vote on “No Billag”, more than 70 per cent of voters said no.

teile.einleitung: A **euphemism** is a word that makes something unpleasant sound nicer. Instead of “die”, for example, people say “pass away”, which sounds gentler.
wichtigste: A euphemism replaces an unpleasant expression with a **milder** one.
The word comes from Greek and means something like “speaking well”.
Examples: “pass away” instead of “die”, “let go” instead of “fire”.
The opposite, an insulting term, is called a **dysphemism**.
Euphemisms can be considerate, but they can also hide something.

abschnitte.text: Some things are sad, embarrassing or unpleasant. Then people like to choose a friendlier word. Instead of “die” they say “pass away” or “leave us”. Instead of “old” they might say “elderly”. Expressions like these are called **euphemisms**, from the Greek “eu” (good) and “phemi” (I say).

People often use euphemisms out of **politeness** and consideration. If you write to a grieving family, you choose your words carefully. With illness or mishaps, too, people do not want to hurt anyone. In such cases euphemisms help people treat each other kindly.

But euphemisms can also **hide** something. Companies talk about “letting people go” when people lose their jobs. Instead of a price rise, they talk about a “price adjustment”. In politics and advertising it is therefore worth listening carefully. You can ask yourself: what does this word really mean?

The opposite of a euphemism is a **dysphemism**. This deliberately describes something in an insulting or rude way, such as “banger” for a car or “goggle box” for the television. Euphemisms and dysphemisms both show that words do not just name something, they also express an attitude.

gewusst: A word that makes something sound nicer can itself start to sound unpleasant over time. Then a new, milder word is often invented.
The word “toilet” was also originally a refined way of putting it; it comes from French.

teile.einleitung: The Benrath line is an important border between German dialects. It separates areas where people say “maken” from areas where people say “machen” (to make). It is named after the place Benrath, today part of the city of Düsseldorf.
wichtigste: The **Benrath line** is a dialect border in Germany.
It is named after the pair of words “maken” and “machen” (to make).
To the north people say “maken”, to the south “machen”.
It separates **Low German** from **High German**.
The reason is the **High German consonant shift** (the second sound shift).

abschnitte.text: The **Benrath line** runs roughly from west to east right across Germany. It is named after **Benrath**, a district of Düsseldorf on the Rhine. North of the line people speak **Low German** dialects, often also called Plattdeutsch. To the south lie the **High German** dialects. There people say “machen” instead of “maken”.

The difference arose through the **second sound shift**. This was a change in pronunciation that began in the south more than a thousand years ago. In it, for example, k became ch, t became s and p became f. This change did not reach the north. That is why people there still say “maken”, “Water” and “Schipp” today, while in the south it is “machen”, “Wasser” and “Schiff” (make, water, ship).

The Swiss dialects belong to **Alemannic** and so to High German in the wider sense. Here the sound shift went especially far. That is why in Swiss German people say “Chind” instead of “Kind” (child) and “Chuchi” instead of “Küche” (kitchen). As well as the Benrath line there are other lines, for example the **Uerdingen line** between “ik” and “ich” (I).

gewusst: English is related to Low German: that is why English also has “make” and “water”.
A line on a language map that separates two forms of a word is called an **isogloss**.

teile.einleitung: An acrostic is a poem with a hidden word. If you read the first letters of the lines from top to bottom, they make a word or a name.
wichtigste: In an acrostic the first letters of the lines make a word.
Often the word is a name or the subject of the poem.
You read the first letters from top to bottom.
The term comes from Greek.
Acrostics are a popular writing exercise at school.

abschnitte.text: In an **acrostic**, each line or verse begins with a particular letter. If you read the **first letters** from top to bottom, they make a **word**. Often it is a **name** or the subject of the poem. An example for the German word SOMMER (summer): the first line begins with S, the second with O, the third with M and so on.

The word comes from **Greek**. “Akron” means tip or beginning, and “stichos” means verse or line. So an acrostic is a poem in which the tips of the verses reveal something. Such poems have existed since **ancient times**. Poets sometimes hid their own name in them or the name of a person to whom they dedicated the poem.

At school people often write an acrostic of their own **first name**. You write the letters one below the other and find a word or sentence for each letter that suits the person. This is a good exercise for finding fitting words and writing creatively. An acrostic does not have to rhyme.

gewusst: In German the plural of Akrostichon is Akrosticha.
Acrostics are sometimes used as secret messages that you only discover if you look closely.

teile.einleitung: The ambulance service helps people who are ill or injured. In Switzerland you call it on 144. It comes with an ambulance and brings help as quickly as possible.
wichtigste: The emergency number for the ambulance service is 144.
The ambulance service comes with an ambulance vehicle.
On the phone you say who is calling, what has happened and where.
You only hang up when the person on the phone tells you to.
Calling 144 is free and works even without credit.
Other emergency numbers: police 117, fire brigade 118, Rega 1414.

abschnitte.titel: What does the ambulance service do?
abschnitte.text: The **ambulance service** is made up of trained **paramedics**. They treat ill and injured people right where they are. Then they take the person to hospital in the **ambulance**. In serious cases an emergency doctor sometimes comes along too.

If you dial **144**, an emergency control centre answers. Stay calm and say **who** you are, **what** has happened and **where** you are. Also say how many people are injured. Only hang up when you are told to. The experts on the phone will explain what you can do until help arrives.

In Switzerland there are several **emergency numbers**. **117** calls the police, **118** the fire brigade and **144** the ambulance service. **1414** alerts Rega, the air rescue service with helicopters. In cases of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** helps on 145. The European emergency number **112** also works in Switzerland.

After the call you stay with the person if it is safe. Talk to them and watch whether they are **breathing**. If they are breathing but unconscious, the **recovery position** may be needed. If possible, someone is sent out to the road to show the ambulance the **way**.

gewusst: You can call emergency numbers even with a locked mobile phone.
Rega is a foundation and is largely funded by its patrons.

teile.einleitung: The Stop sign is one of the most important road signs. It is red, has eight corners and carries the word STOP. Where it stands, every vehicle must come to a complete stop.
wichtigste: The Stop sign is red and has eight corners.
It says STOP in white letters.
Every vehicle must stop completely before the stop line.
After that you give way to the other vehicles.
This also applies to cyclists.
The sign looks the same in almost every country in the world.

abschnitte.text: The **Stop sign** is an **octagon**. No other road sign uses this shape. That is why you can recognise it even from behind or when there is snow on it. The red **colour** stands for danger and stopping. In the middle it says **STOP** in white letters.

At a Stop sign it is not enough just to drive slowly. You must **stop completely**, even if the road looks clear. Usually there is a white **stop line** and the word STOP painted on the ground. You stop there, look carefully and only drive on when the road is clear.

Stop signs are placed where you **cannot see the junction well**. This may be because of houses, hedges or a bend. Only when you have stopped can you see enough of the road. Anyone who drives through a Stop sign puts others in danger and gets a **fine**.

The Stop sign looks **the same** in most countries. The reason is international **agreements** on road signs. Sometimes the word is written in another language, but the shape stays the same. This means travellers also understand the sign immediately.

gewusst: You cannot mistake an octagon for any other road sign.
The “Give way” sign also has a special shape: it is a triangle standing on its point.

teile.einleitung: A home medicine cabinet, also called a first aid kit for the home, is a collection of medicines and dressings kept at home. With it you can quickly treat small injuries and complaints yourself.
wichtigste: A home medicine cabinet contains dressings and important medicines.
It is kept **dry**, **cool** and **out of reach of children**.
A bathroom is not a good place because of the damp.
Out-of-date medicines are taken back to the **pharmacy** or **chemist’s**.
Medicines never belong in the toilet, the drain or the compost.
In cases of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** helps in Switzerland on **145**.

abschnitte.text: A home medicine cabinet should contain **plasters**, **bandages** and compresses, a **disinfectant** for wounds, scissors, tweezers for splinters and a **thermometer**. Often there are also medicines for pain and fever, a cream for insect bites and a cool pack. Anyone who needs medicines regularly also keeps these within reach. A list of important phone numbers is also helpful.

Medicines do not like **heat** or **damp**. That is why the bathroom, with the steam from the shower, is not a good place. A dry, cool cupboard is better. Above all, the medicine cabinet must be placed or locked so that **small children** cannot get at it. For children even a few tablets can be dangerous, because some look like sweets.

Every packet has an **expiry date**. After that a medicine may work less well or change. That is why you check the medicine cabinet about once a year. You check what has expired and what is missing. You always keep the **patient information leaflet** with the medicines, because it says how to take them correctly.

Out-of-date or unused medicines are taken back to the **pharmacy** or **chemist’s**. There they are disposed of safely, usually in a special incineration plant. They never belong in the toilet, the drain or the compost, because their active ingredients can get into the **water** and harm fish and other animals.

If someone has accidentally swallowed medicines or cleaning products, **Tox Info Suisse** can help. The advice centre can be reached day and night on **145**. In a serious emergency you call the ambulance service on **144**. It is important to stay calm and have the packet ready.

gewusst: Every year Tox Info Suisse advises tens of thousands of callers, often about children.
Some medicines need to be kept in the fridge; it then says so on the packet.

teile.einleitung: Night-time quiet is the time in the evening and at night when it should be quiet. This lets everyone sleep and rest.
wichtigste: During night-time quiet you avoid making noise.
It often lasts from about 10 pm until early morning.
The exact times are in the rules of the **municipality** and in the **house rules**.
Many places also have a **lunchtime quiet** period and quiet on Sundays.
Good sleep is important for health and learning.
Consideration for the neighbours makes living together easier.

abschnitte.text: In the evening many people get tired and go to bed. So that they can rest well, it should be quiet at **night**. This time is called **night-time quiet**. Then you play quietly, do not run through the flat, turn music and the television down and do not slam doors. In flats you often hear noises through walls and ceilings.

In Switzerland the exact times are usually set by the **municipality**, for example in its **police regulations**. Night-time quiet often begins at **10 pm** and lasts until 6 or 7 in the morning. The **house rules** of a block of flats also often name quiet times. Many places also have a **lunchtime quiet** period and especially quiet **Sundays** and public holidays.

During **sleep** the body recovers. The brain sorts out what you experienced and learned during the day. Children even do most of their growing at night. Anyone who is often woken by noise is tired the next day, finds it harder to concentrate and gets ill more easily. That is why quiet at night is important for everyone.

Some neighbours work at night and sleep during the day instead. Babies and people who are ill also need quiet at other times. That is why it helps to always show a little **consideration**. For a birthday party you can let the neighbours know beforehand. On special days such as **1 August** or New Year’s Eve, some exceptions are usual.

gewusst: School-age children need much more sleep than adults, often ten hours or more.
According to experts, noise is one of the most common causes of arguments between neighbours.

teile.einleitung: A password is a secret word or a secret string of characters that you use to log in to an account. It works like a key, which is why only a few people may know it.
wichtigste: A password protects your account like a key protects your home.
Only you and your parents know your password.
A good password is **long** and hard to guess.
Every account needs its **own** password.
Real companies never ask for your password by email.
**Two-factor authentication** gives extra protection.

abschnitte.text: Many games, apps and websites have an **account** for each person. So that nobody else can get in, you log in with a **username** and a **password**. The password is like a **key**: anyone who knows it can get into your account, read your messages, write in your name or even buy something.

You tell **nobody** your password, not even your best friend. Friendships can change, and sometimes a password gets passed on. Only your **parents** may know it, so that they can help you. Do not write it on a piece of paper that lies next to the computer.

A good password is **long**, ideally at least twelve characters. It is not a simple word like your name, your birthday or “123456”. A mixture of **capital and small letters**, numbers and special characters is good. One trick is a sentence you can remember, for example using the first letters of a song or a saying.

abschnitte.titel: A separate one for each account
abschnitte.text: Using the same password everywhere is dangerous. If it falls into the wrong hands on one website, all your accounts are open at once. That is why each account has its **own password**. Adults often use a **password manager**, a program that stores all passwords safely. If a password has been given away, you change it immediately.

Many accounts offer **two-factor authentication**. Then as well as the password you need a second proof, for example a code on your mobile phone. It is also important to know that real companies and banks never ask for your password by email or message. Such messages are almost always **fraud**; this is called **phishing**.

gewusst: For years the password “123456” has been one of the most commonly used, and therefore least secure, passwords in the world.
A long password made of several words is often harder to crack than a short one with lots of special characters.

teile.einleitung: A Mofa is a small motorised bicycle that goes no faster than 30 km/h. In Switzerland young people may ride one from the age of 14 if they have the right licence.
wichtigste: By design a Mofa goes no faster than **30 km/h**.
From the age of **14** you can get a **category M** licence.
For this you pass a **theory test**.
Wearing a **helmet is compulsory** on a Mofa.
A Mofa needs a number plate with a valid vignette as proof of insurance.
Where there are cycle paths, Mofas must use them.

abschnitte.text: The word **Mofa** is short for **Motorfahrrad**, motorised bicycle. It looks like a bicycle with an engine or like a small scooter. A Mofa is built so that it reaches no more than **30 km/h**. In the past most had a small petrol engine; today there are also many with an electric motor. Anyone who wants to go faster needs a different vehicle and a different licence category.

For a Mofa you need a **category M driving licence**. You can get it from the age of **14**. For this you pass a **theory test** on traffic rules and signs at the cantonal **road traffic office**. No practical riding test is needed. With the same licence, young people aged 14 and over may also ride slow **e-bikes**.

In Switzerland **wearing a helmet is compulsory** on a Mofa. The helmet must be approved for motorised bicycles. The light must also be switched on during the day. Clothes that are easy to see help drivers to notice you. Because Mofas are slower than cars, they are often overtaken, so you ride attentively and look ahead.

A Mofa needs a small **number plate**. A new **vignette** is stuck on it every year. It shows that there is **third-party liability insurance**. This pays for damage you cause to others. You may not ride without a valid vignette. You are also not allowed to change anything on the Mofa that makes it faster.

Mofas ride on the road and must use **cycle paths** and cycle lanes where there are any. Riding a Mofa on pavements and footpaths is forbidden. Many young people in the countryside use a Mofa to get to school or to their apprenticeship, because the bus does not run often there.

gewusst: In Switzerland the Mofa was especially popular with young people in the 1970s and 1980s.
Anyone who tunes the engine of their Mofa to make it faster is riding without a valid licence and without insurance cover.

teile.einleitung: **Exile literature** mainly means the works of German-speaking writers who had to flee from the Nazis from 1933 onwards. Many carried on writing abroad, including in Switzerland.
wichtigste: On **10 May 1933**, students in many German cities burned books by unwanted authors.
Many writers went into **exile**.
The **Schauspielhaus Zürich** was the most important free German-language theatre.
Brecht’s “Mother Courage and Her Children” had its first performance in Zurich in 1941.
**Thomas Mann** lived in **Küsnacht** on Lake Zurich from 1933 to 1938.
In exile, Anna Seghers wrote the novel “The Seventh Cross”.

abschnitte.text: After the Nazis seized power in 1933, many authors were persecuted because they were Jewish or had different political views. On **10 May 1933**, students in many university towns burned their books. Many fled abroad, into **exile**. They went to neighbouring countries such as Switzerland, France or Denmark, and later often to the USA or South America.

abschnitte.titel: Zurich as a stage of freedom
abschnitte.text: During this time the **Schauspielhaus Zürich** became the most important free German-language theatre. Many actors who had fled performed there, and plays by persecuted authors were staged. In 1941 Brecht’s **“Mother Courage and Her Children”** had its first performance there. The play shows a trader who wants to profit from the war and loses her children in the process.

**Thomas Mann** lived in **Küsnacht** on Lake Zurich from 1933 to 1938, then moved to the USA. In 1952 he returned to Switzerland. **Erich Maria Remarque** had already bought a villa in **Porto Ronco** on Lake Maggiore in 1931 and lived there at times. In these years Switzerland took in some refugees, but it also turned many away at the border.

**Bertolt Brecht** lived in Svendborg in **Denmark** from 1933 to 1939, where he wrote the “Svendborg Poems”. **Anna Seghers** wrote the novel **“The Seventh Cross”** about seven prisoners escaping from a camp. It came out in 1942 and was a worldwide success. Shortly before his death in Brazil, **Stefan Zweig** wrote **“The Royal Game”** (Chess Story), in which a prisoner plays chess in his head.

gewusst: Remarque was buried in Ronco sopra Ascona in Ticino.
Many exiled authors lived in great poverty because abroad they found hardly any readers in their own language.

teile.einleitung: An emergency call is a phone call to get help in a dangerous situation. In Switzerland there are several short numbers for this, which you can dial free of charge from any phone.
wichtigste: **117** is the number for the police.
**118** is the number for the fire brigade.
**144** is the number for the ambulance service.
**112** is the European emergency number and also works in Switzerland.
On the phone you say who you are, where you are and what has happened.
You only dial emergency numbers in a real emergency.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland you reach the **police** on **117**, the **fire brigade** on **118** and the **ambulance service** on **144**. The European emergency number **112** also works. For rescues by helicopter, for example in the mountains, there is **Rega** on **1414**. In cases of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** helps on **145**. All these numbers are free.

abschnitte.titel: What you say on the phone
abschnitte.text: Stay as **calm** as possible and speak clearly. First say **who** you are. Then say **where** you are: the address, the place or what you can see nearby. After that explain **what has happened** and whether anyone is injured. The person on the phone will ask you questions and tell you what you can do.

abschnitte.titel: Do not hang up too soon
abschnitte.text: Only hang up when the person in the **emergency control centre** tells you to. Sometimes they still need important information or explain how you can help until the rescuers arrive. If possible, you then wait in a place where the rescuers can easily find you, or send someone to the front door to bring them in.

Emergency numbers are only for **real emergencies**. Anyone who calls for fun blocks the line. Then perhaps someone in real trouble cannot get through. Rescuers may also set off for nothing. Anyone who deliberately raises a false alarm can be **punished**. If you dialled by mistake, do not simply hang up; say briefly that it was a mistake.

It is good to know the numbers **by heart**. You can practise saying your own address with your parents. Many mobile phones can also make an emergency call when they are locked. In a real emergency the rule is: better to call for help once too often than to wait too long.

gewusst: Rega rescues thousands of people every year, often from the mountains, and is funded by its patrons.
The number 112 works in all countries of the European Union and in many other countries.

teile.einleitung: Cars parked at the side of the road block the view. Anyone who steps out onto the road between them is often seen too late by drivers, especially if they are a child.
wichtigste: Between parked cars you are **hard for drivers to see**.
Children are smaller than most cars.
It is better to cross the road at a place where you can see clearly.
A **zebra crossing** is the safest place.
The rule is: **wait, look, listen, walk**.
Light-coloured clothes and reflective strips make you easier to see.

abschnitte.text: Parked cars stand like a wall at the side of the road. Anyone standing behind them is **invisible** to drivers. If you suddenly step out, the driver has hardly any time to brake. Depending on its speed, a car needs many metres to stop. Children are also **smaller** than the bonnet of many cars and are even harder to see.

Between parked cars you yourself also **cannot see the traffic well**. You do not know whether a car, a bike or a motorbike is coming. Children are also not yet as good as adults at judging speeds and distances. That is why you need a place where you can see well and be seen well.

abschnitte.titel: Where to cross the road instead
abschnitte.text: The safest place to cross the road is at a **zebra crossing** or at traffic lights. At a zebra crossing vehicles must give you **right of way**, but only if they can stop in time. If there is no crossing, you look for a place where no cars are parked and you can see far in both directions.

In Switzerland children learn the rule **“Warte, luege, lose, laufe”**: wait, look, listen, walk. First you stop at the edge. Then you look left, right and left again. You listen to hear whether a vehicle is coming. Only when everything is clear or the vehicles have stopped do you cross the road briskly, without running.

Pedestrians are especially hard to see at **dusk** and in the rain. **Light-coloured clothes**, reflective strips on your jacket and school bag and a reflective band help a lot. Many nursery school children in Switzerland wear a glowing triangle or a high-visibility vest for this. When a car comes, it is best to make **eye contact** with the driver.

gewusst: Drivers can see clothing with reflectors in their headlights from much further away than dark clothing.
You also do not step onto the road from behind a stopped bus or tram, for the same reason as with parked cars.

teile.einleitung: Everyone may decide for themselves whether photos or videos of them are published. This is called the right to your own image. That is why you always ask first before putting a picture of someone on the internet.
wichtigste: The right to your own image is one of the rights of personality.
Anyone who wants to publish a photo of a person needs their permission.
This also applies to friends and your own family.
You may ask at any time for a picture to be deleted again.
For children, the parents have a say.
Once something is on the internet, it often cannot be completely deleted.

abschnitte.text: A picture shows what someone looks like and what they are doing at that moment. That is why your own image is part of your **personality**. In Switzerland the **Civil Code** protects every person’s personality. Anyone who publishes a picture without **permission** can be breaking these rights.

If you want to share a photo, you ask the person **beforehand**. Also tell them where the picture will appear, for example in a group chat or in public. If they say **no**, the picture stays private. You must not simply forward embarrassing or funny pictures either, because they can **hurt** someone.

There are exceptions. At large **events** such as a concert, you are often only a small part of a crowd. Well-known people such as **politicians** also have to expect to be photographed when they appear in public. But their private lives are still protected.

If you find a picture of yourself that you do not want, you may ask for it to be **deleted**. Many platforms have a **report button** for this. If that does not help, you get help from your parents or a teacher. Anyone who uses pictures to humiliate others can even be committing a **criminal offence**.

gewusst: A picture on the internet can be copied and sent on in seconds.
You may not publish videos or voice recordings of a person without permission either.

teile.einleitung: Argumentation means supporting an opinion with good reasons so that others understand it and perhaps adopt it. A good argument consists of a claim, a reason and an example. Anyone who can argue well is more convincing in discussions, essays and everyday life.
wichtigste: According to the school model, an argument consists of a thesis, a reason and an example.
A dialectical essay weighs arguments for and against against each other.
Arguments are often arranged from the weakest to the strongest.
An argument from authority relies on the statement of an expert or an institution.
Fallacies look convincing but are unfair or wrong.
In an argumentum ad hominem you attack the person instead of what they say.
In circular reasoning a claim is justified by itself.

abschnitte.text: **Arguing** means not just stating an opinion but backing it up with reasons. At school you learn a simple model with three parts for this. First comes the **thesis**, that is the claim, for example: school uniforms make sense. Then comes the reason why this is so. Finally, an example makes the argument clear.

There are different ways of supporting an argument. A **factual argument** uses figures or facts that can be checked. An **argument from authority** relies on the statement of an expert or an institution, for example a doctor. An argument from experience tells of your own experiences. A value-based argument relies on generally accepted values such as justice or health.

In a **discursive essay** you examine a question in writing. In a linear essay you argue for one side only. In a **dialectical essay** you weigh arguments for and against and draw a conclusion at the end. The arguments are often arranged from the weakest to the strongest, so that the best argument at the end is especially convincing.

Some arguments sound good but are unfair or illogical. In an **argumentum ad hominem** you attack the person instead of what they say. In a straw man argument you twist the other person’s opinion and then disprove this false version. In an argumentum ad populum you claim something is right just because the majority believes it. **Circular reasoning** justifies a claim with itself, for example: that is correct because it is true.

abschnitte.titel: Arguing in everyday life and in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: You need to argue when discussing in class, when writing letters to the editor or in job applications. In Switzerland arguing plays a special role, because voters often vote on proposals. Before every **popular vote**, arguments for and against are presented in newspapers, on television and in the voting booklet. Even the ancient Greeks taught the art of good speaking, **rhetoric**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A claim that you want to justify.
A text in which you weigh up a question with arguments.
An argument that only seems convincing but is illogical or unfair.
The art of speaking well and convincingly.
What you decide at the end of a line of thought.

gewusst: The names of many fallacies come from Latin; “ad hominem”, for example, literally means “to the person”.
As long as 2300 years ago, the Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote a textbook on rhetoric.
In Switzerland, before every federal vote, there is a booklet setting out the arguments of both sides.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland you can send letters by A Post or by B Post. The difference lies in the speed and the price.
wichtigste: A Post letters usually arrive on the next working day.
B Post is cheaper but takes a few working days longer.
A Post needs a more expensive stamp than B Post.
Swiss Post delivers the letters.
The envelope needs the address, postcode and town.
For important documents there is also registered post.

abschnitte.text: Anyone sending a letter has to decide: should it arrive quickly or should it cost little? With **A Post** a letter is normally with the recipient on the next working day. **B Post** is cheaper, but delivery takes a few days longer. For a birthday card that has to arrive on time, people therefore often choose A Post.

So that the post office knows how fast the letter should travel, it needs the right **stamp**. The stamp for A Post costs more than the one for B Post. Often you also stick a small label with a large “A” on the envelope. You buy stamps at the post office, in some shops or online. The prices also depend on the size and weight of the letter.

A letter only arrives if the **address** is right. This includes the name, the street with the house number, the four-digit **postcode** and the town. The sender’s address is usually at the top left or on the back. If a letter cannot be delivered, the post office sends it back to the sender.

For especially important letters, such as a notice of termination, A Post is often not enough. Then you choose **registered post**. The recipient has to confirm with their signature that they have received the letter. This gives the sender proof. Parcels are also divided into faster and cheaper options.

gewusst: Letters are sorted in large mail centres by machines that can read the addresses.
Postcodes were introduced in Switzerland in 1964.

teile.einleitung: A **narrative** is a story that tells of an experience or an invented plot. At school you learn how to write a narrative that is exciting and lively.
wichtigste: Written narratives are usually in the **simple past**: “She ran off.”
A narrative has an **introduction**, a **main part** with a climax and an **ending**.
The storytelling voice is called the **narrator** and is not the author.
**Direct speech** and well-chosen verbs make a narrative lively.
The surprising twist at the end is called the **punchline**.

abschnitte.text: The **introduction** presents the characters, the place and the time. In the **main part** the most important things happen: the tension rises to the **climax**. In the **ending** the tension is released and the story comes to a close. Some narratives have a **punchline** at the end, a surprising twist that makes you laugh or gasp.

Written narratives are usually in the **simple past**, for example “She opened the door”. For events that happened even earlier you need the **past perfect**: “She had forgotten the key.” If a character tells the story about themselves with “I”, it is a **first-person narrative**. If the story is told with “he” or “she”, it is a **third-person narrative**.

With **direct speech** you write down exactly what a character says and put it in quotation marks: “Where are you?” shouted Lea. Instead of always using “say”, well-chosen verbs such as **whisper**, shout, mumble or ask fit better. Feelings, sounds and smells also make the story come alive. That way the reader can picture everything better.

Many fairy tales begin with the phrase **“Once upon a time ...”**, for example those of the Brothers Grimm. In a **prompt-word story** you are given a few words, for example “thunderstorm, key, dog”. They all have to appear sensibly in the story you invent. In a **picture story** you tell a story to go with a series of pictures.

gewusst: The phrase “Once upon a time” shows that a fairy tale takes place at some unknown time in the past.
A grown-up author can also let a child speak as the narrator.

teile.einleitung: Most people are friendly and helpful. Even so, there is an important rule: you do not go with strangers and you never get into a stranger’s car. Knowing the rules helps you feel safer.
wichtigste: You never go with strangers, even if they are nice.
You never get into a stranger’s car.
You may say no loudly and walk away.
If you need help, you go into a shop or to a woman with children.
Afterwards you tell your parents or your teacher.
You can agree a secret code word with your parents.

abschnitte.text: If a **stranger** wants to give you a lift in their car, you say **“No!”** loudly and clearly and walk away. This also applies if the person is friendly, wants to give you something or says your parents sent them. You do not have to be polite or give a reason. Keep your distance from the car so that nobody can grab you.

Sometimes someone else really does pick up a child, for example a neighbour. So that you can be sure, you agree a **secret code word** with your parents. Only someone who knows the word has been sent by your parents. You do not tell anyone the code word. Without the code word you do not go with them.

If you feel followed or uncomfortable, go where there are lots of people. You can go into a **shop**, a bakery or a restaurant and ask for help. A mother or father with children will also be glad to help. If necessary, you may **shout loudly** or scream. In an emergency you call the police on **117**.

After something like this, you **tell** your **parents**, your teacher or another trusted adult. That is important even if nothing happened. This way the adults can warn other children and, if necessary, inform the police. You have not done anything wrong by telling. You can also get advice by calling **147**.

gewusst: It is best to walk the way to school together with your parents first. That way you know safe places along the way.
The same rule applies on the internet: you do not tell strangers anything and you do not meet them.

teile.einleitung: Alliteration is a figure of speech in which several words that follow each other begin with the same sound. It makes sentences sound good and easy to remember. In old Germanic poetry it was called Stabreim.
wichtigste: In alliteration several words begin with the same initial sound.
A well-known German example is “Milch macht müde Männer munter” (Milk makes tired men lively).
In old Germanic poetry alliteration is called Stabreim.
The Hildebrandslied (Lay of Hildebrand) is an example of alliterative poetry.
Many fixed German phrases, such as “Haus und Hof” (house and home), contain alliteration.
Alliteration makes expressions memorable.

abschnitte.text: In **alliteration**, neighbouring stressed words begin with the same **initial sound**, that is the same sound at the start of the word. A well-known German example is **“Milch macht müde Männer munter”** (Milk makes tired men lively). Here the M is repeated. What matters is the sound, not just the letter. The repetition makes the sentence rhythmic, and it stays in the memory.

German has many fixed phrases with alliteration. They are often called **twin formulas**, because two words are joined with “und” (and). Examples are **“Haus und Hof”** (house and home), **“mit Kind und Kegel”** (with the whole family), “Stock und Stein” (over hill and dale) or “Wind und Wetter” (wind and weather). Many of these phrases are very old and are still used today.

In **old Germanic poetry**, alliteration was the most important verse technique. There it is called **Stabreim**. The stressed syllables with the same initial sound are called **staves**. A well-known example is the Old High German **Hildebrandslied**. Later, **end rhyme**, in which the words at the end of the lines sound the same, took over in German poetry.

Today people still like to use alliteration, especially in **advertising**, in headlines and in names. It sounds witty and sticks in the mind quickly. Tongue twisters are also often based on the same initial sounds, for example the German “Fischers Fritz fischt frische Fische” (Fisherman’s Fritz fishes fresh fish). Anyone who writes can use alliteration to give a text more swing.

gewusst: The word alliteration comes from Latin and means roughly “adding letters”.
Many comic characters have alliterative names so that they are easier to remember.

teile.einleitung: Aluminium is a light metal from which drinks cans, for example, are made. It is worth collecting aluminium, because recycling saves a great deal of energy.
wichtigste: Making new aluminium takes a great deal of electricity.
Melting down used aluminium saves most of this energy, about 95 per cent.
Aluminium can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
Aluminium cans, foil, tubes and pet food trays belong in the aluminium collection.
You can use a magnet to tell aluminium from tinplate.
In Switzerland the cooperative IGORA organises the collection of aluminium packaging.

abschnitte.titel: Lots of energy for new aluminium
abschnitte.text: In nature aluminium does not occur as a pure metal. It is obtained from the rock **bauxite**. First alumina is made from it, then the metal is separated out using electric current. This process is called **electrolysis** and uses huge amounts of electricity. In **recycling**, used aluminium is simply melted down. This saves around 95 per cent of the energy.

Empty **drinks cans**, aluminium foil, tubes, yoghurt pot lids and pet food trays belong in the **aluminium collection**. You remove any large leftovers first. It is handy to squash cans flat so that they take up less room. There are collection points at many municipalities, stations, schools and shops. Aluminium is often put in the same container as tinplate.

Not every can is made of aluminium. Many **tin cans** for food are made of tinplate, which is steel. You can find out with a **magnet**: tinplate sticks to the magnet, aluminium does not. At some collection points both metals are collected together and separated later by machine. Magnetism helps with that too.

Aluminium does **not lose quality** when it is melted down. An old can can become a new can again, over and over. That is why a large part of all the aluminium ever produced is still in use today. In Switzerland the cooperative **IGORA** makes sure that aluminium packaging is collected and recycled.

gewusst: Aluminium is about three times lighter than steel.
In Switzerland the vast majority of aluminium cans are collected and recycled.

teile.einleitung: Road signs tell everyone on the road what they need to watch out for. Warning signs are triangular with a red border and warn of a danger that is coming up soon.
wichtigste: Warning signs are triangles with a red border and a white background.
The point of the triangle points upwards.
They warn of a danger, for example a bend, children or wild animals.
The picture in the middle shows what the danger is.
Warning signs stand before the danger point, so that you have time to prepare.
Round signs are rules, and blue rectangular ones give information.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are different kinds of **road signs**. You can recognise **warning signs** by their shape: they are **triangular**, the point faces upwards, and they have a **red border** and a white background. They mean: **Watch out, danger!** Anyone who sees such a sign drives more carefully and is ready to brake.

In the middle of the triangle, a **picture** shows what the danger is. Two running children warn of **children** near a school. A leaping deer means **wild animals crossing**. A car with wavy lines warns of a **risk of skidding**, and a worker with a shovel of **roadworks**. Other signs show bends, a steep downhill slope or a zebra crossing.

Warning signs do not stand right at the danger but some distance **before** it. This gives drivers and cyclists time to slow down. Sometimes there is an extra plate under the sign that gives the distance or the length of the dangerous stretch. The signs are regulated in the federal **Road Signs Ordinance**.

Not all signs give warnings. **Round** signs with a red border are **rules** or bans, for example a speed limit. Round blue signs tell you what you must do, for example use a cycle path. **Blue rectangular** signs give **information**, for example about a car park. An exception among the triangles is the “Give way” sign: it stands on its point.

gewusst: Many countries in Europe use almost the same warning signs, so you can understand them on holiday too.
The signs are also useful for pedestrians and children: they show where drivers have to be especially careful.

teile.einleitung: At junctions it must be clear who may go first. If no sign and no traffic light says otherwise, in Switzerland priority from the right applies. Whoever comes from the right may go first.
wichtigste: Priority from the right means: whoever comes from the right has right of way.
It applies at junctions without signs and without traffic lights.
The rule applies to cars, bikes and other vehicles.
Signs such as Stop or “Give way” cancel priority from the right.
Anyone coming out of a garage, a farm track or a car park does not have right of way.
Signals from the police take precedence over all rules.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **Road Traffic Act** says: at junctions the vehicle coming from the **right** has right of way. So you always look to the right before driving into a junction. If someone is coming from there, you wait. The rule also applies to **cyclists** coming from the right.

Priority from the right only applies if nothing else has been set. A **Stop sign** or an upside-down triangle meaning “Give way” shows that you must wait. A **yellow diamond** means a main road: whoever drives on it has right of way. **Traffic lights** and hand signals from the **police** take precedence over all signs.

In a **roundabout** there is a special rule: whoever is already in the roundabout has right of way. Anyone who wants to enter must wait. **Trams** and other rail vehicles generally have right of way, because they cannot swerve and can only brake slowly.

Even if you have right of way, you ride **carefully**. Not every driver sees a bike in time. Look the drivers in the eye and only go when you are sure they have seen you. Anyone coming from a **farm track**, a driveway or the pavement must always wait.

gewusst: Priority from the right also applies in car parks and in 30 km/h neighbourhoods, as long as no sign says otherwise.
If vehicles arrive at a junction from all four sides, the drivers have to communicate with signals.

teile.einleitung: The bus takes many people to school, to work or home. To make it work well, there are a few simple rules for getting on and off and during the journey.
wichtigste: First people get off, then the others get on.
At the bus stop you wait at a distance from the road.
Anyone who wants to get off presses the stop button in good time.
During the journey you hold on.
You offer your seat to older people and people with pushchairs.
After getting off, you wait until the bus has driven away before crossing the road.

abschnitte.text: At the **bus stop** you wait calmly and a little way back from the kerb. When the bus pulls in, you do not push to the front. The timetable often shows when the next bus is coming. You have bought your ticket before getting on. This makes getting on quicker.

When the bus stops, people get **off first**. Only then do the others get on. Anyone standing by the door makes room and steps aside. This means there is **no crush**, and everyone gets where they are going more quickly. This rule also applies on the tram and the train.

On the bus you **hold on** to a pole or a handle, because the bus can brake suddenly. You take off your school bag so that it does not hit anyone. You offer your **seat** to older people and people with walking aids or pushchairs. Anyone who wants to get off presses the **stop button** in good time so that the driver knows.

After getting off, you do not run across the road in front of or behind the bus. The bus hides you from the cars, and the cars from you. You **wait** until the bus has **driven away** and then cross the road at the zebra crossing. The rule is: wait, look, listen, walk.

gewusst: The yellow PostBuses have been running in Switzerland for more than a hundred years, even to remote mountain villages.
The famous three-note horn of the PostBus is taken from the overture to Gioachino Rossini’s opera “William Tell”.

teile.einleitung: A **fable** is a short story in which animals usually talk and act like people. At the end there is often a lesson, the **moral**.
wichtigste: Fables are short stories that **teach a lesson**.
The animals have fixed qualities: the **fox** is clever, the ant hard-working.
At the end there is often a **moral**.
The most famous writer of fables in ancient times is **Aesop** from Greece.
In France, **Jean de La Fontaine** wrote many fables in verse.
Well-known ones are “The Fox and the Grapes” and “The Tortoise and the Hare”.

abschnitte.text: In fables, animals talk and think like people. Each animal stands for a particular quality: the **fox** is cunning, the **lion** strong and powerful, the **ant** hard-working. This way human weaknesses and strengths can be shown without pointing a finger at anyone. The stories are short and usually have only two or three characters.

**Aesop** lived in Greece more than 2500 years ago, and many well-known fables go back to him. More than 300 years ago in France, **Jean de La Fontaine** retold many old fables in rhyme. In the German-speaking world, **Gotthold Ephraim Lessing** wrote fables in short prose in the 18th century. But there are fables all over the world.

In “The Crow and the Fox”, the fox flatters the crow until it opens its beak and drops its **piece of cheese**. In “The Fox and the Grapes”, the grapes hang too high, and the fox claims they are too sour for him anyway. In “The Lion and the Mouse”, the little mouse saves the lion by **gnawing through the net**. And in the race, the slow but steady **tortoise** beats the overconfident hare.

A fable wants to teach something. Often there is a sentence at the end that sums up the lesson, the **moral**. In “The Grasshopper and the Ant”, the grasshopper sings all summer long while the ant gathers food. In winter the grasshopper has nothing to eat. The moral: if you plan ahead, you are well prepared. Sometimes, though, you have to work out the lesson for yourself.

gewusst: The saying “sour grapes” comes from the fable of the fox: you run down something you cannot have.
The fable of the lion and the mouse shows that even small creatures can help big ones.

teile.einleitung: Littering means that people simply leave rubbish lying around or throw it away instead of disposing of it properly. The word comes from English and is often used in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Littering means carelessly leaving rubbish lying around or throwing it away.
Rubbish belongs in the bin or is taken home.
Rubbish lying around harms animals and nature.
Cigarette ends contain poisons that get into the soil and water.
In many cantons and municipalities there is a fine for littering.
Clearing up costs the municipalities a lot of money.

abschnitte.text: The English word **litter** means rubbish. **Littering** means that someone simply throws wrappers, cans, bottles or cigarette ends on the ground or leaves them lying around. It happens on streets, in parks, by lakes and in the mountains. Even a small sweet wrapper counts.

Animals sometimes mistake rubbish for food. Birds, fish or cows can swallow pieces of plastic and become ill. Animals can get caught in cans and nets. Over time **plastic** breaks down into tiny pieces, **microplastics**, which stay in the soil and water for a long time. A single **cigarette end** releases poisons into the water.

Municipalities, towns and the railways have to collect the rubbish again. This takes staff, vehicles and a lot of time. In the end everyone pays for it through their **taxes** and fees. People also feel less comfortable in dirty places. Where rubbish is already lying around, others often throw away even more.

In many cantons and municipalities littering is forbidden and punished with a **fine**. The police or other officials can then demand an on-the-spot fine. How much it is varies from place to place. But the aim is not to punish, it is for everyone to dispose of their rubbish properly.

Always throw rubbish into a **bin**. If you cannot find one, put it in your pocket and take it home. You can often collect bottles, cans and paper separately so that they are **recycled**. Many municipalities have clean-up days when school classes and clubs collect rubbish together.

gewusst: Every year Switzerland holds a national Clean-Up Day, when many volunteers collect rubbish.
A glass bottle in nature practically does not break down at all within human timescales.

teile.einleitung: Underinsurance happens when the sum insured is lower than the real value of the insured things. With household contents insurance this means that the insurer pays less if there is a claim.
wichtigste: Household contents insurance covers the things in your home.
You set a sum insured for it.
If your contents are worth more than this sum, you are underinsured.
Then the insurer reduces its payment in the same proportion.
You should check the sum after big purchases or a move.
Insuring for too much does not help: you never get more than the damage.

abschnitte.text: **Household contents** include all the movable things in a home: furniture, clothes, books, appliances, bikes and much more. **Household contents insurance** pays if these things are damaged or lost, for example through fire, water or a **burglary**. Added up, household contents are often worth much more than you think.

An example: the household contents are worth **100,000 francs**, but only **50,000 francs** are insured. That is half. If there is damage of 10,000 francs, the insurer also only pays **half**, that is 5,000 francs. This reduction is called **underinsurance**. It also applies to small claims.

It is best to make a **list** of everything in your home and estimate what it would cost to **buy it all new**. Many insurers offer calculators for this. After a **move**, a marriage or big purchases, you should adjust the sum. Receipts and photos help later to prove damage.

abschnitte.titel: Too much is not good either
abschnitte.text: Anyone who insures their household contents for **too much** pays a higher **premium**. But if there is a claim, they still only get the real damage replaced. This is called **overinsurance**. Some insurers waive the reduction for underinsurance under certain conditions. This is stated in the policy terms.

gewusst: Many people underestimate the value of their clothes, because they have bought them bit by bit over many years.
Insurers usually work with the replacement value, that is the price you would have to pay for an equivalent replacement.

teile.einleitung: Some German words have an h that you cannot hear at all, as in “Bahn” (railway) or “Ohr” (ear). This h shows that the vowel before it is pronounced long. It is called the lengthening h (Dehnungs-h).
wichtigste: The **lengthening h** shows that the vowel before it is **long**.
You cannot hear the lengthening h.
It often comes before **l, m, n or r**, as in “Mehl” (flour), “nehmen” (to take), “Lohn” (wage) and “Jahr” (year).
Examples are Bahn, Hahn, Zahn, Ohr, Uhr, Stuhl and zehn.
Not every long vowel has a lengthening h: “Tal” (valley) or “Schal” (scarf) do not have one.
That is why you have to learn these words carefully.

abschnitte.text: Say the German word “fahren” (to drive) slowly. You do not hear the h. It only shows that the a before it is pronounced **long**. That is why it is called the **lengthening h**: it “stretches” the vowel. Vowels are the letters a, e, i, o and u.

The lengthening h is found in many everyday German words. The train on rails is the **Bahn**, and the bird that crows in the morning is the **Hahn** (cockerel). You bite with your **Zahn** (tooth) and hear with your **Ohr** (ear). You sit on a **Stuhl** (chair), and after nine comes **zehn** (ten). The **Uhr** (clock) also has a lengthening h after the long u.

abschnitte.titel: Before l, m, n and r
abschnitte.text: The lengthening h often comes before the letters **l, m, n or r**. Examples are “Mehl” (flour), “nehmen” (to take), “Lohn” (wage) and “Jahr” (year). This is a good way to remember it, but it is not a fixed rule. Many words with l, m, n or r have no h, for example “Tal” (valley), “Name” (name) or “Ton” (sound). That is why you have to practise words with a lengthening h and remember them well.

Not every long vowel is written with an h. Often it has no sign at all, as in “Tal” (valley) or “Hose” (trousers). Sometimes the vowel is doubled, as in “Meer” (sea), “Boot” (boat) or “Haar” (hair). A long i is usually written as **ie**, as in “Biene” (bee) or “spielen” (to play). A dictionary helps if you are unsure.

There is also a second silent h: the **syllable-separating h**. It comes between two vowels, as in “gehen” (to go), “sehen” (to see) or “drehen” (to turn). There it separates two syllables from each other. This h stays in other forms of the word too: “er geht” (he goes), “sie sieht” (she sees). It is easy to confuse it with the lengthening h.

gewusst: A lengthening h never comes after a short vowel.
Words with a lengthening h are only a small part of all words with a long vowel.

teile.einleitung: “The Rainbow Fish” (in German “Der Regenbogenfisch”) is a picture book by the Bern author and illustrator Marcus Pfister. It was published in 1992 and tells the story of a beautiful fish with glittering scales. The book shows that sharing makes you happier than owning.
wichtigste: **Marcus Pfister** from Bern wrote and illustrated “The Rainbow Fish”.
The picture book was published in **1992**.
The fish has particularly beautiful, **glittering scales**.
In the end he gives his glittering scales away to the other fish.
The message is: **sharing brings friends**.

abschnitte.text: Far out in the ocean lives a fish with scales in all the colours of the rainbow. Some of them glitter like silver. The other fish admire him, but he is proud and will not give away a single scale. So soon nobody wants to play with him any more. He is the most beautiful fish in the ocean, but also the loneliest.

In the end the Rainbow Fish asks for advice. He learns that he should give away his glittering scales. At first it is hard for him, but then he gives away one scale after another. With every scale he becomes happier. In the end he has only one glittering scale left, but lots of friends. The message: **sharing brings friends**.

**Marcus Pfister** from Bern is both author and illustrator. What is special about his book is the real glittering scales in the pictures, which shimmer in the light. “The Rainbow Fish” has been translated into many languages and is one of the best-known Swiss children's books. Later more books about the Rainbow Fish were published, and there is also a cartoon series.

gewusst: The glittering scales in the book are printed with a special shimmering foil.
The Rainbow Fish is one of the best-known picture book characters from Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: An abbreviation is a short form of a word or a group of words. It saves space and time when writing. Depending on the kind, abbreviations in German are written with or without a full stop.
wichtigste: The German “z. B.” means “zum Beispiel” (for example), “usw.” means “und so weiter” (and so on).
“d. h.” means “das heisst” (that is), “bzw.” means “beziehungsweise” (or rather, respectively).
In “z. B.” each part gets a full stop and there is a small space in between.
Abbreviations made of capital letters, such as SBB, are written without full stops.
Units of measurement such as km, kg or cm are abbreviated without a full stop.
If a sentence ends with “usw.”, you only put one full stop.
CH stands for “Confoederatio Helvetica”.

abschnitte.text: Many abbreviations are only written; when reading aloud you say the whole word. They get a **full stop**. Examples in German are **“z. B.”** for “zum Beispiel” (for example), **“usw.”** for “und so weiter” (and so on), **“d. h.”** for “das heisst” (that is) and **“bzw.”** for “beziehungsweise” (or rather). If an abbreviation stands for several words, each part gets a full stop, and there is a small space in between.

Some abbreviations are made of the **first letters** of several words and are also spoken that way. They are usually written in capital letters and **without full stops**, for example **SBB** for Schweizerische Bundesbahnen (Swiss Federal Railways) or AHV for Alters- und Hinterlassenenversicherung (old-age and survivors’ insurance). **Units of measurement** such as km, kg or cm have no full stop either.

abschnitte.titel: At the end of a sentence
abschnitte.text: If a sentence ends with an abbreviation that has a full stop, for example **“usw.”**, you put **only one full stop**. The abbreviation’s full stop is then also the **final full stop**. So you write: “Wir kaufen Äpfel, Birnen usw.” (We are buying apples, pears and so on) and not two full stops one after the other.

You see the country code **CH** on cars and in internet addresses. It stands for the Latin name of Switzerland: **Confoederatio Helvetica**, that is the Swiss Confederation. Because Switzerland has four national languages, the Latin name is neutral and the same for everyone.

gewusst: A word made of first letters that is pronounced like an ordinary word is called an acronym, for example UNO (the German abbreviation for the UN).
Swiss coins say “Helvetia”, the Latin name for Switzerland.
