teile.einleitung: The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, FDPIC for short (EDÖB in German), is the federal supervisory authority for data protection. It makes sure that personal data is handled correctly in Switzerland.
wichtigste: FDPIC is the abbreviation for the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner.
The FDPIC supervises data protection at federal offices and private companies.
It can open investigations and advises the public.
It is also responsible for the principle of transparency in the federal administration.
It works independently and is based in Bern.
For cantonal and municipal authorities, cantonal data protection offices are responsible.

abschnitte.text: The **FDPIC** is an independent federal authority. Its long name shows its two tasks: **data protection** and **transparency** (public access to information). It is based in **Bern** and is supported by a team of experts. The head is elected by the Federal Assembly. The FDPIC reports regularly on its work.

The FDPIC supervises whether **federal offices** and **private companies** keep to the Data Protection Act. If it suspects that a company is processing data wrongly, it can open an **investigation**. Under the revised Data Protection Act, which has applied since 1 September 2023, it can issue binding orders. For example, it can demand that a way of processing data is changed or stopped.

The FDPIC **advises the public**, companies and authorities. On its website you can find explanations on topics such as video surveillance, apps or the **right of access**. It takes reports from people who feel that something is going wrong with data. In certain cases companies must also report data breaches to it.

The second task concerns the federal **Freedom of Information Act**. In principle it allows everyone to see official documents of the federal administration. If an authority refuses access, you can ask the FDPIC for **mediation**. It then mediates between the person and the authority. For cantonal authorities there are separate **cantonal data protection commissioners**.

gewusst: The first federal Data Protection Act came into force in 1993.
Every year the FDPIC publishes an activity report that anyone can read.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland many bikes are stolen every year, often at stations. If you are lucky, you are insured. Usually household contents insurance helps if it has extra cover for theft away from home.
wichtigste: Household contents insurance covers theft from your home or cellar.
For theft outside, for example at the station, you often need extra cover.
This extra cover is called simple theft away from home.
After a theft you first report it to the police.
With the frame number, a bike that is found can be matched to its owner.
A good lock and a fixed object to lock it to give the best protection.

abschnitte.text: A **strong lock** is the best protection. It is best to lock the bike by its frame to a **fixed object**, for example a bike stand. A bike that is only locked by its wheel can easily be carried away. Your bike is also safer in a **bike station** at the railway station.

Every bike has a **frame number**, which is usually stamped underneath the frame. You should write it down and take a **photo** of the bike. The receipt is also important. If the police find a bike, they can use the number to return it to its **owner**.

If your bike has been stolen, you first report the theft to the **police**. You get a confirmation, which the insurer asks for. Then you report the loss to the **insurance company**. Sometimes a bike turns up again after a while, so reporting it is worth it anyway.

**Household contents insurance** pays for a break-in at your home or cellar. But if the bike is stolen outside, for example in front of the station, this is **simple theft away from home**. With many insurers you have to take this out as **extra cover**. For expensive bikes there is also separate bike insurance.

gewusst: Bikes that are not collected for a long time often end up at a lost property office and are later auctioned.
Many stolen bikes are only used for a short time and then left standing somewhere.

teile.einleitung: A **drama** is a text written for the stage. The plot comes from what the characters say and do, and there is no narrator.
wichtigste: The word drama comes from Greek and means “action”.
In 1863 **Gustav Freytag** described the structure in five acts as a pyramid.
At the beginning comes the **exposition**, and at the climax there is often the **peripeteia**.
The **retarding moment** delays the catastrophe.
With epic theatre, **Bertolt Brecht** wanted to make people think critically.
A play text consists of **main text** and **secondary text**.

abschnitte.text: Drama arose in ancient **Greece** at festivals in honour of the god Dionysus. The philosopher **Aristotle** wrote an important study of it, the “Poetics”. The two classic forms are **tragedy**, which ends sadly, and **comedy**, which is cheerful. Later, the three unities of place, time and action were derived from the ancient theory.

In 1863, in “The Technique of the Drama”, **Gustav Freytag** described the structure in five acts. The **exposition** introduces the characters, the place and the conflict. Then the action rises to the **climax**, where the **peripeteia**, the reversal of fortune, often lies. In the fourth act the **retarding moment** raises hope once more. At the end comes the **catastrophe**, the resolution of the conflict.

Some events are hard to show on stage, such as a battle. Then a character standing in a raised position describes what they see. This is called **teichoscopy** or **view from the wall**. In a play text a distinction is made between the **main text**, that is the spoken lines, and the **secondary text** with stage directions, the list of characters and scene details.

In the 20th century **Bertolt Brecht** developed **epic theatre**. The audience was not meant to feel along with the characters but to think critically about what was happening. For this he used the **alienation effect**: songs, banners or actors who speak directly to the audience. That way you always notice that you are sitting in a theatre.

gewusst: Friedrich Schiller wrote the play “William Tell” in 1804. In Interlaken it has been performed for many years as the Tell play.
With Max Frisch and Friedrich Dürrenmatt, Switzerland had two world-famous playwrights in the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: **Franz Hohler** is a Swiss writer, cabaret artist and songwriter. He writes for adults and for children, for example the well-known children’s book “Tschipo”.
wichtigste: Franz Hohler was born in **Biel** in **1943**.
He is a **writer**, **cabaret artist** and **songwriter**.
His children’s book **“Tschipo”** came out in 1978.
His text **“Totemügerli”** is written in an invented Bernese dialect.
He has lived in **Zurich** for many years.

abschnitte.text: Franz Hohler was already performing his own cabaret shows when he was young. **Cabaret** combines humour, music and thinking about society and politics. Hohler often accompanies his songs on the **cello**. His text **“Totemügerli”** became famous: it sounds like Bernese German but is made up almost entirely of invented words. Even so, when you listen, you feel you understand the story.

The children’s book **“Tschipo”** came out in 1978. The boy Tschipo dreams so strongly that in the morning he finds a piece of his dream in his bed, for example sand from an island. This leads him and his family into many crazy adventures. The book shows Hohler’s love of imagination, in which something ordinary suddenly turns into something wonderful.

Hohler writes novels, stories, poems and plays. In the story **“The Reconquest”** from 1982, wild animals return to Zurich and take over the city. Many of his texts are short, playful and surprising. They are often set in Switzerland and show everyday life from an unusual angle. He has received many prizes for his work.

gewusst: “Totemügerli” contains words that do not exist at all, and yet everything sounds like real Bernese dialect.

teile.einleitung: Batteries supply electricity for toys, clocks and torches. Used batteries do not belong in the general rubbish but back in the shop.
wichtigste: You take used batteries to a collection box.
Every shop that sells batteries has such a box.
Batteries contain substances that can harm nature.
Valuable metals are recovered from collected batteries.
With lithium batteries it is best to tape over the terminals.
Button cells must be kept out of reach of small children.

abschnitte.text: A **battery** stores energy in chemical form and releases it as electricity. Inside are metals such as zinc, manganese, nickel or lithium. Some of these substances are **harmful to the environment** if they get into the soil or the water. That is why batteries must not go in the rubbish bag.

In Switzerland every shop that sells batteries must also take used ones back. There is usually a **collection box** by the exit or at the till. Returning them is **free**, because when you buy them you already pay a small fee for disposal, the **advance disposal fee**. Municipal collection points also accept batteries.

The collected batteries are sorted and processed in special plants. Metals such as **zinc**, iron and manganese are recovered. These can be used for new products. At the same time, toxic substances are disposed of safely. In this way recycling protects nature and saves raw materials.

**Lithium batteries** from mobile phones or toys can catch fire if their terminals touch. That is why you tape over the terminals with a bit of sticky tape. Small **button cells** are dangerous for small children because they can be swallowed. Keep them in a safe place. Anyone who often needs batteries can use **rechargeable batteries**, which can be recharged again and again.

gewusst: In Switzerland the organisation INOBAT organises the collection and recycling of batteries.
A single rechargeable battery can be recharged many hundreds of times and so replaces many disposable batteries.

teile.einleitung: **Drama** is one of the three great genres of literature, alongside epic (narrative) literature and poetry. It includes all texts written for the theatre.
wichtigste: The three genres of literature are **epic**, **lyric** and **dramatic** literature.
In drama there is normally **no narrator**.
The plot comes about through **dialogue** and acting on stage.
**Stage directions** say how lines should be spoken and acted.
Plays are usually divided into **acts** and **scenes**.

abschnitte.text: Literature is often divided into three **genres**. **Epic** literature tells a story, for example in novels and fairy tales. **Lyric** poetry includes poems with verses and often rhymes. Finally, **drama** shows a plot on stage. A dramatic text is called a **drama**, a play or a stage play.

In drama there is normally no narrator telling the story. Instead, the **characters** speak for themselves. A conversation between characters is called a **dialogue**. If a character speaks alone and says their thoughts out loud, this is called a **monologue**. The audience understands the plot from what it hears and sees.

As well as the spoken lines, a play text also contains **stage directions**. They are usually printed in italics or put in brackets. They tell you, for example, how a character speaks, where they go or what the stage looks like. They are not spoken. But they help the actors with their acting.

A play is divided into larger parts, the **acts**, and these in turn into **scenes**. A new scene often begins when a character comes on or goes off. The best-known forms are serious **tragedy** and cheerful **comedy**. Mixed forms are called **tragicomedy**, a form that Friedrich Dürrenmatt, for example, liked to use.

gewusst: Many plays are more than 2000 years old and are still performed today, for example plays from ancient Greece.
The Schauspielhaus Zürich is one of the best-known theatres in the German-speaking world.

teile.einleitung: An **inflectional morpheme** is a small building block of a word that adapts the word’s form to the sentence. In the German “du gehst” (you go), the “-st” shows that the second person singular is meant.
wichtigste: A **morpheme** is the smallest building block of a word that has a meaning or a function.
**Inflection** means that words change their form in a sentence.
Inflectional morphemes show **person**, **number**, **case** or **tense**.
They do not make a new word, only a different **word form**.
Building blocks that make new words, on the other hand, are called **derivational morphemes**.

abschnitte.text: Words can be broken down into building blocks. The smallest building block that has a meaning or a grammatical job is called a **morpheme**. For example, the German word “Kinder” (children) is made of “Kind” (child) and “-er”. “Kind” carries the meaning, while “-er” shows the **plural**. Building blocks like “-er” are called **inflectional morphemes**.

**Inflection** means bending a word into a different form. In German, verbs are **conjugated**: ich geh**e**, du geh**st**, er geh**t**, wir geh**en** (I go, you go, he goes, we go). Nouns, articles and adjectives are **declined**, for example in the genitive “des Mann**es**” (of the man). The endings show person, number, case or tense, for example “-te” in “spielte” (played) for the past. The word stays the same; only its **form** changes.

A **derivational morpheme** such as “-heit” or “un-” makes a new word with its own meaning: “frei” (free) becomes “Freiheit” (freedom). An inflectional morpheme does not do this: “gehst” and “geht” are both forms of “gehen” (to go). That is why you find “Freiheit” in the dictionary as a word of its own, but not “gehst”. Inflectional morphemes usually come right at the end of a word.

gewusst: Some forms are shown without an ending, just with an umlaut: “die Mutter” (the mother), “die Mütter” (the mothers).
With “der Lehrer” (the teacher) and “die Lehrer” (the teachers) you cannot see any difference in the noun itself, only in the article.

teile.einleitung: An address says where someone lives. It is important so that letters arrive and help can find the way. At the same time it is personal information that you do not tell just anyone.
wichtigste: An address is made up of name, street, house number, postcode and town.
In Switzerland the postcode has four digits.
You should know your address by heart, for example in case of an emergency.
On the internet you never tell strangers your address.
If someone asks for it in a chat, you show the message to your parents.
Photos can also give away where you live.

abschnitte.titel: How an address is made up
abschnitte.text: A complete **address** includes the person’s name, the street with the **house number**, the **postcode** and the town. In Switzerland the postcode has four digits. The first digit roughly shows the region; for example, 1 stands for western Switzerland and 8 for the area around Zurich. In blocks of flats, the name on the letterbox helps the postman find the right recipient.

abschnitte.titel: Why you should know it by heart
abschnitte.text: If you get lost or need help in an emergency, it is good if you can say your **address**. Your parents’ phone number is important too. Anyone who calls the emergency services must say exactly where something has happened. So practise your address at home until you know it for sure.

On the internet you never know for sure who is really writing. A completely different person can be hiding behind a nice profile. That is why you **never** give **strangers** your address, your school or your phone number. If someone asks for it in a chat, you do not reply and you show the message to your parents or another **trusted adult**. You may also block such contacts.

It is not only words that give away where you live. **Photos** sometimes show street signs, house numbers or your school in the background. Many mobile phones also save the **location** in pictures. So before you share a picture, you look at it carefully. In the settings you can switch off the location information for photos.

gewusst: Postcodes were introduced in Switzerland in 1964.
Some apps show your location to others without you noticing. That is why it is worth looking at the settings with your parents.

teile.einleitung: The bike bell is a small but important part of a bike. With it you can warn others that you are coming. In Switzerland a bell is part of a bike’s required equipment.
wichtigste: With the bell you warn others that you are coming.
In Switzerland every bike must have a bell.
It must be easy to hear.
You use it when necessary, not all the time.
With pedestrians you ring early and in a friendly way.
The bell does not replace being careful.

abschnitte.text: Bikes are very **quiet**. Pedestrians often do not hear a bike coming from behind. With the **bell** you draw attention to yourself. This lets others make **room** for you or stop. This is especially important on paths that bikes and pedestrians share.

In Switzerland the bell is part of a bike’s **compulsory equipment**. This also includes two **brakes**, reflectors and, at night, lights. Anyone riding without a bell can get a **fine**. That is why a bike sold in a shop usually already has a bell.

You ring **in good time**, not only when you are right behind someone. Otherwise the person might get a fright and take a wrong step. A short ring is usually enough. Ringing all the time seems **rude**. When overtaking, you ride past slowly and with enough distance.

Not everyone hears the bell. Some people wear **headphones**, others do not hear well. Children sometimes jump suddenly to the side. That is why you ride **carefully** despite the bell and are ready to brake. The bell is a warning, not a right of way.

gewusst: There are bike bells in many shapes, from the classic ringer to the small bell with a bright tone.
In some towns there are signs on popular paths reminding cyclists to ride slowly and considerately.

teile.einleitung: Nosebleeds are common and usually harmless. With a few simple steps you can usually stop one quickly yourself.
wichtigste: With a nosebleed you tilt your head **forwards**.
You pinch the soft **sides of the nose** together for a few minutes.
Do not tilt your head back, or blood will run into your throat.
A cold cloth on the **back of the neck** can also help.
Common causes are dry air, nose picking or a knock.
If the bleeding does not stop, a doctor is needed.

abschnitte.text: At the front of the nose there are many fine **blood vessels** just under the thin **mucous membrane**. They can easily be injured. This happens, for example, with **dry air** in winter, when picking your nose, when blowing your nose hard, with a cold or from a knock while playing. In children nosebleeds are especially common and almost always harmless.

Sit down and tilt your **head slightly forwards**. With your thumb and index finger, pinch the soft **sides of your nose** together and breathe through your mouth. Keep up the pressure for about **ten minutes** without checking in between. A **cold cloth** or cool pack on the back of the neck can help, because cold makes the vessels narrow. Afterwards you do not blow your nose for a while.

In the past people often tilted their head back. That is wrong. Then the blood runs into the **throat** and the stomach, and that can make you feel sick and vomit. You also can no longer see how heavily it is bleeding. Stuffing cotton wool deep into the nose is not a good idea either.

If the bleeding does not stop after about **20 minutes**, if it is very heavy or if it comes after a serious **accident** to the head, medical help is needed. Anyone who often has nosebleeds for no reason should have it checked. In an emergency in Switzerland you can reach the ambulance service on **144**.

gewusst: The spot at the front of the nose that bleeds especially often has its own name in medicine: Kiesselbach’s area (Locus Kiesselbachi).
For people who often have nosebleeds in winter, more humid air in the room sometimes helps.

teile.einleitung: Quiet times are times when you should not make unnecessary noise. This lets everyone sleep and rest. In Switzerland, in many buildings, night-time quiet begins at 10 pm.
wichtigste: Night-time quiet usually begins at 10 pm.
It often lasts until 6 or 7 in the morning.
Many municipalities also have a lunchtime quiet period.
On Sundays and public holidays it should be especially quiet.
The exact times are in the house rules or in the municipality’s regulations.
Consideration for the neighbours is the most important thing.

abschnitte.text: In many Swiss municipalities, **night-time quiet** applies from **10 pm** until 6 or 7 am. During this time you should not listen to loud music, drill or have noisy parties. Televisions and voices on the balcony can also disturb people. Anyone who has to work early needs their **sleep**.

Many house rules have a **lunchtime quiet** period, often from about 12 to 1 pm. On **Sundays** and public holidays, noisy jobs such as mowing the lawn or hammering are usually not allowed. In some buildings you are not supposed to do washing on Sundays either. The rules are not the same everywhere.

The **municipality** often regulates noise in its police regulations. For rented flats there are also **house rules**. They say, for example, when the laundry room may be used. Under **tenancy law**, anyone who rents a flat must show consideration for the neighbours.

If you are planning a **party**, it helps to let the neighbours know beforehand. If someone keeps disturbing you, you first speak to them **in a friendly way**. Often the other person does not even know they are being loud. If that does not help, you can contact the **management** or the landlord.

gewusst: In blocks of flats you often hear footsteps and music through ceilings and walls better than you think.
For some celebrations, such as 1 August or New Year’s Eve, municipalities allow noise for longer than usual.

teile.einleitung: An adjective is a word that describes what someone or something is like. In German it is also called an Eigenschaftswort or Wiewort. With adjectives you can say whether something is big, red, sour or slow.
wichtigste: Adjectives describe what someone or something is like.
Other German names for them are Eigenschaftswort and Wiewort.
German examples are “gross” (big), “klein” (small), “weiss” (white), “sauer” (sour) and “langsam” (slow).
In German, adjectives are written with a small letter.
Most adjectives can be compared: “gross, grösser, am grössten” (big, bigger, biggest).
In front of a noun, the German adjective changes its ending: “der grosse Hund” (the big dog), “die grosse Katze” (the big cat).
Words such as “singen” (to sing) or “laufen” (to run) are not adjectives but verbs.

abschnitte.text: An **adjective** tells us more about people, animals and things. It answers the question “What is something like?”. Fresh snow, for example, is **“weiss”** (white), a lemon tastes **“sauer”** (sour), and a snail is very **“langsam”** (slow). Without adjectives our descriptions would be rather boring.

A good trick in German: you put the word between an article and a noun, for example “der ___ Hund” (the ___ dog). If the word fits, as in “der laute Hund” (the loud dog), it is usually an adjective. In the series “klein, laut, singen, warm” (small, loud, sing, warm), **“singen”** is not an adjective but a verb. You do not say “der singen Hund”. In German, adjectives are also written with a small letter.

Many adjectives can be **compared** in order to compare things. The basic form is called the positive: “gross” (big). The first level is called the **comparative**: “grösser” (bigger). The highest level is called the **superlative**: “am grössten” (biggest). Some adjectives have special forms, such as “gut, besser, am besten” (good, better, best) or “viel, mehr, am meisten” (much, more, most).

There are adjectives for colours such as “rot” (red), “blau” (blue) and “weiss” (white). Others describe taste, such as “süss” (sweet), “salzig” (salty), “sauer” (sour) and “bitter” (bitter). Others again say something about size, shape, feelings or character, for example “rund” (round), “fröhlich” (cheerful) or “mutig” (brave). Many adjectives have an opposite: “heiss” and “kalt” (hot and cold), “schnell” and “langsam” (fast and slow).

If an adjective stands in front of a noun in German, it gets an ending: “der rote Ball”, “ein roter Ball”, “mit dem roten Ball” (the red ball, a red ball, with the red ball). This change is called **declension**. If the adjective comes after the verb “sein” (to be), it has no ending: “Der Ball ist rot” (The ball is red). Adjectives can also describe how someone does something, for example: “Sie rennt schnell” (She runs fast).

begriffe.erklaerung: Another German word for adjective (literally “property word”).
The first level of comparison, for example “grösser” (bigger).
The highest level of comparison, for example “am grössten” (biggest).
Changing the ending of a word depending on the sentence.

gewusst: Some adjectives cannot sensibly be compared at all, for example “tot” (dead) or “schwanger” (pregnant).
Nouns can be made from many adjectives, such as “die Schönheit” (beauty) from “schön” (beautiful).
Ordinal numbers such as “erste” (first) or “zweite” (second) also behave like adjectives in a sentence.

teile.einleitung: A bike helmet protects your head in a fall. But it only helps if it fits properly. It must sit straight on your head, and the chin strap must be fastened.
wichtigste: The helmet sits straight and covers the forehead.
The chin strap is always fastened.
About one finger fits between the strap and the chin.
The helmet must not wobble, but it must not pinch either.
After a bad fall you need a new helmet.
In Switzerland a helmet is not compulsory for ordinary bikes, but it is strongly recommended.

abschnitte.text: In a fall the **head** often hits the ground. Inside, the helmet is made of a hard **foam** that cushions the impact. This protects the **brain** better. Head injuries are among the most serious consequences of bike accidents.

The helmet sits **straight** on your head and covers your forehead. It should not slip back onto your neck. The **straps** meet under the ears. The **chin strap** is fastened, and one finger fits between the strap and your chin. With the little wheel at the back you adjust the helmet so that it does not wobble.

abschnitte.titel: When you need a new helmet
abschnitte.text: After a **bad fall** you must replace the helmet, even if you cannot see any damage. The foam may be broken inside. When your head grows, you also need a **bigger helmet**. Over the years the material ages, so you should change your helmet after a few years.

For ordinary bikes and slow e-bikes, a helmet is **not compulsory** in Switzerland. But accident prevention experts **recommend** it to everyone. For **fast e-bikes** up to 45 kilometres per hour a helmet is compulsory. A helmet also protects you when skiing, inline skating or riding a scooter.

gewusst: A helmet with scratches on the outside may still be fine; what matters is that the foam inside is not damaged.
Light-coloured helmets with reflectors also make you easier to see.

teile.einleitung: A cycle path is a path meant for bikes. You can recognise it by the round blue sign with a white bike. Cycle paths separate bikes from car traffic and make cycling safer.
wichtigste: The “cycle path” sign is blue and round and shows a white bike.
Round blue signs are mandatory signs: they say what you must do.
If there is a cycle path, cyclists must use it.
E-bikes and Mofas may also use the cycle path.
A cycle lane is a lane marked in yellow at the edge of the road.
In Switzerland red signposts show cycle routes.

abschnitte.text: The sign for a **cycle path** is a **blue circle** with a white bike. Round blue signs are called **mandatory signs**; they tell you to do something. Anyone riding a bike must use the cycle path. Cars may not drive or park there.

Road signs have fixed shapes. **Red circles** forbid something, for example no vehicles allowed. **Triangles** warn of dangers. **Blue circles** say what you must do, and blue rectangles give information. Anyone who knows these shapes can understand many signs from far away.

A **cycle path** is usually separate from the carriageway. A **cycle lane**, on the other hand, is on the road and is marked with a **yellow line** and a bike symbol. Sometimes bikes and pedestrians share a path; then the sign shows both symbols. On such paths you take particular care of pedestrians.

In Switzerland there are many well signposted **cycle routes**. You can recognise them by **red signposts** with white writing. Some routes run right across the whole country. Municipalities and cantons keep expanding their cycle paths so that more people can cycle safely.

gewusst: Since 2018 the promotion of cycle paths has been in the Federal Constitution; the people voted in favour.
Many cycle signposts also show the number of kilometres to the next place.

teile.einleitung: Phishing is a kind of fraud on the internet. Fraudsters send fake emails, text messages or other messages to try to get passwords, card numbers or money.
wichtigste: Phishing comes from the English word “fishing”.
The fraudsters pretend to be the post office, a bank, a parcel service or an authority.
Often you are supposed to click on a link and enter data there or pay something.
Banks and the post office never ask for passwords by email or text message.
Do not open suspicious messages, do not reply, and delete them.
Anyone who has already entered data contacts their bank at once and changes the password.

abschnitte.text: In **phishing**, fraudsters cast out a fishing line, so to speak. They send out a huge number of fake messages and hope that someone will bite. If the fraud comes by text message, it is also called **smishing**. The aim is always the same: the fraudsters want your **personal data** or your money.

**Time pressure** is typical: “Otherwise your parcel will be sent back” or “Your account will be blocked”. Often only a small amount is asked for, for example 2 francs. The sender looks real, but the **web address** in the link is strange. Sometimes the text also has mistakes in it. If you are not expecting a parcel, the message is especially suspicious.

**Never click on unknown links** and do not enter any data there. Delete the message or show it to an adult first. If you want to know whether it is genuine, go yourself to the real website of the post office or the bank. A **secure password** and two-step login give your accounts extra protection.

In Switzerland the **Federal Office for Cybersecurity** deals with attacks from the internet. You can report suspicious messages there. Anyone who has lost money should inform their **bank** immediately and report it to the **police**. The faster you act, the more likely it is that the damage can be limited.

gewusst: The “ph” instead of “f” in the word phishing is a play on words from the language of computer enthusiasts.
Fake websites sometimes look so like the original that only a single letter in the address is different.

teile.einleitung: An anglicism is a word or phrase from English that is used in another language. German has a great many anglicisms, for example “chatten” (to chat), “Party” or “Computer”.
wichtigste: Anglicisms are words from English in another language.
Since the end of the Second World War the influence of English has grown greatly.
English verbs are conjugated according to German rules: “chatten”, “gechattet” (to chat, chatted).
English words ending in y form their German plural with s: “Partys”, “Babys”.
Before that, French was for a long time the most important source language.
Some words sound English but are not used that way in English at all.

abschnitte.text: Languages keep taking words from each other. Such words are called **loanwords**. For a long time **French** was the most important source of loanwords for German. After **1945** the influence of the **USA** and Great Britain grew in politics, business, technology and pop culture. Since then a particularly large number of new words have come from **English**, for example from music, sport and the computer world.

When German takes over an English verb, it is usually conjugated like a **weak German verb**. “To chat” becomes **“chatten”**: “ich chatte, du chattest, wir haben gechattet” (I chat, you chat, we have chatted). So the participle is formed with “ge-” and “-t”. In the same way people say “gejoggt” (jogged) or “gestreamt” (streamed). This is how foreign words adapt to German grammar.

German rules also apply to the **plural**. Since the spelling reform, English words ending in **“-y”** form their plural with **“-s”**. So in German you write **“Partys”** and **“Babys”**, not “parties” as in English. In German, English nouns are written with a capital letter, for example “das Team” or “der Computer”.

Some words sound English but are used differently in English or not at all. They are called **false anglicisms**. The best-known example is **“Handy”** for a mobile phone. In English it is called a “mobile phone” or “cell phone”. In Switzerland there are also many loanwords from **French**, such as **“Velo”** (bike) or “Trottoir” (pavement).

gewusst: “Beamer” for a projector is also a false anglicism.
The other way round, English has also taken German words, for example “kindergarten” and “rucksack”.

teile.einleitung: Chiasmus is a figure of speech in which parts of a sentence are arranged crosswise. What comes first in the first half comes last in the second half. This creates a striking sentence that is easy to remember.
wichtigste: In a **chiasmus**, parts of a sentence are arranged **crosswise**.
The name comes from the Greek letter **chi**, which looks like an X.
An example is “Art is long, and short is our life”.
Chiasmus often emphasises a contrast.
The opposite is **parallelism**, with the same order.

abschnitte.text: In a **chiasmus**, two parts of a sentence mirror each other. In the example “Art is long, and short is our life” (in German “Die Kunst ist lang, und kurz ist unser Leben”), first comes a noun and then an adjective. In the second half it is the other way round: first the adjective, then the noun. If you join the matching words with lines, you get a cross. The sentence comes from Goethe's “Faust”.

The name comes from the Greek letter **chi**. It looks like our X. Just like the lines in the letter, the parts of the sentence cross over in a chiasmus. Another well-known example is: “I eat to live, and do not live to eat.” Sentences like this stick in the memory.

Chiasmus makes a sentence striking and rhythmic. It often emphasises a **contrast**, for example long and short. In that case it is related to **antithesis**, which sets opposites against each other. The counterpart of chiasmus is **parallelism**. There the order stays the same, for example: “Art is long, life is short.”

gewusst: Chiasmus is also popular in speeches and advertising slogans, because it is easy to remember.
As early as ancient times, teachers of rhetoric described chiasmus as an ornament of speech.

teile.einleitung: A fire in a block of flats is dangerous, above all because of the smoke. Anyone who knows how to behave correctly can protect themselves and others.
wichtigste: In a fire you immediately call the fire brigade on 118.
You never use the lift; you escape by the stairs.
The lift can get stuck if the power fails, and it can fill with smoke.
Smoke is often more dangerous than the flames.
You close doors behind you so that fire and smoke do not spread.
If the stairwell is full of smoke, you stay in the flat and make yourself noticed at the window.

abschnitte.text: In a fire the order is: **alert, rescue, extinguish**. First you call the **fire brigade** on **118** and say where the fire is. Then you get yourself and others to safety. You only try to put out a very small fire, and only if you do not put yourself in danger.

In a fire the **power can fail**. Then the **lift** gets stuck between two floors. The lift shaft also acts like a chimney: it can quickly fill with **smoke**. Anyone stuck in the lift can no longer escape. That is why you always use the **stairs**. In many buildings there is a sign next to the lift saying this.

The greatest danger in a fire is **smoke**. It contains poisonous gases that you cannot smell, and it stops you seeing. Because smoke rises, the air near the floor stays breathable for longer. That is why you move bent down low or crawling. You close doors behind you, because a closed door holds back fire and smoke for a while.

abschnitte.titel: If the way out is blocked
abschnitte.text: If the **stairwell** is already full of smoke, you do not go out. You stay in the flat, close the door and seal gaps with wet cloths. You make yourself noticed by the fire brigade at the **window**. A **smoke alarm** warns early with a loud sound and gives you valuable time to escape. In Switzerland the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention and fire safety experts recommend fitting smoke alarms in every flat.

gewusst: A smoke alarm costs little and can save lives, because it also wakes you up when you are asleep.
Tall buildings sometimes have a special firefighters’ lift that only the fire brigade may use.

teile.einleitung: Why is the German word “Hund” (dog) written with a d, even though you hear a t at the end? This is because of final devoicing. With a simple trick you can still always find the right letter.
wichtigste: At the end of a German word, b, d and g are pronounced hard, like p, t and k.
This is called **final devoicing** (Auslautverhärtung).
With the **lengthening test** you can find the right letter.
In “Hunde” (dogs), “Kinder” (children) and “Räder” (wheels) you can hear the d clearly.
In “Körbe” (baskets) and “gelbe” (yellow) you hear the b, and in “Berge” (mountains) and “Zwerge” (dwarfs) the g.
That is why you write “Hund”, “Rad”, “Korb”, “Berg” and “gelb”.

abschnitte.text: Say “Hund” (dog), “Wald” (forest) or “Berg” (mountain) out loud. At the end you hear a hard t or k. But a d or a g is written. This is because in German soft sounds at the end of a word are pronounced hard. Experts call this **final devoicing**. The **final sound** is the last sound of a word.

The best trick is the **lengthening test**. You make the word longer, and then you can hear the letter clearly. With nouns you form the plural: “Hund” becomes “Hunde”, “Kind” (child) becomes “Kinder”, “Rad” (wheel) becomes “Räder”. With adjectives you add a noun: “gelb” (yellow) becomes “gelbe Blumen” (yellow flowers). With verbs the infinitive helps: “er gibt” (he gives) comes from “geben” (to give).

The test works with a great many words. “Wald” (forest) goes to “Wälder”, “Pferd” (horse) to “Pferde”. For the basket in which you carry bread, “Korb”, the plural “Körbe” helps. The dwarf from the fairy tale, “Zwerg”, becomes “Zwerge”. And mountains such as the Matterhorn or the Säntis show that “Berg” (mountain) is written with a g.

In **Middle High German**, about 800 years ago, people often wrote words the way they spoke them. For “Tag” (day) people wrote “tac”, but in the plural “tage”. Later it became the rule that a word should look the same in all its forms. That is why today “Tag” is written with a g. This makes it easier to recognise related words.

Not all languages have final devoicing. In English “dog” and “dock” sound different. In German, on the other hand, “Rad” (wheel) and “Rat” (advice) sound almost the same. Dutch, Polish and Russian also have final devoicing. Anyone learning German therefore has to remember the spelling with the help of the lengthening test.

gewusst: “Rad” (wheel) and “Rat” (advice) sound the same but have completely different meanings.
The lengthening test also helps with other questions, for example whether a word is written with a double consonant.

teile.einleitung: The apostrophe is a small mark that looks like a raised comma. It usually shows that letters have been left out of a word. But many people also put it where it does not belong at all.
wichtigste: The apostrophe is a **mark of omission**: it stands for letters that have been left out.
In the German “Wie geht's?” (How are you?), the “'s” stands for the word “es” (it).
With common forms such as “geht's”, you may also leave out the apostrophe.
The German genitive of names is normally formed without an apostrophe: “Annas Buch” (Anna’s book).
If a name ends in s, ss, x, z or tz, an apostrophe is used in the German genitive: “Klaus' Velo” (Klaus’s bike).
The plural s gets no apostrophe in German, not even with abbreviations: “CDs”.
Contractions such as “ins”, “am” or “zum” are written without an apostrophe.

abschnitte.text: When people speak quickly, they often swallow letters. In writing this can be shown with an apostrophe. In German, “Ich habe es” (I have it) becomes “Ich hab's”, and “Wie geht es?” (How is it going?) becomes “Wie geht's?”. The apostrophe sits exactly where the letters are missing. That is why it is also called a **mark of omission**.

The **genitive** shows whom something belongs to. With German names you simply add an s: “Annas Buch” (Anna’s book), “Peters Velo” (Peter’s bike). But if a name ends in s, ss, x, z or tz, you cannot add another s. Then you only put an apostrophe: “Klaus' Velo” (Klaus’s bike), “Max' Mütze” (Max’s cap). The form “Anna's Buch”, as in English, is only a rare exception in German.

In German the plural s never gets an apostrophe. So you write “CDs”, “Autos” (cars) and “Handys” (mobile phones). There is also no apostrophe in contractions of a preposition and an article: “ins” from “in das” (into the), “am” from “an dem” (at the), “zum” from “zu dem” (to the). These words are so common that they count as perfectly normal words. A wrongly placed apostrophe is jokingly called a **Deppenapostroph** (idiot’s apostrophe) in German.

With shortened forms of “es” (it), the apostrophe is often optional. You may write “Wie geht's?” or “Wie gehts?”. Both are correct. The only important thing is to be consistent within a text. Apostrophes are found especially often in poems and songs, because there they improve the rhythm.

The word “apostrophe” comes from **Greek**. The ancient Greek “apostrophos” means roughly “turned away”. The word came into German via Latin. On a Swiss or German keyboard the apostrophe is usually on the same key as the question mark.

gewusst: An apostrophe and a comma look almost the same, but the apostrophe is at the top.
In English the apostrophe is normal in the genitive (possessive); in German it is usually wrong there.

teile.einleitung: **Friedrich Dürrenmatt** was one of the best-known Swiss writers of the 20th century. His plays and crime novels are read and performed all over the world.
wichtigste: Dürrenmatt was born in the canton of Bern in **1921** and died in Neuchâtel in **1990**.
His best-known play is **“The Visit”**.
In **“The Physicists”** (1962), three physicists pretend to be mad in a sanatorium.
In the crime novel **“The Judge and His Hangman”**, Inspector **Bärlach** investigates.
He often wrote **tragicomedies**, in which seriousness and comedy come together.
Dürrenmatt was also a **painter** and draughtsman.

abschnitte.text: Friedrich Dürrenmatt was born in **1921** in Konolfingen in the **Emmental**; his father was a pastor. He studied in Bern and Zurich and at first wanted to become a painter. Then he decided to write. From the 1950s he lived in **Neuchâtel**, where he died in **1990**. Today the **Centre Dürrenmatt** there shows his paintings and drawings.

In this play the rich **Claire Zachanassian** returns to her poor home town of **Güllen**. She offers the town a billion if someone kills **Alfred Ill**. He had betrayed her when she was young. At first everyone is outraged, but slowly the townspeople give in to temptation. The play asks how much justice and morals are worth when money is involved.

In the comedy **“The Physicists”** from 1962, three physicists live in the sanatorium “Les Cerisiers” and pretend to be mad. The physicist **Möbius** wants to protect the world from his dangerous discoveries this way. But the plan fails. In his **“21 Points on The Physicists”**, Dürrenmatt wrote that a story has only been thought through to the end when it has taken the **worst possible turn**. In the play, this turn happens by chance.

Dürrenmatt also wrote exciting crime novels. In **“The Judge and His Hangman”**, the sick Inspector **Hans Bärlach** investigates in Bern and on Lake Biel. He uses the culprit as a tool to bring an old enemy to justice. “The Pledge” is another well-known crime novel of his. Many of his books are read in schools and have been made into films.

gewusst: Dürrenmatt called many of his plays comedies, even though they ask very serious questions.
The Centre Dürrenmatt in Neuchâtel was built by the Ticino architect Mario Botta.

teile.einleitung: A **foreign word** is a word that has been taken from another language and still seems foreign. You can often recognise it by its spelling or pronunciation, as with the German words “Chauffeur” (driver) or “Rhythmus” (rhythm).
wichtigste: A **foreign word** still gives away its origin through its spelling or pronunciation.
If a word has fully adapted, it is called a **loanword**, for example the German “Fenster” (window).
Many foreign words in German come from **Latin**, **Greek**, **French** and **English**.
Latin words ending in “-um” often form their German plural with “-en”: Museen (museums), Daten (dates).
In Switzerland many words from French are common, such as “Trottoir” (pavement).

abschnitte.text: Languages are constantly borrowing words from each other. A **foreign word** still seems foreign: in German, “Chauffeur” is spelt the French way and “Computer” the English way. A **loanword**, on the other hand, has fully adapted. “Fenster” comes from the Latin “fenestra”, but today it sounds completely German. Often the line between the two is blurred.

Many foreign words from science and education come from **Greek** or **Latin**. The German “Bibliothek” means a collection of books and is written with “th”. “Atmosphäre” (atmosphere) comes from “atmos” (vapour) and “sphaira” (ball). “Rhythmus” contains the letter h twice, and the y is pronounced like the German ü. Latin words ending in “-um” have special plural forms: “Museum” becomes “Museen” and “Datum” becomes “Daten”.

In Switzerland a particularly large number of words from **French** are in use. People say “Trottoir” for the pavement, “Velo” for the bicycle, “Perron” for the railway platform and “Glace” for ice cream. “Trottoir” comes from the French verb “trotter”. “Ingenieur” (engineer) also keeps the French spelling with “-ieur” and is pronounced roughly “Inschenjör”.

Today many new German words come from **English**, especially from technology, sport and music. They are called **anglicisms**, for example “Computer”, “Team” or “Download”. Some words only sound English but are not actually used that way in English. The best-known example is **“Handy”**: in English you say “mobile phone”.

gewusst: “Handy” is a false anglicism: the word looks English, but in English it is not used for a mobile phone.
Many Swiss expressions such as “Velo” or “Billett” (ticket) are not immediately understood in Germany.

teile.einleitung: The alphabet is the fixed order of all the letters of a writing system. Our alphabet begins with A and ends with Z and has 26 letters. It is also called the ABC, after its first three letters.
wichtigste: Our alphabet has 26 letters from A to Z.
The first letter is A and the last is Z.
After M comes N, and S stands between R and T.
German also has the umlauts Ä, Ö and Ü.
The word alphabet comes from the Greek letters alpha and beta.
Dictionaries and phone lists are arranged in alphabetical order.
Our alphabet is called the Latin alphabet and is the most widely used in the world.

abschnitte.text: An **alphabet** is a writing system in which each sign stands roughly for one sound. The letters have a fixed order: A, B, C, D, E and so on to Z. Our alphabet has **26 letters**. Each letter exists as a capital letter and as a small letter, for example A and a.

The first alphabetic writing systems were created more than 3000 years ago in the Middle East. The **Phoenicians** developed a script that the Greeks adopted and added vowels to. The name also comes from the Greeks: **alpha** and **beta** are their first letters. The Romans turned it into the Latin alphabet that we use today.

When you put words in alphabetical order, you look first at the first letter. That is why “apple” comes right at the front if the other words begin with later letters. If the first letters are the same, you compare the second, then the third. With the German words Hut, Haus, Hund and Hase (hat, house, dog, hare), **Hase** comes first, because a comes before au, u and ut. This is how dictionaries, lists of names and indexes are arranged.

As well as the 26 letters, German has the **umlauts** Ä, Ö and Ü. In Germany and Austria there is also the Eszett, a special letter for a sharp s sound. In Switzerland the Eszett is not used; instead people write ss, so “gross” (big) rather than with the Eszett. French, Italian and Romansh, the other national languages of Switzerland, also use the Latin alphabet with their own signs such as é or à.

abschnitte.titel: Other writing systems of the world
abschnitte.text: Not all languages use our alphabet. In Greece people write with the **Greek alphabet**, and in Russia with the Cyrillic one. Arabic and Hebrew are written from right to left. Chinese is not an alphabet at all, because there the characters stand for whole words or syllables. But the Latin alphabet is the most widespread writing system in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for the alphabet.
The German letters Ä, Ö and Ü with two dots.
Arranged in the order of the alphabet.
A sound such as A, E, I, O or U.

gewusst: At school many children learn the ABC with a song so that they remember the order better.
The sentence “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” contains all 26 letters.
The J and the W did not yet exist in the Romans’ original alphabet.

teile.einleitung: The Halbtax, or Half Fare travelcard, is a pass for public transport in Switzerland. Anyone who has one pays only about half the price for most tickets.
wichtigste: With the Half Fare travelcard most tickets cost about half price.
It is valid on trains, buses, trams, many boats and mountain railways.
The Half Fare travelcard is personal and valid for one person only.
You buy it for a certain period, usually a year.
It is worth it for anyone who travels on public transport fairly often.
Today the Half Fare travelcard is stored on the **SwissPass**.

abschnitte.titel: What the Half Fare travelcard is
abschnitte.text: The word **Halbtax** means “half fare”, that is half price. With this pass you buy a ticket but only pay about half the normal price. This applies to single tickets, day passes and many other offers. The Half Fare travelcard has existed in Switzerland for many decades, and a great many people own one.

The Half Fare travelcard is not only valid with **SBB**. Many other railways, PostBuses, town buses, trams and boats also give the reduction. You also get a discount on many **mountain railways**. Some railways or special offers have their own rules, so it is worth checking the railway’s information.

The Half Fare travelcard belongs to exactly one person. You may not lend it to anyone. Today it is stored on the **SwissPass**, a red card with a photo. When tickets are checked, you show the card or your phone with the app. Anyone travelling at half price without a valid pass has to pay a surcharge.

The Half Fare travelcard itself costs money. It is worth it if you travel so much in a year that the saving is bigger than the price of the pass. Anyone who travels almost every day often chooses the **General Abonnement**, **GA** for short. With it you can travel all over Switzerland without individual tickets.

gewusst: The Half Fare travelcard is one of the most popular passes in Switzerland; a large part of the population owns one.
Since 2015 the Half Fare travelcard and the GA have been stored on the SwissPass; before that there were separate cards for them.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who rents a flat draws up a **handover report** when moving in and when moving out. It records the condition of the flat and what was already broken. This protects you later from arguments and unnecessary costs.
wichtigste: The handover report describes the condition of the flat.
The tenant and the landlord go through the flat together.
Existing defects are written down precisely, ideally with photos.
Both sign, and both get a copy.
Whatever is in the report was already broken before.
This means you do not have to pay for someone else’s damage when you move out.

abschnitte.text: A **handover report** is a document that is filled in when a rented flat is handed over. Room by room, you record what the walls, floors, windows, kitchen and bathroom look like. The number of **keys** and the meter readings are also noted. In Switzerland this is often also called the **flat inspection**.

When moving in you look carefully: scratches in the parquet, marks on the wall, a crack in the washbasin. Every such **defect** goes into the report. Dated photos help as well. If you only notice something later, you report it to the landlord quickly and **in writing**.

When moving out, the flat is inspected together again. The condition is compared with the report from moving in. The tenant does not have to pay for damage that was already there before. Normal **wear and tear**, such as walls that have faded slightly after many years, is part of living somewhere and is not at the tenant’s expense.

Many landlords ask for a **rent deposit**. In Switzerland it may be at most three months’ rent and is kept in an account in the tenant’s name. After moving out you get the money back if there is no new damage. So a careful report also helps you get your deposit back in full.

gewusst: You should only sign a report if you agree with what it says.
If there is an argument later, the signed report is an important piece of evidence.

teile.einleitung: Service charges are costs of a rented flat that come on top of the actual rent, for example for heating, hot water or the caretaker. Swiss tenancy law has an important rule about them.
wichtigste: Service charges pay for services around the flat, such as heating and hot water.
The landlord may only charge them if they are **listed individually** in the tenancy agreement.
If they are not in the contract, they are considered **included in the rent**.
Often you pay a monthly **payment on account**.
Once a year a **statement** arrives with the actual costs.
Tenants may see the receipts.

abschnitte.text: The **rent** pays for the use of the flat itself. In addition there are costs for things you need all the time: **heating**, **hot water**, cleaning the stairwell, the **caretaker**, the lift or charges for water and sewage. These are called **service charges**. Electricity in your own flat is usually paid directly to the electricity company.

The **Code of Obligations** says: the landlord may only charge service charges if they are expressly agreed in the **tenancy agreement**. Each item must be named **individually**, for example “heating” or “caretaker”. If the contract says nothing at all about them, the service charges are considered **included** in the rent. The landlord cannot then charge them on top.

Often you pay a fixed amount for the service charges every month along with the rent. With a **payment on account**, this is an advance payment. Once a year the landlord draws up a **statement** with the real costs. If you have paid too much, you get money back; otherwise you have to pay the difference. With a **flat rate**, the amount stays fixed and there is no statement.

Tenants have the right to see the **receipts** for the service charge statement. This lets you check whether everything is correct. If the statement shows a large extra payment, it is worth taking a close look. Advice centres such as the tenants’ association or the **conciliation authority** can help with questions.

gewusst: In many flats heating costs are the largest part of the service charges.
Anyone who heats economically and does not shower for too long can lower their own service charges when there is a statement on account.

teile.einleitung: Anaphora is a rhetorical figure of speech. In it, sentences, parts of sentences or lines that follow each other begin with the same word. This emphasises a statement and makes it easier to remember.
wichtigste: In anaphora a word is repeated at the beginning of sentences.
One pattern is “Who …, who …, who …”.
Anaphora is one of the figures of repetition.
Epiphora, on the other hand, repeats words at the end.
Anaphora can be found in speeches, poems, songs and advertising.

abschnitte.text: In **anaphora** the same word or group of words comes at the **beginning** of several sentences or lines. A typical pattern is **“Who …, who …, who …”**. An example: “Whoever laughs, whoever sings, whoever dances is welcome.” The word anaphora comes from Greek and means roughly “carrying back” or “taking up again”.

The repetition gives the text a clear **rhythm**. The message has a **powerful** effect and stays in your head. That is why speakers like to use anaphora to emphasise their most important message. It is also often found in **poems**, songs and **advertising**.

Anaphora has a counterpart, **epiphora**. There a word is repeated at the **end** of sentences that follow each other, for example “I am tired, you are tired, everyone is tired”. Both belong to the **figures of repetition**. So when you examine a text, you look at whether the repetition comes at the beginning or at the end.

gewusst: In linguistics anaphor means something different, namely a reference back, for example through a pronoun such as “he”.

teile.einleitung: A payment on account (Akontozahlung) is an advance payment towards costs that you will only know exactly later. At the end there is a final statement, and you either pay a bit more or get money back.
wichtigste: Akonto means advance payment or payment on account.
The word comes from Italian and means “on account”.
If you rent a flat, you often pay the service charges on account every month.
Once a year the service charge statement arrives with the real costs.
If you have paid too little, you pay the difference; otherwise you get a refund.
There are also payments on account for taxes and electricity.

abschnitte.text: The word **akonto** comes from the Italian “a conto” and means “on account”. So you pay an amount now, even though the exact costs have not been fixed yet. The amount is an **estimate**. Only later, when everything has been added up, do you know how much it really cost.

abschnitte.titel: Service charges in a rented flat
abschnitte.text: Anyone who rents a flat often pays **service charges** on top of the actual rent. These include, for example, heating, hot water, the caretaker or cleaning the stairwell. Because these costs vary depending on the winter and how much is used, you pay a fixed amount **on account** every month. Once a year the management sends the **service charge statement** with the real costs.

In the statement, the payments on account are compared with the real costs. If the winter was cold and a lot of heating was used, the money may not be enough. Then there is an **extra payment** to make. If you have paid more than necessary, you get a **refund**. It is different with a **flat rate**: this is not settled at the end of the year; you always pay the same amount.

The system is also used for **taxes**. Many cantons send provisional bills, and you pay in instalments in advance. The final bill only comes once the tax return has been checked. It is similar with some electricity or gas bills. Anyone making payments on account should put some money aside for the final statement.

gewusst: You may look at the service charge statement carefully: tenants have the right to see the receipts for it.
If the payments on account are set too low, a large extra payment may come at the end of the year.

teile.einleitung: Motor vehicle liability insurance is insurance that every car, motorbike and other motor vehicle in Switzerland must have. It pays for damage that you cause to other people with the vehicle.
wichtigste: Motor vehicle liability insurance is **compulsory** in Switzerland.
Without it you do not get **number plates**.
It pays for damage you cause to **others**.
It does not cover damage to your own car.
For that there is voluntary **comprehensive insurance** (Kasko).
The obligation is set out in the federal **Road Traffic Act**.

abschnitte.text: Being **liable** means that you have to take responsibility for damage and pay for it. Anyone who causes an accident with a car can do great damage to other people: to their vehicle, to their house or to their health. Such costs can be very high. **Motor vehicle liability insurance** covers these costs so that the people harmed are sure to get their money.

The federal **Road Traffic Act** requires every motor vehicle to have liability insurance. The road traffic office only issues the **number plates** if there is **proof of insurance**. If the insurance ends, the insurer reports this to the office and the plates must be handed in.

abschnitte.titel: What it pays and what it does not
abschnitte.text: Liability insurance pays for damage to **others**: to the other party’s car, to fences or street lamps, and the costs when people are injured. It does not pay for damage to **your own car**. For that there is voluntary **partial cover**, for example for hail or theft, and **fully comprehensive cover**, which also covers damage you cause to your own car.

You pay a yearly **premium** for the insurance. How much it is depends, for example, on the car, your age and previous accidents. Anyone who causes a lot of damage often has to pay more. Young new drivers usually pay more, because statistically they have accidents more often.

abschnitte.titel: When the person responsible is missing
abschnitte.text: Sometimes someone drives off after an accident, or a vehicle is not insured at all. For such cases Switzerland has the **National Guarantee Fund**. It makes sure that injured people still receive compensation. This means nobody is left without protection if they are involved in an accident through no fault of their own.

gewusst: Mofas also need liability insurance; this is shown by the yearly vignette on their number plate.
Liability insurance also pays if someone else drives your car with your permission and causes an accident.

teile.einleitung: A registered letter is a letter whose delivery the post office records precisely. The recipient has to confirm with their signature that they have received the letter.
wichtigste: With registered post the recipient confirms receipt with their signature.
If nobody is at home, the post office puts a collection notice in the letterbox.
The post office keeps registered items for 7 days.
For letters from authorities, a letter is often deemed to have been delivered on the last day of this period.
With a tracking number you can follow where the letter is at the moment.
Important letters such as notices of termination are often sent by registered post.

abschnitte.text: A **registered letter** is a letter sent with **proof**. The post office registers the letter when it is handed in and records when and to whom it was handed over. The recipient confirms with their **signature** that they have received it. This means the sender can later prove that the letter arrived. Registered post costs more than an ordinary letter.

If nobody is at home when the letter is delivered, the postman or postwoman puts a **collection notice** in the letterbox. It says where you can collect the letter, usually at a post office. The post office keeps the item for **7 days**. If you do not collect it, it goes back to the sender. You can also send another person with a **written authorisation** to collect it.

For letters from **authorities** or courts there is an important rule. Anyone who has to expect such a letter, for example because proceedings are under way, cannot avoid it. If they do not collect the registered letter, it is still deemed to have been delivered on the **last day of the period**. This is called **deemed delivery**. Time limits for replying then start to run anyway.

Letters where **proof** matters are sent by registered post. These include notices ending a tenancy, an insurance policy or a job. Authorities also often send important decisions by registered post. With the **tracking number** on the receipt you can follow online where the letter is at the moment.

gewusst: With a notice of termination, what often counts is not when it was sent but when the letter reaches the recipient. That is why it is better to send it early.
Anyone going on holiday can ask the post office to hold their letters and so will not miss a collection deadline.

teile.einleitung: Mail forwarding is a post office service after you move house. The post office then forwards letters and parcels that are still sent to your old address to your new address for a certain time.
wichtigste: Mail forwarding helps after a move.
Letters to your old address go to your new address for a period you choose.
You can set up forwarding online or at the post office counter.
You should set it up a few days before you move.
You still tell all important offices your new address.
You also report your move to the **municipality**.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who moves often still gets post at their old address at first. With **mail forwarding** you let the **post office** know. It then forwards letters and often parcels too to the new address for a period you choose. This means no important bill or invitation gets lost. You can set up forwarding for one person or for the whole household.

You can set up mail forwarding with Swiss Post **online** or at the **counter** of a post office. You give the old and the new address and choose from when and for how long post should be forwarded. It is best to do this a few days before the move. Depending on how long it lasts, the service costs something.

Mail forwarding only lasts for a certain time. That is why you still tell everyone your **new address**: family and friends, your school or employer, the bank, the **health insurance fund** and insurance companies. You also have to change magazine subscriptions. This way, after the forwarding ends, post comes straight to the right address.

In Switzerland you must also report a move to the **municipality**. You deregister with the old municipality and register with the new one, usually at the **residents’ registration office**. There is a short time limit for this. In many cantons this can now be done online with the **eUmzugCH** service. If you move within the same municipality, you only report the new address.

gewusst: If you ask, the post office can also hold your post, for example during a long holiday, and deliver it all at once later.
Letters that cannot be delivered are sent back by the post office to the sender, if the sender’s address is on the envelope.

teile.einleitung: An **email** is an electronic letter that reaches its destination over the internet in seconds. If you know a few rules, you can write clear and polite messages.
wichtigste: The **subject line** shows straight away what it is about.
In the **CC** field further people get a copy, and everyone sees their address.
The other recipients cannot see addresses in the **BCC** field.
Files are sent as an **attachment**.
The **@** is called the at sign; in German it is jokingly called the “Klammeraffe” (spider monkey).
Text in CAPITAL LETTERS comes across like shouting.

abschnitte.titel: How an email is set out
abschnitte.text: Every email has a **To** field for the recipient's address. Below it is the **subject**, which you can already see in the inbox. A clear subject such as “Question about maths homework” helps with sorting and finding it again. Then come the greeting, the text and the sign-off. At the end there is often a **signature** with your name and contact details.

“CC” stands for “carbon copy”. Anyone in the CC field receives a copy for information, and everyone can see their address. “BCC” means “blind carbon copy”. These recipients remain invisible to the others. For group emails to lots of people, BCC therefore protects **privacy**.

An email address consists of a name, the **at sign @** and the domain, for example “anna@beispiel.ch”. The ending “.ch” stands for Switzerland. Photos or documents are added as an **attachment**. You should not open attachments from unknown senders, because they can contain harmful programs.

If you address someone formally, you also write politely in an email, for example “Guten Tag Frau Keller” (Good day, Mrs Keller) or “Sehr geehrte Frau Keller” (Dear Mrs Keller). At the end “Freundliche Grüsse” (Kind regards) is suitable. Write briefly and clearly and without CAPITAL LETTERS, because that comes across like shouting. Read the message through once more before sending it. After all, you cannot get an email back once it has been sent.

gewusst: The first email was sent by the American Ray Tomlinson in 1971. He also chose the @ as the separator.
In Switzerland people often say “das Mail” (neuter), while in Germany they usually say “die Mail” (feminine).

teile.einleitung: The Baroque is a period of art and literature in the 17th century. The time was marked by the Thirty Years’ War, by diseases and by great uncertainty. That is why many poems reflect on transience and death, while others celebrate splendour and the joy of life.
wichtigste: Baroque literature belongs mainly to the **17th century**.
One background is the **Thirty Years’ War** (1618 to 1648).
Important motifs are **vanitas**, **memento mori** and **carpe diem**.
Andreas Gryphius wrote the sonnet “All is vanity”.
In 1624 Martin Opitz set out rules for poetry in his “Book of German Poetics”.
Grimmelshausen’s “Simplicissimus” is a **picaresque novel**.
A **sonnet** has two quatrains and two tercets.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word **“vanitas”** means vanity or emptiness. What is meant is that everything earthly passes away: wealth, beauty and power. This fits the saying **“memento mori”**, “Remember that you must die”. The opposite motif is often **“carpe diem”**, “Seize the day”. That is why paintings from this time often show hourglasses, candles and wilting flowers.

**Andreas Gryphius** (1616 to 1664) lived through the Thirty Years’ War himself. His poems are about suffering, death and transience. His best-known sonnet is called “All is vanity”. The **sonnet** was a favourite form in the Baroque. It has 14 lines: two four-line verses, the **quatrains**, and two three-line verses, the **tercets**.

In 1624 **Martin Opitz** published the “Book of German Poetics”. In it he demanded, among other things, that the stress of words and the stress of the verse should match. His set of rules shaped German poetry for more than a hundred years. In 1617 the **Fruitbearing Society** had already been founded in Weimar. It was the first and largest German language society and aimed to promote the German language and clean it of foreign words.

Hans Jakob Christoffel von **Grimmelshausen** wrote the novel “The Adventurous Simplicissimus”. It tells the life of Simplicius during the **Thirty Years’ War**. The novel shows clearly the misery of that time. It belongs to the genre of the **picaresque novel**. Such a novel tells the adventures of an outsider who battles his way through the world. The model for it came from Spain.

The Baroque is not only found in books but also in buildings and music. Baroque churches are magnificent, with lots of gold, stucco and ceiling paintings. In Switzerland the **abbey church of Einsiedeln** and the **abbey church (cathedral) of St Gallen** are well-known examples. In music, Johann Sebastian Bach is one of the most famous Baroque composers. Splendour and transience belong closely together in this period.

gewusst: The word “Baroque” probably comes from the Portuguese “barroco”, an irregularly shaped pearl.
The term “Baroque” was at first meant disapprovingly and meant something like “bombastic” or “overloaded”.

teile.einleitung: **Derivation** is a way of forming new words. You attach a building block such as “-heit” or “un-” to an existing word. In German this is called **Ableitung**.
wichtigste: In German, derivation is called **Ableitung**.
New words are created with **affixes**, that is prefixes and suffixes.
A part added at the front is called a **prefix**, and one added at the end is called a **suffix**.
From “frei” (free) and “-heit” you get the noun “Freiheit” (freedom).
A suffix can change the word class, but a prefix usually cannot.
As well as derivation there is **compounding**, for example “Haustür” (front door).

abschnitte.text: Many words are made up of several parts. The core is called the **stem** or base, for example “frei” (free), “les” (read) or “Glück” (luck). If you add an **affix** to it, you get a new word with a new meaning. An affix cannot stand on its own as a word. This process is called derivation, in German Ableitung.

A **prefix** comes before the stem. Examples in German are “un-”, “ver-”, “be-” and “ent-”. “Glück” (luck) becomes “Unglück” (bad luck), and “kaufen” (to buy) becomes “verkaufen” (to sell). The word class usually stays the same: “Glück” and “Unglück” are both nouns. But the meaning changes, sometimes into the opposite.

A **suffix** comes after the stem. Common German suffixes are “-heit”, “-keit”, “-ung”, “-lich” and “-bar”. Suffixes often change the word class: the adjective “frei” (free) becomes the noun “Freiheit” (freedom), and the verb “lesen” (to read) becomes the adjective “lesbar” (readable). With nouns, the suffix even decides the article.

In **compounding** two independent words are joined: “Haus” (house) and “Tür” (door) give “Haustür” (front door). In derivation, on the other hand, there is always a building block that is not a word on its own. Both ways make the German vocabulary very rich. They often appear together, for example in “Schulleitung” (school management).

gewusst: German nouns ending in “-heit”, “-keit” and “-ung” are always feminine: die Freiheit (freedom), die Heiterkeit (cheerfulness), die Zeitung (newspaper).
German nouns ending in “-chen” and “-lein” are always neuter. That is why it is “das Mädchen” (the girl) and “das Büchlein” (the little book).

t1y7fz8r.t: Surcharge for travelling without a ticket

teile.einleitung: Anyone travelling on a tram, bus or train without a valid ticket has to pay a surcharge if they are checked. This is much more expensive than a ticket. That is why it is worth always buying a ticket before the journey.
wichtigste: On public transport you need a valid ticket or pass.
You buy the ticket before getting on.
If you are checked without a valid ticket, you pay the fare and a surcharge.
Anyone caught several times pays more.
Anyone who has forgotten their pass can often show it later and pays less.
Children under 6 travel free when accompanied.

abschnitte.text: Someone who travels without a **valid ticket** is called a fare dodger in everyday language. If there is a **check**, you have to pay the fare and a **surcharge**. Checks take place on trams, buses and trains. The inspectors may ask for an **identity document** to take down your details.

abschnitte.titel: Expensive, and more expensive each time
abschnitte.text: The surcharge is much higher than a normal ticket. Anyone caught without a ticket several times pays a **higher surcharge** each time. The transport companies in Switzerland keep a joint **register** for this. Anyone who does not pay receives reminders and must expect further costs.

Anyone who has a personal **pass** but has forgotten it also has to pay something first when checked. If you can **show** the pass later, most of the money is often refunded. You then only pay a smaller **processing fee**. Since the SwissPass was introduced, the pass is usually stored on a card.

Children under **6** travel free with someone aged 12 or over. From 6 they need a **ticket**, usually at half price. With the **Junior Card** or the Children’s Co-Travel Card, children travel cheaply with their parents or grandparents. From 16 you pay the normal price.

gewusst: In many towns you have to buy your ticket before getting on; there is often no machine on the tram itself.
Today you can also buy tickets on your mobile phone with an app.

teile.einleitung: An essay, or composition, is a longer text that you write on a topic at school. It can tell a story, describe something or give reasons for an opinion. To be easy to read, it needs a clear structure.
wichtigste: An essay has an **introduction, a main part and an ending**.
The main part is usually the longest part.
The introduction leads into the topic and arouses interest.
The ending rounds off the text without completely new arguments.
**Paragraphs** organise the thoughts clearly.
A **common thread** means that the thoughts are logically connected.

abschnitte.text: Every essay consists of three parts. The **introduction** briefly leads into the topic and arouses curiosity. The **main part** contains the actual content, for example the action or the arguments. That is why it is much longer than the other parts. The **ending** rounds off the text, for example with a conclusion or a look ahead.

A good essay has a **common thread**, in German a “red thread”. This means that each part builds sensibly on the one before. Nothing jumps suddenly back and forth. The readers can easily follow the thoughts. Words such as “first”, “then”, “also” or “therefore” help to link the sentences.

**Paragraphs** make a text clear. Each paragraph deals with one thought or one step in the action. When something new begins, you start a new line. A text without paragraphs looks like a grey wall and is tiring to read. You should not bring in completely new arguments in the ending, because there you can no longer justify them.

Before writing it is worth making a plan. You collect ideas, for example in a **mind map** or as key words. Then you sort them for the introduction, main part and ending. After writing you read the text through again. This lets you find mistakes in spelling and sentence structure and cut out repetitions.

A good title makes you curious without giving everything away. Often a short, slightly mysterious title works better than a long one. There are different kinds of essay: the **story**, the **description**, the **report** and the **discursive essay**. In a discursive essay you weigh up arguments for and against something. Each kind has its own rules, but the basic structure stays the same.

gewusst: The German word “Aufsatz” used to mean something you “set up” in writing, that is a draft.
Many professional writers revise their texts several times before they are satisfied.

teile.einleitung: An identity card or a passport shows who you are. If you lose an identity document, you must report the loss to the police and order a new one.
