wichtigste: You report a lost identity document to the police.
The document is then entered in the search system and blocked.
A document reported as lost is invalid, even if you find it again.
You apply for a new document at the responsible office in the canton.
Anyone who loses their document abroad contacts the police and the Swiss embassy or consulate.
A copy of your document at home can help.

abschnitte.text: With an **identity card** or a **passport** you can prove who you are. You need them for travelling abroad, for some dealings with the authorities or when opening a bank account. An identity document contains your name, date of birth, photo and other information. That is why it is valuable and should be kept safe.

If the document has gone, you report the loss to the **police**. They enter it in the **search system**. This blocks it so that no one else can use it. If you find the document later, it is still **invalid**. You may not use it any more. The police issue a confirmation that the loss has been reported.

Then you order a new document. In most cantons you make an appointment at the **passport office** for this. A new photo is taken there, and you give your fingerprints if you are ordering a passport. For children, the parents must give their consent. The new document arrives by post after a few days. It costs money, and the price depends on the type of document.

If the document is lost on a journey, you report it to the local police. Then you contact the **Swiss embassy** or a consulate. There you get help to travel home, for example a provisional travel document. A **copy** or a photo of the document makes the process much easier.

gewusst: An identity card for children and young people under 18 is valid for five years, and for adults for ten years.
For some years now the Swiss passport has contained a chip with the person’s data.

teile.einleitung: A comic tells a story with lots of pictures that are read one after another. What the characters say is written in speech bubbles. There are comics for children and adults, and some characters are famous all over the world.
wichtigste: What a character says is written in a **speech bubble**.
Words such as “Bang!” or “Crash!” show a **sound**.
German-language comics are read from left to right and from top to bottom.
**Asterix** gets his strength from the magic potion.
**Snowy** is a dog, a white fox terrier.
The Swiss comic family **Moll** has existed since 1952; their dachshund is called Tschips.
**Garfield** the cat loves lasagne.

abschnitte.text: The **speech bubble** shows what a character says. A small tail points to the person who is speaking. Thoughts are often in a **thought bubble**, which looks like a cloud. Comics show noises with **sound words** such as “Bang!”, “Crash!” or “Whoosh!”. This way you can almost hear the bang as you read.

A comic is made up of many individual pictures called **panels**. German-language comics are read like a text: in each row **from left to right**, then the next row underneath. Between the pictures something often happens that you have to imagine yourself. Japanese comics, called **manga**, are read from right to left instead.

**Asterix** is a small Gaul from a village that holds out against the Romans. He gets his enormous strength from the **magic potion** made by the druid Getafix. He was created by René Goscinny and Albert Uderzo from France. **Tintin** is a young reporter from the comics by the Belgian artist Hergé. His faithful companion is **Snowy**, a white fox terrier.

The best-known Swiss comic family is the **Moll family**. Papa Moll has existed since **1952**; he was created by the illustrator Edith Oppenheim-Jonas. The family includes the three children Fritz, Willy and Evi and the dachshund **Tschips**. Papa Moll always wants to help, but things often go wrong. The comic character Titeuf, by the Geneva artist Zep, comes from French-speaking Switzerland.

**Garfield** is a fat, lazy cat from the USA. He likes sleeping, hates Mondays and loves eating **lasagne** most of all. Garfield appears in newspapers as a short **comic strip** with just a few pictures. As well as such strips, there are comic books, albums and whole novels in comic form, which are called **graphic novels**.

gewusst: The name Asterix refers to the little star symbol in writing called an “asterisk”.
Comics are also called the “ninth art”.

teile.einleitung: The Enlightenment was a period in the 18th century in which many people demanded to think for themselves instead of simply believing what the Church or rulers said. Reason was to guide life. These ideas shaped literature, science and politics throughout Europe, including in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement in the **18th century**.
In 1784 Immanuel Kant called it “man’s emergence from his self-incurred immaturity”.
Its motto is **“Sapere aude”**: “Have the courage to use your own understanding”.
Important values were reason, tolerance and education.
Bodmer and Breitinger from Zurich argued with Gottsched from Leipzig about the art of poetry.
Albrecht von Haller from Bern wrote the poem “Die Alpen” (The Alps) in 1729.

abschnitte.text: The name “Enlightenment” means that it should become light inside people’s heads. People should no longer follow authorities blindly but use their own understanding. In 1784 the philosopher **Immanuel Kant** wrote the essay “An Answer to the Question: What is Enlightenment?”. In it he calls the Enlightenment the emergence from self-incurred **immaturity**. Immature means someone who does not dare to think for themselves.

The Latin saying **“Sapere aude”** literally means “Dare to be wise”. It comes from the Roman poet Horace. Kant translated it as “Have the courage to use your own understanding”. This sentence became the motto of the whole period. The thinkers of the Enlightenment believed that education could make people freer and better.

The writers wanted to entertain people and teach them at the same time. That is why **fables**, in which animals show a lesson, were popular. Gotthold Ephraim Lessing wrote the play “Nathan the Wise”. In it, with the famous parable of the rings, he argues for **tolerance** between Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The Leipzig scholar Johann Christoph Gottsched laid down strict rules for poetry.

In Zurich, **Johann Jakob Bodmer** and **Johann Jakob Breitinger** disagreed with the scholar Gottsched. They defended imagination and the marvellous in poetry. The dispute became known as the literary quarrel between Leipzig and Zurich. **Albrecht von Haller** from Bern wrote the poem “Die Alpen” (The Alps) in 1729. It praises the simple life of the mountain people and awakened enthusiasm for the Swiss mountains.

The ideas of the Enlightenment also changed politics. Many people demanded rights for all people and limits on the power of rulers. These ideas influenced the American Declaration of Independence and the **French Revolution** of 1789. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who was born in Geneva, was also one of the well-known thinkers of this time. Human rights and democracy have important roots here.

gewusst: In France at this time a huge **encyclopedia** was created, which was meant to collect the knowledge of the world.
Haller’s poem “Die Alpen” helped to make travellers from all over Europe want to visit the Swiss mountains.

teile.einleitung: Active and passive are two ways of building a sentence. In the active, the focus is on who does something: the cook cuts the vegetables. In the passive, the focus is on what happens: the vegetables are cut by the cook.
wichtigste: In the active, what matters is who is acting.
In the passive, the action is more important than the person doing it.
The German process passive is formed with “werden” and the past participle (Partizip II).
The German state passive is formed with the auxiliary verb “sein”.
The accusative object of the active sentence becomes the subject in the passive.
The passive is often used in factual texts.
The technical term for active and passive is Genus Verbi (voice).

abschnitte.text: Many actions can be described from two points of view. In the **active**, the person acting is the subject: “Der Koch schneidet das Gemüse” (The cook cuts the vegetables). In the **passive**, the thing affected moves to the front: “Das Gemüse wird vom Koch geschnitten” (The vegetables are cut by the cook). The person acting can be named with “von” (by) or left out completely.

The most common passive in German is the **process passive** (Vorgangspassiv). It is formed with a form of “werden” and the past participle, for example “wird geschnitten” (is cut). The **accusative object** from the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence. The tense stays the same: the active example sentence above becomes the passive sentence with “wird … geschnitten”. In the perfect tense you get forms such as “geschrieben worden” (been written).

As well as the process passive, German has the **state passive** (Zustandspassiv). It is formed with the auxiliary verb “sein” and describes the result of an action. “Die Tür wird geschlossen” (The door is being closed) shows something happening. “Die Tür ist geschlossen” (The door is closed), on the other hand, shows the state afterwards. So you have to pay close attention to whether a process or a state is meant.

There is also a passive with no subject at all, the **impersonal passive**: “Am Samstag wird getanzt” (On Saturday there will be dancing). Here all that matters is that something happens, not who does it. Another form is the **recipient passive** with “bekommen” (to get): “Er bekommt das Paket geschickt” (He gets the parcel sent to him). Here the focus is on the person who receives something.

You find the passive very often in factual texts, newspaper reports and instructions. There the action is usually more important than the person doing it. An example is a sentence saying that a road is being rebuilt, because who exactly is building it often does not matter. But too many passive sentences make a text heavy, so a good mixture is best.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sentence form in which the subject does something itself.
A sentence form in which something happens to the subject.
A German verb form such as “geschnitten”, “geschrieben” or “gemacht” (cut, written, made).
A part of the sentence you ask about with “Wen?” or “Was?” (Whom? What?).

gewusst: Not every verb can form a passive; for example “haben” (to have) or “besitzen” (to own) cannot.
The word passive comes from the Latin “pati”, which means “to suffer” or “to undergo”.
Even verbs without an object, such as “tanzen” (to dance), can form an impersonal passive.

teile.einleitung: Where does the word “deutsch” (German) actually come from? It has a long history and originally simply meant “belonging to the people”.
wichtigste: The word “deutsch” goes back to the Old High German **“diutisc”**.
“diutisc” is derived from **“diot”**, which means “people”.
At first it meant the **language of the people**, as opposed to Latin.
Only later did it also become a name for the country and its people.
Other languages call the Germans something quite different, for example “allemand” in French.

abschnitte.text: In the early Middle Ages scholars and monks wrote almost only in **Latin**. But ordinary people spoke various Germanic dialects. A word was needed for this language of the people: **“diutisc”**, derived from “diot”, meaning “people”. So “deutsch” was at first not the name of a country but meant “the way the people speak”.

An important witness is **Notker** from the monastery of **St Gallen**. He lived around the year 1000 and translated Latin texts into the language of the people so that his pupils could understand them better. Because of this work he was given the nickname “the German”. The word for “German” already appears in his texts.

Over time the word came to mean not just the language but also the people who spoke it. Much later still, the name of the country **“Deutschland”** (Germany) came about. By the way, the word for “people” is also hidden in the old name **Dietrich**, which means something like “ruler of the people”.

Not all languages took over the word “deutsch”. The Italian **“tedesco”** does come from the same root. The French **“allemand”**, on the other hand, comes from the **Alemanni**, a Germanic people. The Alemanni also settled in what is now German-speaking Switzerland, which is why our dialects are called Alemannic.

gewusst: The English word “Dutch” has the same origin as “deutsch”.
The word “deutsch” first referred to a language and only much later to a country.

teile.einleitung: A letter is a written message to another person or to a company. Personal letters are written to friends and family, formal letters for example to authorities or companies. There are fixed rules for formal letters.
wichtigste: For an unknown company, the German greeting is “Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren” (Dear Sir or Madam).
In Switzerland formal letters end with “Freundliche Grüsse” (Kind regards).
The polite German forms “Sie”, “Ihnen” and “Ihr” (you, your) are always written with a **capital letter**.
“du” and “dein” (informal you, your) are written with a small letter, though a capital is also allowed in letters.
The place and date are in the letterhead, and the **subject line** comes before the greeting.
After a greeting with a comma, German continues with a small letter, except for nouns.
With a **cover letter** you apply for an apprenticeship.

abschnitte.text: You write a **personal letter** to people you know well. There you may write casually, for example “Liebe Lea” (Dear Lea) and “Herzliche Grüsse” (Warm wishes). You write a **formal letter** to companies, schools or authorities. There are fixed rules for its structure and language. This makes the letter seem polite and tidy.

At the top are the sender’s address and the recipient’s address. Then come the **place and date**, so that later you know when and where the letter was written. After that comes the **subject line**: it says in a few words what the letter is about. Only then comes the **greeting**. At the end there is the closing phrase, the name and the signature.

If you do not know the name of the person to contact, you write **“Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren”** (Dear Sir or Madam). If you know it, it is for example “Sehr geehrte Frau Meier” (Dear Ms Meier). After the greeting there is a **comma**. That is why in German you continue on the next line with a small letter, unless the first word is a noun or the polite form. At the end, in Switzerland it is usually **“Freundliche Grüsse”** (Kind regards).

The polite form **“Sie”** (you) and the forms that go with it, such as “Ihnen” or “Ihr”, are always written with a capital letter. This shows the difference from “sie”, meaning they, several people. According to the rules, the words **“du”** and “dein” (informal you, your) are written with a small letter. In letters and emails a capital letter is also allowed. Many people find that especially friendly.

Anyone looking for an **apprenticeship** writes a **cover letter**, also called a motivation letter. In it you explain why you are interested in the job and why you are suitable. Together with your **CV** and school reports it forms your **application file**. A clean letter without mistakes makes a good first impression.

gewusst: In Switzerland postcodes have four digits.
With Swiss Post, a letter sent by A Post arrives faster than one sent by B Post.

teile.einleitung: **Matches** are small wooden sticks with a head that catches fire when it is rubbed. They are useful for lighting a candle or a fire. Because a fire can quickly start from them, they belong in the hands of adults.
wichtigste: A match is made of a wooden stick and a match head.
A safety match only lights if you strike it on the striking surface of the box.
If you find matches, you give them to an adult.
Fire can quickly lead to a blaze.
In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on 118.
Matches are not toys.

abschnitte.text: The **match head** contains substances that get hot and ignite when rubbed. On the **striking surface** of the box there is red **phosphorus**. If you strike the head across it, the friction makes so much heat that a small flame flares up. Then the wooden stick carries on burning.

In the past there were matches that would light on any rough surface. They contained poisonous **white phosphorus**, which made the workers in the factories ill. In the 19th century the **safety match** was developed in Sweden. It only lights on the matching striking surface. In 1906 several countries agreed in a convention in **Bern** to ban white phosphorus in matches.

abschnitte.titel: What do you do if you find matches?
abschnitte.text: If matches are lying around somewhere, you do not take them to play with. You give them to an **adult**. Even a tiny flame can set curtains, paper or dry grass alight. A fire becomes big and dangerous in a short time. The **smoke** is dangerous too, because it is poisonous.

If there is a fire, the rule is: **alert, rescue, extinguish**. First you shout loudly for help and get someone to call the fire brigade on **118**. Then you get yourself to safety and go outside. If there is smoke, you stay close to the floor, because the air is better there. You never go back into a burning house.

gewusst: A match only burns for a few seconds before it reaches your fingers.
The Bern Convention of 1906 was one of the first international agreements to protect workers.

teile.einleitung: Many German words are made up of two words. Often there is a small sound between the two parts that joins them, like the “s” in “Arbeitsplatz” (workplace). This joining piece is called a linking element.
wichtigste: A word made of other words is called a compound.
The linking element sits where two parts of the word meet.
Common linking elements are s, es, n, en, er and e.
A linking element is not a case ending like the genitive.
Many compounds manage without a linking element at all, for example “Haustür” (front door).
Switzerland has some linking elements of its own, as in “Zugsverspätung” (train delay).

abschnitte.text: In German you can join words together like building blocks. This creates **compounds**, for example “Haustür” (front door), “Schulweg” (way to school) or “Arbeitsplatz” (workplace). The last part is called the **base word**; it decides the word class and the gender. The first part is called the **modifier**; it says more precisely what is meant. So an “Arbeitsplatz” is a place where you work.

The **joint** is the seam between the two parts. Sometimes there is an extra sound there, the **linking element**. Examples are “Arbeit**s**platz” (workplace), “Sonne**n**schein” (sunshine), “Kind**er**garten” (nursery school), “Tag**es**licht” (daylight) and “Hund**e**hütte” (dog kennel). If there is nothing in between, as in “Haustür”, it is called a **zero link**.

The “s” in “Arbeitsplatz” looks like a genitive ending, but it is not one. “Arbeit” (work) is feminine and forms its genitive without an “s”: “der Arbeit”. So the linking element has no grammatical meaning in the sentence. It often makes the word easier to pronounce. Which link a word gets does not follow a simple rule; people usually just learn it along the way.

In Swiss Standard German there are some links that are different in Germany. In Switzerland people say “Zugsverspätung” (train delay) or “Zugsabfahrt” (train departure), while in Germany it is usually “Zugverspätung”. “Schweinsbraten” (roast pork) with a linking s is also usual in Switzerland and Austria. Differences like these are among the **Helvetisms**. Both forms are correct in their own country.

gewusst: Sometimes a letter even disappears when words are put together: “Schule” (school) and “Buch” (book) become “Schulbuch” (school book).
A word such as “Bundesrat” (Federal Council) contains the linking element “es”.

teile.einleitung: An allomorph is a variant of a morpheme. So different forms have the same job in a word but look different. A good example is the plural endings in German.
wichtigste: A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that has a meaning or a job.
Allomorphs are different forms of the same morpheme.
The German plural endings “-e”, “-er” and “-en” are allomorphs.
“Tische” (tables), “Kinder” (children) and “Frauen” (women) all express the plural.
Which form is used depends on the word.

abschnitte.text: Words can be broken down into smaller building blocks. The smallest building block that has a **meaning** or a **grammatical job** is called a **morpheme**. The German word “Kinder” (children) is made of “Kind” (child) and the ending “-er”. “Kind” carries the meaning, and “-er” shows that there is more than one. Both parts are morphemes.

Sometimes a morpheme has several forms. These variants are called **allomorphs**. The best-known example is the **plural**. In German there are various endings for it: **“-e”** as in “Tische” (tables), **“-er”** as in “Kinder” (children), **“-en”** as in “Frauen” (women) and **“-s”** as in “Autos” (cars). They all have the same job, namely to express the plural.

Which allomorph is used depends on the particular **word**. Often you simply have to learn it. Sometimes the **sound**, that is the sounds around it, also decides. In English, for example, the plural ending sounds slightly different in “cats”, “dogs” and “horses”, even though it is written almost the same. The science that studies such building blocks is called **morphology**.

gewusst: The word allomorph comes from Greek: “allos” means “other” and “morphe” means “form”.

teile.einleitung: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm were two brothers from Germany who collected and wrote down many old fairy tales around 200 years ago. Their “Children’s and Household Tales” is one of the best-known books in the world. But the brothers were also important language researchers.
wichtigste: The Brothers Grimm were called **Jacob and Wilhelm**.
They came from **Germany** and lived, among other places, in Kassel.
Their collection is called **“Children’s and Household Tales”**.
Their fairy tales include Little Red Riding Hood, Hansel and Gretel, Rapunzel and Rumpelstiltskin.
They also began a large **German Dictionary**.
Jacob Grimm is considered one of the founders of **German studies**.

abschnitte.text: **Jacob Grimm** was born in 1785 and his brother **Wilhelm** in 1786. Both were born in Hanau in Hesse. They studied law and were very interested in old texts and language. For a long time they lived and worked in **Kassel**. The two brothers stayed close to each other all their lives.

The Brothers Grimm had people tell them fairy tales and wrote them down. They heard many stories from women and men around them. In 1812 the first volume of the **“Children’s and Household Tales”** was published. In later editions it was mainly Wilhelm who revised the texts so that they sounded more beautiful and suited children better. The fairy tales were translated into a great many languages.

**Little Red Riding Hood** takes cake and wine to her sick grandmother in the forest. The first time, **Hansel** scatters white pebbles that shine in the moonlight so that he and Gretel can find their way home. **Rapunzel** lets her long hair down from the tower that has no stairs. In **The Frog Prince** the king’s daughter drops a golden ball into the well. And in **Rumpelstiltskin** the miller’s daughter has to spin straw into gold.

The Brothers Grimm were not only collectors of fairy tales. They researched the history of the German language. Jacob Grimm is considered one of the founders of **German studies**, the study of the German language and literature. Together they began the **German Dictionary**. It was so huge that it was only finished more than a hundred years after their deaths.

As professors in Göttingen, in 1837 the brothers and five colleagues protested against a king who had abolished the constitution. This group is called the **Göttingen Seven**. The professors lost their jobs because of it. Later Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm lived in **Berlin**. Many people admired them for standing up for justice and freedom.

gewusst: The Brothers Grimm appeared on the former 1000 Deutschmark note.
The Brothers Grimm’s German Dictionary was only completed in 1961.

teile.einleitung: A report gives factual information about an event that really happened. It answers the most important questions without decorating anything. Reports are found in newspapers, at insurance companies and at school.
wichtigste: A report answers the **W questions** (in English the 5 Ws): Who? What? When? Where? How? Why?
The language is **factual and precise**.
Feelings and decorations do not belong in a report.
The events are told in **chronological order**.
The opening under the headline of a newspaper report is called the **lead**.
A report is a kind of **factual text**.

abschnitte.text: A good report answers the **W questions**: Who was involved? What happened? When and where did it happen? How did it happen? Why did it come about? With these questions you can check whether the report is complete. If an answer is missing, an important piece of information is missing. Often people also ask about the consequences.

A report gives information about **facts**. That is why you write factually and precisely. A good sentence would be: “On Monday at 8 o’clock two bikes collided.” It gives the time and what happened without feelings. Sentences such as “It was terrible!” or sound words such as “Crash!”, on the other hand, belong in a story. In German you usually write in the **simple past** (Präteritum).

After an accident the insurance company often needs an **accident report**. It should record what happened as objectively as possible. The events are described in **chronological order** so that everything can be followed exactly. Your own feelings and guesses do not belong in it. A small sketch can also help.

In a newspaper a report often begins with a short opening in bold print under the headline. This is called the **lead** or standfirst. It sums up the most important points in a few sentences. Anyone who reads only the lead already knows what it is about. Then come the details, the most important first.

abschnitte.titel: Reports at school and in an apprenticeship
abschnitte.text: After a **taster apprenticeship** or a work placement, people often write a **placement report**. In it you record factually which kinds of work you got to know in the company. It is handed in at school or used for job applications. Because a report gives information about a real event, it counts as a **factual text** and not as a made-up, literary text.

gewusst: The police also write reports after operations; in Switzerland these are called Rapporte.
Journalists often build reports like an upside-down pyramid: the most important thing right at the top.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who moves to another municipality must deregister with the old municipality and register with the new one. This way the authorities always know where someone lives.
wichtigste: You deregister at the residents’ registration office of your previous municipality.
In the new municipality you register within a time limit.
The canton sets the time limit for registering; it is often 14 days.
In many municipalities you can also report a move online.
Swiss citizens usually need their certificate of origin to register.
The post office, health insurance fund and other offices should also be told the new address.

abschnitte.text: Every municipality in Switzerland keeps a **register of residents**. It shows who lives in the municipality. The **residents’ registration office** is responsible for it; sometimes it is called residents’ services. The municipality needs this information, for example, for taxes, for school and for the right to vote. That is why it needs to know when someone leaves or arrives.

Anyone moving away deregisters with the **old municipality**. You say when you are moving out and where to. Swiss citizens get back their **certificate of origin** if it was deposited with the municipality. The certificate of origin shows in which municipality you have your place of citizenship. Deregistering is also important when moving abroad.

At your new place of residence you register **within the time limit** set by the canton. This is often 14 days after moving in. You bring an identity document, your certificate of origin or, for foreign nationals, the residence permit, and sometimes the tenancy agreement. In many municipalities you can conveniently deregister and register online with the **eUmzugCH** service.

Once you have dealt with the municipality, not everything is done yet. The **post office** can forward letters to your new address. The health insurance fund, bank, employer and school also need the new address. Anyone who has a dog or owns a car must re-register these too. A list helps you not to forget anything.

gewusst: For taxes in Switzerland, what usually counts is where you live at the end of the year: if you move in December, you pay tax for the whole year in the new place.
There are more than 2000 municipalities in Switzerland, and each keeps its own register of residents.

teile.einleitung: Old High German is the oldest written stage of High German. It is dated roughly from 750 to 1050. After it comes Middle High German.
wichtigste: Old High German is dated roughly from 750 to 1050.
It is the oldest stage of High German recorded in writing.
It was followed by Middle High German and later New High German.
Old High German was not a single language but consisted of several dialects.
Many texts were written in monasteries, including in St Gallen.

abschnitte.text: Languages change over time. That is why different **stages** of German are distinguished. The oldest stage recorded in writing is **Old High German**, from about **750 to 1050**. It is followed by **Middle High German**, the language of the age of knights, and later by **New High German**, from which today’s language developed.

Old High German was **not a single language**. There were several dialects, for example **Alemannic**, Bavarian and Franconian. There was not yet a common written language. Alemannic was spoken in the area of today’s German-speaking Switzerland, in south-west Germany and in Alsace. The **Swiss German dialects** come from this Alemannic.

At that time it was mainly **monks** who could read and write. That is why most texts were written in **monasteries**, and often their purpose was to understand Latin texts. Among the best-known examples are the **Abrogans**, a word list, and the **Hildebrandslied** (Lay of Hildebrand). In the monastery of **St Gallen**, the monk **Notker the German** translated Latin works into Old High German around the year 1000.

gewusst: The word “deutsch” (German) goes back to an old word meaning “belonging to the people”.
A person today would hardly understand an Old High German text without practice.

teile.einleitung: In online shopping you pay over the internet for goods, services or things in games and apps. Even if you only tap a button, it costs real money.
wichtigste: Purchases in games and apps also cost **real money**.
Children ask their **parents** first before every purchase.
Such purchases in apps are called **in-app purchases**.
Parents can block purchases on devices or require a password.
In Switzerland there is no general right to cancel online purchases.
Watch out for fake online shops.

abschnitte.text: You can buy almost anything on the internet: clothes, books, games, music or holidays. You choose something, put it in the **basket** and pay, for example with a card or a payment app. It is convenient because you do not have to go to a shop. But precisely because it is so easy, you can quickly spend more money than you planned.

Many games on a tablet or mobile phone are free at first. Later, though, they offer coins, gems, characters or new levels for money. These are called **in-app purchases**. The colourful game currencies do not look like money, but they cost **real francs**. That is why you always ask your **parents** first before you buy anything.

Children and young people under 18 are usually only allowed to make bigger purchases **with their parents’ consent**. Parents can set mobile phones and tablets so that every purchase needs a **password** or is blocked completely. It helps to agree together how much money you may spend on games, for example from your own **pocket money**.

Unlike in the European Union, in Switzerland there is **no general right of withdrawal** for online purchases. Whether you can return something depends on the shop’s **terms and conditions**. That is why you read what the seller says about it before buying. Many shops offer returns voluntarily.

There are **fake online shops** that take your money and deliver nothing. Warning signs are extremely low prices, no address for the seller and payment in advance only. Emails or messages asking for passwords or card details are also often fraud. This is called **phishing**. If in doubt, ask an adult.

gewusst: Some games are designed so that you keep spending small amounts, which add up to a lot of money.
Experts advise always converting game currencies into francs in your head so that you see the real price.

teile.einleitung: In German, the words “Das” and “Dass” sound exactly the same but are spelt differently. The form with one s can be an article or a pronoun, while the form with a double s is always a conjunction. With a simple replacement test you can almost always find the right spelling.
wichtigste: The form with one s can be an **article**, a **relative pronoun** or a **demonstrative pronoun**.
The form with a double s is a **conjunction**, a joining word meaning “that”.
If the word can be replaced by “welches” (which) or “dieses” (this), it is written with one s.
If the replacement does not work, the double-s form is usually meant.
The double-s form introduces a subordinate clause, which is separated off by a comma.
The conjunction “sodass” (so that) is always written with a double s.

abschnitte.text: The one-s form can be a **definite article**, like “the” in English. Then it comes directly before a noun: “Das Buch liegt hier” means “The book is lying here”. An article is always written with one s. Here you can usually replace it with “dieses” (this). If a noun comes straight after it, the matter is clear.

The one-s form can also stand in for a noun. In the sentence “Das Velo, das dort steht, gehört mir” (The bike that is standing there belongs to me), the second one refers to the bike. It is a **relative pronoun** and can be replaced by **“welches”** (which). In “Das glaube ich” (I believe that), the word points to something specific. It is a **demonstrative pronoun**, a pointing word, and can be replaced by “dieses” (this).

The double-s form is a subordinating **conjunction**, meaning “that”. It joins a main clause to a subordinate clause, as in “It is nice that you are here”. In German there is usually a **comma** before it. It often follows verbs such as to say, to hope, to know or to believe. So in “He says that he is tired” the German word for “that” must be written with a double s; writing it with one s here is a typical mistake.

If you are unsure, do the **replacement test**. Try replacing the word with “welches” (which) or “dieses” (this). If the sentence still sounds right, you write it with one s. If it sounds wrong, you write it with a double s. Example: “Ich hoffe, welches du kommst” (I hope which you come) sounds wrong, so here the double-s form is correct.

abschnitte.titel: At the start of a sentence, and sodass
abschnitte.text: A subordinate clause with the double-s form can also come at the beginning: “Dass du kommst, freut mich” means “That you are coming makes me happy”. Then it is written with a capital letter, because it is at the start of the sentence. If a joining word expresses a result, you write **“sodass”** or, as two words, “so dass”, as in “It rained heavily, so that we stayed inside”. In both cases you always need a double s.

gewusst: Before the spelling reform of 1996, the conjunction was written in Germany with a different letter at the end, the sharp s (Eszett), but in Switzerland it had long been written with ss.
Mixing up the one-s and double-s forms is one of the most common spelling mistakes in German.

teile.einleitung: “Grüezi” is the best-known greeting in German-speaking Switzerland. With this little word you show other people that you notice them and that you are being friendly to them.
wichtigste: “Grüezi” is a greeting from German-speaking Switzerland.
You say it mainly to people you address formally with “Sie”.
If you greet several people, you say “Grüezi mitenand”.
Among friends and in the family people tend to say “Hoi” or “Sali”.
In western Switzerland people greet each other with “Bonjour”, and in Ticino with “Buongiorno”.
A greeting in the stairwell makes living together friendlier.

abschnitte.text: The word “Grüezi” is a short form. In the past people said “Gott grüez i”, which means roughly “God greet you”. Over time the greeting got shorter and shorter. Today hardly anyone thinks of the old meaning. It is similar with the southern German “Grüss Gott”.

In Switzerland it depends on whom you are greeting. You say **Grüezi** to adults you do not know well, that is to people you address formally with **“Sie”**. To friends and children people tend to say **Hoi**, **Sali** or **Salü**. In Bern you often hear **Grüessech**. When saying goodbye, people say for example “Uf Widerluege” (goodbye) or “Tschüss” (bye).

Switzerland has four national languages. In **western Switzerland** people greet each other with “Bonjour”, in **Ticino** with “Buongiorno” or “Ciao”. In Romansh people say **“Allegra”**. Anyone travelling in another part of the country will please people if they greet them in their language.

A greeting is a sign of **respect**. Anyone who greets the neighbours in the stairwell is showing: I see you, we live here together. That way you get to know each other over time and are more likely to help each other. On hikes in the mountains, even people who do not know each other at all often greet each other. A friendly look goes with it.

gewusst: Abroad, “Grüezi” is seen as typically Swiss and often appears on postcards and souvenirs.
In Romansh the greeting is “Allegra”, which means something like “Be glad”.

teile.einleitung: German grammar describes the rules by which words are formed and put together into sentences. It explains word classes, tenses, cases and sentence structure. If you know the grammar, you can speak more clearly and write with fewer mistakes.
wichtigste: Grammar is the set of rules of a language.
German has four cases: nominative, genitive, dative and accusative.
There are six tenses, from the present to the future perfect.
The word classes include nouns, verbs, adjectives, pronouns and conjunctions.
In standard German the preposition “wegen” (because of) takes the genitive.
After “als” in a comparison the nominative is used: “Er ist grösser als ich” (He is taller than I am).
In Switzerland standard German applies with a few special features, such as ss instead of Eszett.

abschnitte.text: **Grammar** is something like the rules of the game of a language. It explains how words change their form and how they are put together into sentences. It includes **morphology**, which deals with word forms, and sentence structure, also called syntax. The most important reference work for the German language is the **Duden**.

The words of a language are divided into **word classes**. Nouns name things, living beings or ideas, verbs describe actions and adjectives describe qualities. Pronouns stand in place of a noun; for example, “dessen” (whose) in “der Mann, dessen Hund bellt” (the man whose dog is barking) is a **relative pronoun**. Words such as “obwohl” (although) or “weil” (because) are called subordinating conjunctions and introduce subordinate clauses.

German has six **tenses**: present, simple past, perfect, pluperfect, future and future perfect. The pluperfect of “ich gehe” (I go) is “ich war gegangen” (I had gone) and describes something that happened before another past action. “Sie wird angekommen sein” (She will have arrived) is the **future perfect** and expresses that something will be finished in the future. There are also verb forms such as the present participle, for example “lachend” (laughing).

Nouns, pronouns and adjectives change depending on the **case**. There are four cases: nominative, genitive, dative and accusative. Prepositions often decide the case: “mit” (with) takes the dative, “für” (for) the accusative, and “wegen” (because of) the genitive in standard German. So the correct form is “wegen des Regens” (because of the rain). In comparisons with “als” (than) the nominative is used: “Er ist grösser als ich” (He is taller than I am).

A **light verb construction** (Funktionsverbgefüge) is a fixed combination of noun and verb, for example “zur Verfügung stellen” (to make available) instead of “bereitstellen” (to provide). Such expressions often appear in official texts. In Switzerland people speak dialect in everyday life but usually write standard German. Swiss standard German has a few special features, such as words like “Velo” (bike) or “parkieren” (to park) and ss instead of Eszett.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rules for how a language is built.
A group of words with similar jobs, such as nouns or verbs.
The grammatical form of a word, for example the dative.
The study of sentence structure.
A fixed combination of noun and verb, for example the German “in Frage stellen” (to call into question).

gewusst: The word grammar comes from the Greek “grammatike”, the art of reading and writing.
In the Middle Ages grammar was one of the seven liberal arts taught at schools.
In the dialect of many Swiss people there is hardly any simple past; the past is usually told using the perfect.

teile.einleitung: How long does a story last? Here we distinguish between two times: the **discourse time**, which is how long it takes to read, and the **story time**, which is how long the plot lasts.
wichtigste: The **discourse time** is the time you need to read or tell the story.
The **story time** is the period of time the plot covers.
You can read a book about many years in just a few hours.
Skipping time **compresses** it; describing it in detail **stretches** it.
With **flashbacks** a story jumps into the past.

abschnitte.text: The **discourse time** is measured in pages or in reading time. The **story time** is how long the plot lasts within the story. A novel can describe a character’s whole life over 80 years, but you read it in a few hours. The other way round, a single minute can be described over many pages.

If the discourse time is shorter than the story time, this is called **time compression**: “Three years passed.” If both last about the same, the telling **matches** the time, for example in a conversation in direct speech. If the discourse time is longer, it is called **time stretching**. This happens when an exciting moment is described with lots of thoughts and details.

Not every story is told in order. In a **flashback** you find out what happened earlier. A **flash-forward** gives away what will happen later. Jumps like these make a story exciting and help you understand the characters better.

gewusst: The novel “Ulysses” by James Joyce tells of a single day in 1904 over many hundreds of pages.
A short sentence such as “Many years later” can skip decades in a story.

teile.einleitung: A smoke alarm is a small device on the ceiling that detects smoke. As soon as smoke gets into it, it beeps very loudly. This means people are warned of a fire in time, even when they are asleep.
wichtigste: When you are asleep you cannot smell smoke.
The smoke alarm gives a very loud warning sound when there is smoke.
In a fire, the poisonous smoke is usually more dangerous than the flames.
Smoke alarms belong on the ceiling, ideally in the middle of the room.
You should test the alarm regularly and change the battery.
In Switzerland the emergency number for fire is 118.

abschnitte.text: A fire produces a lot of **smoke** with poisonous gases. Just a few breaths can make you unconscious. Many people who die in fires are overcome not by the fire but by the **smoke**. When you are asleep you notice nothing, because your **nose** does not warn you then.

Inside the smoke alarm there is a small **measuring chamber** with light. If smoke gets in, the light is scattered and the alarm goes **off**. Because smoke rises, it is fitted on the **ceiling**. Bedrooms, children’s rooms and the hall are especially important.

Most smoke alarms have a **test button**. If you press it, the device beeps. This is how you check whether it still works. If the alarm beeps quietly and regularly, the **battery** is usually almost flat. After about ten years you should replace the whole device.

If you hear the alarm, you leave the flat immediately and close the **doors** behind you. If there is a lot of smoke, you move low down near the floor, because the air is better there. Never use the **lift**. Outside you call the **fire brigade** on **118**.

gewusst: In Switzerland smoke alarms in flats are not compulsory everywhere, but accident prevention experts recommend them.
In Germany smoke alarms are compulsory in all federal states.

teile.einleitung: In a library you can borrow books, magazines, films and audiobooks or read them there. Almost every Swiss municipality or school has one. Some libraries are very old and are World Heritage Sites.
wichtigste: In a library you can **borrow** books.
For this you usually need a **library card**.
Someone who works there is called a **librarian**.
Anyone who brings a book back late often pays a **late fee**.
In a **toy library** (Ludothek) you borrow games.
The **Abbey Library of St Gallen** has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

abschnitte.text: In the library you borrow books for a certain time. For this you usually need a **library card**. This way the library knows who has which book. Every book has a **return date**. Anyone who keeps it too long has to pay a **late fee** in many libraries. You can often renew the loan too.

**Librarians** arrange the books and help people look for them. Every book has a **shelf mark**, a kind of address on the shelf. On the shelf the books stand side by side, so you only see the narrow **spine** with the title and author. With a computer catalogue you can quickly find out whether a book is there. Today many libraries also lend e-books.

In Switzerland many municipalities have a **Ludothek**, a toy library. There you do not borrow books but board games, toys and ride-on vehicles. The word comes from the Latin “ludus”, game. This lets you try out lots of games without buying them. That saves money and space.

abschnitte.titel: The Abbey Library of St Gallen
abschnitte.text: The **Abbey Library of St Gallen** is one of the oldest libraries in the world. It belonged to the monastery of St Gallen and owns very old books written by hand. Its magnificent Baroque hall is famous. The **abbey precinct** has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1983. The **Swiss National Library** in Bern, on the other hand, collects publications about Switzerland and from Switzerland.

There were already large libraries in ancient times. The most famous was the **Library of Alexandria** in Egypt. Before printing existed, monks copied books by hand in monasteries. That is why books were very valuable at that time. The word “Bibliothek” (library) comes from Greek and means roughly “bookcase”.

gewusst: Above the entrance to the Abbey Library of St Gallen there is a Greek word meaning “pharmacy of the soul”.
In the Abbey Library of St Gallen visitors wear felt slippers to protect the wooden floor.

teile.einleitung: Empty glass bottles and jars are not rubbish but a valuable raw material. Anyone who takes them to the bottle bank helps to make new glass from them.
wichtigste: Empty bottles and jam jars belong at the bottle bank.
Glass can be melted down and shaped again and again.
Waste glass is sorted by the colours clear, green and brown.
Each colour becomes glass of the same colour again.
You remove lids and corks before putting glass in.
Drinking glasses, window glass and porcelain do not belong in the bottle bank.

abschnitte.text: An empty **jam jar**, a wine bottle or a little vinegar bottle does not belong in the rubbish bag. Almost every municipality has a **bottle bank** with large containers. That is where you put the glass in. You do not have to rinse it thoroughly, but it should be empty. You take off metal lids and corks first.

The containers usually have three openings: for **clear**, **green** and **brown** glass. The colours are melted down separately. This makes glass of exactly the same colour again. Even a few coloured pieces would discolour clear glass. Glass of other colours, for example blue, usually goes in with the green glass.

Glass is made from **quartz sand**, soda and lime. Waste glass is crushed, cleaned and melted at very high temperatures. New bottles and jars are shaped from it. The special thing is that glass does not lose quality in the process. It can be recycled **as often as you like**. Because broken glass melts more easily than the raw materials, recycling also saves energy.

abschnitte.titel: What does not belong in it
abschnitte.text: Not all glass may go into the container. **Drinking glasses**, window glass, mirrors, light bulbs, ceramics and **porcelain** have a different make-up and melt differently. Even small pieces of them can ruin a whole load of new glass. These things belong in the general rubbish or in the collection for building rubble, depending on the municipality. Also, you only put glass in at the permitted times, because it is noisy.

gewusst: In Switzerland a very large share of glass bottles is collected and recycled, well over nine out of ten.
Recycled glass is as good as new: a bottle can become a bottle again and again.

teile.einleitung: For many children, the way to school is the first journey they make on their own. On the way they learn to move safely in traffic. In Switzerland the saying “Warte, luege, lose, laufe” (wait, look, listen, walk) helps with this.
wichtigste: At the edge of the road you first stop and wait.
“Luege” means look, “lose” means listen.
Only when everything is clear do you cross the road.
It is best to cross the road at the zebra crossing.
Light-coloured clothes and reflective strips make children easier to see.
Many children already go to nursery school alone or with friends.

abschnitte.text: The saying comes from **Swiss German**. First you **wait** at the edge of the road. Then you **look** left and right and **listen** to hear whether a car is coming. Only when the vehicles have stopped or the road is clear do you **walk** briskly across. You should not run, or you might trip.

In Switzerland **zebra crossings** are yellow. There pedestrians have **right of way**. Even so, you wait until the cars really stop. A car needs a **braking distance** and cannot stop immediately. It helps to look the driver in the eye.

It is best for parents to practise the way to school with their child before the child goes alone. You choose the **safest** route, even if it is a bit longer. Children are smaller than adults and are hard to **see** between parked cars. That is why you cross the road where you can see well and be seen.

Many children walk to school with **friends**. The way to school is not only a route but also time to chat and discover things. The **municipality** makes sure that the way to school is reasonable. For very long or dangerous routes there is sometimes a **school bus**.

gewusst: In Switzerland many nursery school children wear a glowing triangle or a high-visibility vest so that they can be seen easily.
Children can only judge the speeds and distances of cars properly from about the age of ten.

teile.einleitung: German words such as “Wasser” (water), “Tasse” (cup) or “Fluss” (river) are written with a **double s**. In Switzerland this is particularly easy, because the sharp s (Eszett) is never used here and ss is always written instead.
wichtigste: After a **short vowel** you often write ss, as in “Wasser” (water).
In Switzerland you **always write ss**, never the sharp s.
In Germany and Austria the sharp s is used after long vowels.
That is why in Switzerland people write “gross” (big), “heiss” (hot) and “Strasse” (street).
The conjunction **“dass”** (that) is written with ss everywhere.

abschnitte.text: Say the word slowly and listen carefully. If the vowel before the s is **short**, two s usually follow. This applies to “Wasser” (water), “Tasse” (cup), “Kissen” (cushion), “Schlüssel” (key), “Nuss” (nut) and “Schloss” (castle). You can also hear it when you split the word into syllables: “Was-ser”, “Tas-se”. This rule applies throughout the German-speaking world.

In Germany there is still a special letter, the **sharp s** (Eszett). There it is written after long vowels and after sounds such as “ei” or “au”. In Switzerland this letter is not used; people simply write **ss**. That is why in Switzerland people write “gross” (big), “heiss” (hot), “Fuss” (foot) and “Strasse” (street). This applies in schools, newspapers and public offices.

The sharp s gradually disappeared in Switzerland in the 20th century. First schools stopped using it, and later the newspapers too. The “Neue Zürcher Zeitung” was one of the last to switch, in 1974. In Liechtenstein, too, people write ss today. One reason was probably that Swiss typewriters needed room for French and Italian letters.

Here are some German words with ss: Wasser, Tasse, Kissen, Schlüssel, Nuss, Schloss, Fluss, essen (to eat), wissen (to know). And typically Swiss: gross, heiss, Fuss, Strasse, Gruss (greeting). A trick for the word “dass”: if you can replace it with “welches” (which), you write “das” with one s. Otherwise you write “dass”.

gewusst: In Switzerland “Masse” is written both for a large quantity and for measurements, as in “Massband” (tape measure). In Germany you can see the difference in the spelling; in Switzerland only from the context.
Since 2017 there has also officially been a capital letter for the sharp s, but it is not needed in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Early New High German is a stage of the German language that is dated roughly from 1350 to 1650. During this time the language of the Middle Ages slowly changed into the German we know today.
wichtigste: Early New High German lasted roughly from 1350 to 1650.
It comes between Middle High German and New High German.
Printing helped a shared written language to spread.
Martin Luther’s translation of the Bible was read very widely and shaped the language.
In this period “min niuwes hus” became “mein neues Haus” (my new house).
The Swiss dialects have kept many old sounds, such as “Huus” for “Haus” (house).

abschnitte.text: Languages are always changing. That is why experts divide the history of German into **language stages**: Old High German, Middle High German, Early New High German and New High German. **Early New High German** forms the bridge between the language of the knights and minstrels and the German of today. The boundaries cannot be drawn precisely, so people say “roughly 1350 to 1650”.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz invented **printing** with movable type. Now books could be made much faster and more cheaply. Printers wanted as many people as possible to be able to read their books, so they adapted the spelling. The **Reformation** brought many pamphlets and sermons to the people. Martin Luther’s translation of the **Bible** into German became especially important.

Many sounds changed during this time. The long vowels i, u and ü turned into the double sounds ei, au and eu. This change is called **diphthongisation**: “zit” became “Zeit” (time) and “hus” became “Haus” (house). The other way round, some double sounds turned into simple long vowels, as with “guot”, which became “gut” (good). This second change is called **monophthongisation**.

The Swiss dialects did not take on the new double sounds. That is why in Swiss German people still say “Ziit”, “Huus” and “Lüüt” (people) today. A great deal was printed in Switzerland during this time, too. In 1531 Christoph Froschauer in Zurich published a complete German Bible, the **Zurich Bible**. Over time, the shared written language also became established in Switzerland.

gewusst: Our phrase “mein neues Haus” (my new house) would have sounded roughly like “min niuwes hus” in the Middle Ages.
The habit of writing nouns with a capital letter only spread gradually in the early modern period.

teile.einleitung: The internet connects computers all over the world. You can use it to learn, play and talk to others, but you also see things there that are frightening or not true.
wichtigste: The internet is a worldwide network of computers.
You can find knowledge, games, videos and news there.
Not everything on the internet is true or made for children.
If something frightens you, you tell an adult.
You do not give away personal details such as your address or phone number.
Children and young people can reach the Pro Juventute advice service on **147**.

abschnitte.text: The **internet** is a huge network. Millions of computers, mobile phones and other devices are connected to each other through it. The data travels through cables, by radio and even via satellites. The **World Wide Web** with its websites is only one part of it. Emails and video calls also run over the internet.

abschnitte.titel: What you can do with it
abschnitte.text: On the internet you can look up almost anything: how an animal lives, what time the train leaves or what the weather will be like. You can listen to music, watch films, play games and stay in touch with family and friends. Many schools use the internet for lessons. It is important to agree your **screen time** with your parents.

Sometimes on the internet you see pictures or videos that are shocking or make you sad. That is not your fault. It is best to close the window and tell an **adult** you trust, for example your parents or your teacher. Talking about fear helps. If you would rather talk to someone you do not know, you can call **147** in Switzerland.

Anyone can write something on the internet. That is why not everything is **true**. Some news is made up; this is called **fake news**. It helps to ask: who wrote this? Does it also appear in other, well-known places? People in chats are also not always who they claim to be.

On the internet, do not give **personal data** such as your address, school or phone number to strangers. Do not send photos to people you do not know. Never meet up alone with someone you only know from the internet. A good password protects your accounts.

gewusst: The first computers were already linked into a network in the USA around 1969, and the internet later grew out of it.
The World Wide Web was invented around 1990 at the research centre CERN near Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The **first sound shift** was a big change in pronunciation a very long time ago. Because of it, the Germanic languages, which include German and English, became different from Latin or Greek.
wichtigste: The first or **Germanic sound shift** separated Germanic from the other Indo-European languages.
It happened more than 2000 years ago; the exact date is unknown.
For example, p became f: Latin “pater”, English “father”.
K became h: Latin “centum”, German “hundert” (hundred).
**Jacob Grimm** described the rules in 1822; this is called **Grimm’s law**.
In 1875, **Karl Verner** explained apparent exceptions with stress.

abschnitte.text: Many languages of Europe and Asia are related to each other. This family is called **Indo-European**. It includes Latin, Greek, the Slavic languages and the Germanic languages. The Germanic languages, such as German, English, Dutch or Swedish, split off through a regular change in the consonants: the **first sound shift**.

Certain stop sounds turned into friction sounds: **p** became **f**, **t** became a sound like the English “th”, and **k** became **h**. You can see this by comparing words: Latin “pater” and English “father”, Latin “tres” and English “three”, Latin “centum” and German “hundert”. Other sounds shifted too, so d became t: Latin “duo”, English “two”. Latin kept the old sounds.

**Jacob Grimm**, known for the fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm, was also a language scholar. In 1822 he described the regular matches that today are called **Grimm’s law**. The Danish scholar Rasmus Rask had noticed something similar before him. Some words seemed not to follow the rules. In 1875, **Karl Verner** showed that this depended on the original **stress**. This is called **Verner’s law**.

Much later came the **second sound shift**. It separated High German from English and Dutch: English “two”, but German “zwei”. It went furthest in the south of the German-speaking area. That is why many Swiss German dialects say “Chind” instead of “Kind” (child) and “Chäs” instead of “Käse” (cheese).

gewusst: Thanks to the sound shift you can spot relatives: Latin “piscis” and German “Fisch” (fish) belong together.
The V in the German word “Vater” (father) is pronounced like an f, which still shows the shift from p to f today.

teile.einleitung: Behind every book there are people who created it. The author writes the text, and the illustrator draws the pictures. A publisher makes sure that it becomes a finished book.
wichtigste: The person who writes the text is called the **author**.
The person who draws the pictures is called the **illustrator**.
A company that publishes books is called a **publisher**.
Erich Kästner wrote “Emil and the Detectives”.
Michael Ende wrote “Jim Button”, and Otfried Preussler “The Robber Hotzenplotz”.
For “The Gruffalo”, Julia Donaldson wrote the text and Axel Scheffler drew the pictures.
For “The Very Hungry Caterpillar”, Eric Carle was both author and illustrator.

abschnitte.text: The **author** thinks up a story and writes it down. For non-fiction books the author collects knowledge and explains it clearly. Some authors write under a different name, a **pseudonym**. The word “author” comes from the Latin “auctor”, which means originator.

The **illustrator** paints or draws the pictures for a book. These pictures are called **illustrations**. Sometimes the author and illustrator work closely together, like Julia Donaldson and Axel Scheffler on “The Gruffalo”. Some people can do both: **Eric Carle** wrote and designed “The Very Hungry Caterpillar”. His pictures are made from colourful, painted pieces of paper stuck together.

A **publisher** turns a text into a finished book. Among the people who work there are **editors**. They read the text, give advice and look for mistakes. The publisher has the book printed and sells it to bookshops. The author and illustrator receive part of the money for it.

Many children’s books have been popular for decades. **Erich Kästner** wrote “Emil and the Detectives”, “Lottie and Lisa” and “Dot and Anton”. **Michael Ende** wrote “Jim Button and Luke the Engine Driver”, “Momo” and “The Neverending Story”. **Otfried Preussler** wrote “The Robber Hotzenplotz”, “The Little Witch” and “The Little Ghost”.

Famous children’s books were also created in Switzerland. **Johanna Spyri** wrote the stories about “Heidi”, which are known all over the world today. For the picture book “A Bell for Ursli” (Schellen-Ursli), Selina Chönz wrote the text and **Alois Carigiet** painted the pictures. Marcus Pfister from Bern is the author and illustrator of “The Rainbow Fish”.

gewusst: Copyright protects texts and pictures: you may not simply copy them and pass them off as your own.
The names of the author and illustrator are usually on the book cover.

teile.einleitung: A rent deposit is a sum of money that tenants pay as security when they move in. It protects the landlord in case damage or unpaid bills are left at the end.
wichtigste: The rent deposit is **security** for the landlord.
For flats it may be at most **three months’ rent**.
The money goes into a **blocked account** in the tenant’s name.
The landlord may not use the money on their own.
After moving out, the tenant gets the deposit back with interest if everything is in order.
Instead of money, you can often take out **rent deposit insurance**.

abschnitte.text: When you move in, the landlord often asks for a **rent deposit**. It is a security. If the tenant leaves damage that they have to pay for when moving out, or has not paid the rent, the landlord can draw on it. If everything is in order, the tenant gets the money back.

The Swiss **Code of Obligations** says exactly where the deposit must go: into a **savings account** or deposit at a bank, in the **tenant’s name**. This is called a **blocked account**. So the landlord may not simply take the money into their own account. The bank only releases it if both agree or if a court or authority decides.

For **flats** the deposit may be at most **three months’ rent**. The interest on the blocked account belongs to the tenant. For business premises higher amounts are also allowed. Many landlords ask for exactly the permitted three months’ rent, which can be a lot of money for young people moving out for the first time.

After the **flat is handed back**, the landlord checks whether there is any damage. If neither has any claims left, they sign the release and the tenant receives the money. If the landlord does not make a legal claim within one year of the end of the tenancy, the tenant can ask the bank to return the money.

Anyone who does not have the money all at once can often take out **rent deposit insurance**. Then you pay a premium every year, and the insurer guarantees the amount to the landlord. This is convenient, but over the years you pay money that you do not get back. If the insurer has to pay for damage, it later reclaims the money from the tenant.

gewusst: Legally, the deposit remains the tenant’s money, even though they cannot get at it during the tenancy.
The rule that the money must be held in the tenant’s name is in Article 257e of the Code of Obligations.

teile.einleitung: Cyberbullying means that someone is repeatedly insulted, humiliated or left out via the internet or a mobile phone. It hurts just as much as bullying in the playground. But there are ways to fight back.
wichtigste: Cyberbullying is bullying through chats, social networks or messages.
It can happen around the clock, and many people see it.
Screenshots are evidence and help later.
The most important thing is to show it to a trusted adult.
You can block the bullies and report them to the provider.
Anyone watching should not join in and should not forward anything.

abschnitte.text: In **cyberbullying**, a person is torn down **again and again** through digital means. This happens, for example, in a **class chat**, on social networks or through messages. People spread nasty comments, embarrassing pictures or lies, or they deliberately leave someone out of a group. A single argument is not bullying. What is typical is that it goes on for a long time and one person is left on their own.

Bullying on the internet does not stop after school. It can go on **around the clock**, even at home. Lots of people see it, and pictures or texts can be passed on quickly. Sometimes the people affected do not even know who is behind it. This frightens many people and can make them very sad.

It is important not to insult them back. It is better to take **screenshots** of the messages, because they are **evidence**. Then you show everything to a **trusted adult**, such as your parents or a teacher. They can help to make the bullying stop. You can **block** the bullies and **report** them to the provider. You can also get advice by calling **147**, the Pro Juventute helpline.

In cyberbullying, many people are often watching. Anyone reading along can make a big difference: you **do not forward anything**, you do not join in and you show the person affected that they are not alone. You can also tell an adult. That is not telling tales but **helping**. In Switzerland some actions in cyberbullying, such as threats or insults, can also be criminal offences.

gewusst: Screenshots show who wrote what and when. That is why they are so valuable when you get help.
Many schools in Switzerland have rules for class chats so that everyone treats each other with respect.

teile.einleitung: House rules set out how people in a block of flats can live well together. They say, for example, when it should be quiet, how the laundry room is used and that the stairwell must be kept clear.
wichtigste: The house rules apply to everyone who lives in the building.
They are often part of the tenancy agreement.
The stairwell is an **escape route** and must be kept clear.
They cover quiet times, the laundry room, rubbish and tidiness.
Anyone who keeps to them shows consideration for the neighbours.
If there are problems, people first talk to each other in a friendly way.

abschnitte.text: In a building with many flats, everyone shares the **stairwell**, the cellar, the laundry room and often a garden. So that there are no arguments about this, the landlord or the management writes **house rules**. They are usually handed over together with the tenancy agreement. Anyone who moves in promises to keep to these rules.

No boxes, bikes or pushchairs may stand around in the stairwell. The reason is that it is an **escape route**. In a fire everyone must be able to get out quickly and safely, even in smoke when you can hardly see anything. The **fire brigade** needs room for its hoses and to carry people. Things standing around can also catch fire themselves.

In many Swiss buildings there is a shared **laundry room**. A rota shows who may do their washing on which day. After washing you tidy up and clean the filter. There are also rules for rubbish: rubbish bags only go out on collection day, and you separate paper, glass and other materials.

The house rules often name times when the building should be quiet, for example at **night** and sometimes over lunchtime. Then you play quietly, do not play music loudly and do not run noisy machines. The municipality often has its own rules about noise too.

If you are annoyed with a neighbour, it is best to talk to them **in a friendly way** first. Many problems are quickly solved like this. If that does not help, you can contact the **management** or the landlord. Anyone who keeps breaking the house rules can, in the worst case, lose their flat.

gewusst: The shared laundry room with a washing rota is seen as typically Swiss and is rather rare abroad.
Fire brigades warn that even a single object in the stairwell can become a trip hazard in smoke.

teile.einleitung: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz developed printing with movable type. This invention changed the world: books could now be produced much faster and more cheaply. In this way knowledge and ideas spread all over Europe.
wichtigste: Around 1450 **Johannes Gutenberg** developed printing with movable type in **Mainz**.
The **type** consisted of individual letters made of metal.
Before that, books were mostly copied by hand.
The **Gutenberg Bible** is famous.
Printing encouraged more uniform German spellings.
**Basel** became an important centre of printing.

abschnitte.text: Before printing, books were usually copied by hand. This was often done by monks in monasteries. A single book sometimes took months or years. That is why books were very expensive and rare. Only a few people owned books of their own.

**Johannes Gutenberg** from Mainz had a brilliant idea. He cast individual letters from metal, which are called **type**. He put these together into words and pages. With a **printing press** he pressed paper onto the inked type. Afterwards the type could be taken apart again and used for new pages. That is why people speak of **movable type**.

The most famous work from Gutenberg’s workshop is the **Gutenberg Bible**. It was printed in the 1450s and is in Latin. Today only a few copies still exist, and they are very valuable. The Bible shows how beautiful and even printed pages already looked at that time.

Printed texts reached large areas. The printers wanted as many people as possible to be able to read their books. That is why they used spellings that could be understood beyond individual regions. In this way printing encouraged **more uniform spellings** in German. The Reformation also benefited: Martin Luther’s writings and his translation of the Bible spread quickly.

Soon after Gutenberg’s invention, printing works were set up in many towns. **Basel** became one of the most important centres of printing in Europe. There, for example, the printer **Johann Froben** worked, who printed works by the scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam. The town had a university and was well placed on the Rhine. That helped the book trade.

gewusst: In China people were printing centuries before Gutenberg, first with wooden blocks and later also with movable characters made of clay.
The unit for type size is still called the “point” today and comes from the age of metal type.

teile.einleitung: Quotation marks are punctuation marks that frame direct speech, quotations or titles. In Switzerland people use angled double marks that look like small double arrows pointing outwards; they are called guillemets. There are clear rules for punctuation around direct speech in German.
wichtigste: The angled double marks used in Switzerland are called guillemets.
In everyday German, quotation marks are also called Gänsefüsschen (little goose feet).
If the introducing clause comes first, a colon follows: Lea sagt: “Ich komme.” (Lea says: “I am coming.”)
If the introducing clause comes after, a comma follows the closing quotation mark: “Komm mit”, sagt Lea. (“Come along”, says Lea.)
Question marks and exclamation marks belonging to the speech stay inside the quotation marks.
An introducing clause inserted in the middle stands between two commas.
Quotation marks also mark titles and sometimes show irony.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, quotation marks are usually written as angled double marks that point outwards. These marks are called **guillemets**. The name comes from French. In Germany, on the other hand, people often put one mark at the bottom at the beginning and one at the top at the end. In everyday German, quotation marks are also called **Gänsefüsschen** (little goose feet), because they look like the tracks of geese’s feet.

If the **introducing clause comes first**, it is followed by a **colon**, and the full stop goes inside the quotation marks: **Lea sagt: “Ich komme.”** (Lea says: “I am coming.”) If the **introducing clause comes last**, the full stop of the speech is dropped. After the closing quotation mark there is a **comma**: **“Komm mit”, sagt Lea.** (“Come along”, says Lea.)

**Question marks** and **exclamation marks** belong to the speech and stay inside the quotation marks. A comma still follows afterwards: **“Kommst du?”, fragt Tim.** (“Are you coming?”, asks Tim.) If the speech is interrupted by the introducing clause, this stands between **two commas**, which are outside the quotation marks: **“Morgen”, sagte Lea, “gehen wir baden.”** (“Tomorrow”, said Lea, “we are going swimming.”)

Quotation marks are not only needed for direct speech. They also mark **word-for-word quotations** and the **titles** of books, films or newspapers, for example: Ich lese “Heidi” (I am reading “Heidi”). Putting a single word in quotation marks can express **distance** or **irony**. Then the reader notices that the word is not meant literally.

gewusst: For a quotation inside a quotation, single quotation marks are used; in Switzerland these are single angled marks.
Guillemets are also used in French and Italian, that is in other national languages of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A notice of termination ends a contract, for example a tenancy agreement for a flat. Swiss tenancy law has precise rules so that tenants are protected.
wichtigste: A flat can only be given notice **in writing**.
The landlord must use a **form** approved by the canton.
Without this form the notice is **void**, that is invalid.
For flats a notice period of three months usually applies.
Notice is given for certain dates that are set in the contract or usual in the area.
A notice can be challenged before the **conciliation authority**.

abschnitte.titel: What a notice of termination is
abschnitte.text: With a **notice of termination**, one party to a contract says: I want to end the contract. This exists for tenancy agreements, employment contracts or subscriptions. The **tenancy law** in the Swiss **Code of Obligations** contains special rules for flats. They are meant to stop anyone suddenly finding themselves out on the street.

If the **landlord** gives notice, they must use an **officially approved form**. The canton decides what this form looks like. Among other things, it says how the tenants can defend themselves. If the form is missing, the notice is **void** and does not count at all. For a family home, the notice must be sent separately to both spouses.

The **tenant** must also give notice in writing, but without a special form. A signed letter is enough. It is best to send it by **registered post** so that you can prove when it arrived. If two spouses live in the family home, both must sign.

For flats a **notice period** of three months usually applies. Notice is given for a **date** that is in the contract or usual in the area. It is important that the notice reaches the other party before the notice period begins. Anyone who wants to move out earlier can often suggest a suitable **replacement tenant**.

If you think a notice is unfair, you can challenge it before the **conciliation authority** for tenancy matters. You have **30 days** to do this after receiving the notice. The authority tries to find an agreement. Sometimes the tenancy can also be **extended** if moving out would be very hard.

gewusst: A letter giving notice is usually only deemed delivered when it could be collected, not when it was sent.
In Switzerland most people rent their homes, which is why tenancy law matters to a great many people.

teile.einleitung: A lot of personal things are stored on a mobile phone: photos, messages and contacts. A screen lock makes sure that nobody can get at them without permission.
wichtigste: A screen lock protects your data from strangers.
Without a lock, anyone who finds your phone can see your photos and messages.
You can use a code, a pattern, your fingerprint or your face.
A good code is not easy to guess, so not 1234 or your birthday.
You do not tell anyone your code except your parents.
The phone should lock itself after a short time.

abschnitte.text: A lot of private things are stored on a **mobile phone**: photos, chats, contacts and often logins for apps too. Without a **screen lock**, anyone who picks up the phone can see everything. That can happen if you leave it lying around or lose it. A lock protects your **data** and also that of your friends who have written to you.
