There are several ways to lock a phone. The best known is a **number code**, the PIN. Some devices allow a **pattern** that you draw with your finger. Many phones also recognise your **fingerprint** or your **face**. Even then you also need a code in case the recognition does not work.

A code is only useful if nobody can guess it. Numbers like **1234**, 0000 or your date of birth are too easy. A code with six digits that do not follow a pattern is better. You tell **nobody** your code, not even your best friend. Only your parents may know it. Make sure nobody is looking over your shoulder when you type it in.

In the settings you can set the phone to **lock automatically** after a short time. No private messages should appear on the lock screen. Many phones have a function to **locate** them if they get lost. With it you can lock the device remotely or even wipe it. It is worth setting up this function with your parents.

gewusst: After several wrong attempts many phones lock themselves for a while, so that nobody can simply try out every code.
A six-digit number code has a million possible combinations.

teile.einleitung: A ballad is a poem that tells an exciting story. Like a poem it has verses and often rhymes, but like a story it also has a plot. Many ballads by Goethe, Schiller and Fontane are still learned at school today.
wichtigste: A **ballad** is a poem that tells a story.
It combines features of a poem, a story and a play.
1797 is called the **year of ballads**, because Goethe and Schiller wrote many ballads.
Goethe wrote “The Erl-King” and “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice”.
Schiller wrote “The Diver”, “The Pledge” and “The Glove”.
Theodor Fontane wrote “John Maynard” and “Herr von Ribbeck of Ribbeck in Havelland”.
Conrad Ferdinand Meyer from Zurich wrote “The Feet in the Fire”.

abschnitte.text: A **ballad** tells a story in verse, with suspense and often a dramatic ending. Like a **poem**, it has verses and rhymes. Like a **story**, it has a plot. And often characters speak directly to each other, as in a **play**. That is why Goethe called the ballad the “primal egg” of poetry, which contains all three forms.

In **“The Erl-King”** a father rides late through the night and the wind with his sick child. The child hears the Erl-King luring him, but the father sees only mist and willows. When he reaches the farm, the child is dead. In **“The Sorcerer’s Apprentice”** an apprentice puts a spell on a broom so that it fetches water. But he can no longer stop it, and only the old master ends the chaos.

In **“The Diver”** a king throws a golden cup into a whirlpool in the sea. A young squire brings it up, but on his second dive he does not come back. In **“The Pledge”** a friend pledges his life for a condemned man. The condemned man returns in time despite all obstacles. The tyrant is so impressed by this **loyalty** that he pardons them both.

**Theodor Fontane** wrote famous ballads in the 19th century. In **“John Maynard”** a ship is on fire on Lake Erie. The helmsman stays at the wheel until the ship reaches the shore and everyone is saved, and he himself dies. In **“Herr von Ribbeck of Ribbeck in Havelland”** a landowner loves giving pears to children. He has a pear placed in his grave with him, and a new pear tree grows from it.

In **1797** Goethe and Schiller competed with each other. In a short time they wrote many of their most famous ballads, such as “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice”, “The Diver” and “The Glove”. That is why this year is called the **year of ballads**. Well-known ballads were also written in Switzerland: **Conrad Ferdinand Meyer** from Zurich wrote “The Feet in the Fire”.

gewusst: The word “ballad” originally comes from a dance song and is related to the Italian “ballare”, to dance.
Many ballads were set to music, for example Goethe’s “The Erl-King” by Franz Schubert.

teile.einleitung: In subletting, a tenant rents out their flat or a room to another person. This is allowed in Switzerland, but only with the landlord’s consent.
wichtigste: Subletting is regulated in the Code of Obligations.
The tenant needs the landlord’s consent.
The landlord may only refuse for certain reasons.
One reason is an excessively high rent for the subtenant.
The main tenant remains responsible to the landlord.
If the main tenancy ends, the sublet also ends.

abschnitte.text: In **subletting** there are three people involved: the **landlord**, the **main tenant** and the **subtenant**. The main tenant has a contract with the landlord. They then make a second contract themselves with the subtenant. You can sublet the whole flat or just a **room**, for example while you are abroad.

Anyone who wants to sublet must **ask** the landlord and tell them the terms, such as the rent and how long it will last. The landlord may only say no for certain **reasons**. For example, if the tenant will not tell them the terms. Or if the subtenant would have to pay an **excessively high** rent. The landlord may also refuse if the sublet would cause them significant disadvantages.

The **main tenant** remains responsible to the landlord. If the subtenant does not pay or breaks something, the landlord has to turn to the main tenant. That is why you should choose the subtenant carefully and make a **written contract**. It states how long the sublet lasts and what it costs.

Anyone who rents out their flat for short periods to tourists through **online platforms** is usually subletting too. This also needs the landlord’s **consent**. Some municipalities and cantons have extra rules for this. Anyone who rents out without permission even risks having their tenancy **terminated**.

gewusst: A shared flat, known in German as a WG, is often also a form of subletting.
Towards the main tenant, the subtenant has similar rights to an ordinary tenant.

teile.einleitung: **Epic** or narrative literature is literature that tells stories. It includes all texts in which someone tells a story, from a short fairy tale to a thick novel.
wichtigste: Narrative literature is one of the three genres, alongside **poetry** and **drama**.
A typical feature of narrative literature is a **narrator**.
A **novel** is a longer narrative text and belongs to narrative literature.
Other forms are the fairy tale, fable, legend, novella and short story.
The oldest works of narrative literature are long heroic poems, the **epics**.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Greek “epos”, which means “word” or “story”. In narrative literature there is always a **narrator** who tells us about characters, places and events. That makes it different from drama, where the characters speak for themselves on stage. It is different from poetry because it is usually not written in verse.

Narrative literature includes long and short texts. The **novel** is long and often has many characters and storylines. The **novella** is shorter and centres on one special event. The **short story**, **fairy tale**, **fable**, **legend** and **anecdote** are also short. What they all have in common is that a story is told.

The oldest works of narrative literature are the **epics**. These are long stories in verse about heroes and gods. Famous ones are the “Iliad” and the “Odyssey”, which are said to be by the Greek poet **Homer**. In the Middle Ages, for example, the “Song of the Nibelungs” was written in the German-speaking world.

Important narrative works were also written in Switzerland. **Johanna Spyri** wrote the novels about **Heidi**, which became world famous. **Jeremias Gotthelf** wrote about life in the Emmental. **Gottfried Keller** from Zurich wrote novels and novellas, such as “Clothes Make the Man”.

gewusst: Johanna Spyri’s Heidi books have been translated into a great many languages.
Even a fable of only a few sentences belongs to narrative literature, because it too tells a story.

teile.einleitung: Anyone cycling at night or when visibility is poor needs lights. There must be a white light at the front and a red light at the back. This lets others see that you are there and which way you are going.
wichtigste: At the front there is a white light.
At the back there is a red light.
You need lights at night, at dusk, when visibility is poor and in tunnels.
A bike also needs reflectors at the back and on the pedals.
The light must be easy to see but must not dazzle.
Without lights you risk a fine and, above all, an accident.

abschnitte.text: The **white light** at the front shows others that you are coming towards them. It also helps you to see the road. The **red light** at the back shows that you are riding in front of someone. Cars have the same colours. This way everyone knows immediately which **direction** you are going in.

Lights are compulsory from **dusk** until daybreak. They must also be switched on in rain, fog or snow and in **tunnels**. In autumn and winter it gets dark early, often already on the way home from school. That is why it is better to switch the lights on once too early than too late.

As well as lights, a bike needs **reflectors**. At the back there is a red reflector, and on the **pedals** there are orange reflectors. They light up when the light from cars falls on them. Reflectors in the **spokes** make the bike visible from the side too.

There are **fixed lights**, often powered by a dynamo, and clip-on lights with a **rechargeable battery** or ordinary batteries. Clip-on lights are allowed, but you must have them with you. Before setting off you check that they **work**. A rechargeable battery should be charged in good time.

gewusst: A bike light should be adjusted so that it points slightly forwards onto the road, so that it does not dazzle anyone.
Modern LED lights use much less electricity than old light bulbs and last longer.

teile.einleitung: The Brünig-Napf-Reuss line is an important border between Swiss dialects. It roughly divides German-speaking Switzerland into a western and an eastern part. It is named after a pass, a mountain and a river.
wichtigste: The **Brünig-Napf-Reuss line** divides German-speaking Switzerland into west and east.
It is named after the **Brünig Pass**, the **Napf** and the **Reuss**.
Many differences between the dialects run along the line.
The **Röstigraben**, on the other hand, means the border with the French-speaking Romandie.
All the dialects of German-speaking Switzerland belong to **Alemannic**.

abschnitte.text: The line is named after three landmarks. The **Brünig** is a pass between the Bernese Oberland and Obwalden. The **Napf** is a mountain in the area between the Emmental and the Entlebuch. The **Reuss** is a river that flows through Lucerne and later into the Aare. If you join these points, you get roughly the border between west and east.

West of the line lie, for example, the Bernese dialects, and east of it the Zurich dialects, for instance. Many words, sounds and forms differ on the two sides. Experts speak of a **bundle of language borders**, because several differences come together here. But the border is not sharp: there are often transitions, and not every feature follows the line exactly.

The Brünig-Napf-Reuss line separates dialects within German-speaking Switzerland. The **Röstigraben** is something else: it means the border between German-speaking Switzerland and the French-speaking **Romandie**. All the dialects of German-speaking Switzerland belong to **Alemannic**. Especially old-fashioned forms are found in the Valais, in what is called **Highest Alemannic**.

gewusst: Many people in German-speaking Switzerland can tell from just a few words which region someone comes from.
The dialect borders in Switzerland often follow old borders of rule and transport routes.

teile.einleitung: Waste paper is used paper that is collected and recycled. In this way old newspapers and exercise books become new paper.
wichtigste: Newspapers, magazines, exercise books and leaflets belong in the paper collection.
New paper is made from waste paper.
Recycled paper needs less wood, water and energy.
You tie the paper into bundles with string and without plastic.
Tissues, baking paper and drinks cartons do not belong in it.
In many municipalities cardboard is collected separately.

abschnitte.text: Old **newspapers**, magazines, exercise books, leaflets, letters and books without covers go into the **paper collection**. The paper should be clean and dry. You stack it and tie it into a bundle with **string**. Sticky tape and plastic bags are not wanted, because they cause problems during processing. When collections take place is shown in the municipality’s rubbish calendar.

abschnitte.titel: What does not belong in it
abschnitte.text: Not everything that looks like paper can be recycled. **Tissues** and kitchen roll are often dirty. **Baking paper** and coated paper are hard to break down. **Drinks cartons** also do not belong in the paper collection, because they contain layers of plastic and sometimes aluminium. In many municipalities cardboard is collected separately from paper.

Paper is made of fine **fibres**, which mostly come from wood. In the paper mill, waste paper is broken down with water into a pulp. Printing ink and other materials are removed. New sheets of paper are made from the pulp. The fibres can be reused several times, but they get a little shorter each time. That is why new fibres are often mixed in too.

For **recycled paper**, fewer trees have to be cut down. It also needs less water and energy than paper made from fresh wood. Exercise books and toilet paper made from recycled paper can often be recognised by an eco-label. In many Swiss municipalities, school classes or clubs collect the waste paper and earn money for their funds.

gewusst: Paper fibres can be recycled several times before they become too short.
In Switzerland a large share of used paper and cardboard is collected and recycled.

teile.einleitung: The Abrogans is a word list from the 8th century. It translates Latin words into Old High German and is considered the oldest surviving book in the German language. The oldest manuscript is kept in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.
wichtigste: The Abrogans is a Latin and Old High German word list.
It was created in the 8th century.
It is considered the oldest surviving book in the German language.
The oldest manuscript is kept in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.
It gets its name from the first Latin word in the list.

abschnitte.text: In the early Middle Ages, monks wrote mainly in **Latin**. The **Abrogans** helped them to understand Latin words. Next to each Latin word there is an **Old High German** word. Such a list is called a **glossary**. It was created in the **8th century** and is considered the **oldest surviving book in the German language**.

The list begins with the Latin word **“abrogans”**. It means something like “modest” or “humble”. The whole work was named after this first word. For language research the Abrogans is very valuable, because it shows what German looked like more than 1200 years ago.

The oldest surviving manuscript is kept in the **Abbey Library of St Gallen**. This library is one of the oldest in the world and owns many medieval manuscripts. The **Abbey precinct of St Gallen** is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Visitors wear felt slippers in the magnificent Baroque hall to protect the floor.

gewusst: The St Gallen manuscript of the Abrogans also contains one of the oldest translations of the Lord’s Prayer into German.

teile.einleitung: An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning to another word. The opposite of big is small, and the opposite of day is night. Antonyms help us to express differences clearly.
wichtigste: An antonym is an opposite word, that is a word with the opposite meaning.
Big and small, hot and cold, loud and quiet are antonyms.
There are antonyms among adjectives, nouns, verbs and other word classes.
The opposite of open is close.
Some words have different opposites depending on their meaning.
The counterpart of the antonym is the synonym, a word with the same meaning.
In German many opposites are formed with prefixes such as un-, for example “freundlich” and “unfreundlich” (friendly and unfriendly).

abschnitte.text: An **antonym** is a word that means exactly the opposite of another word. The word comes from Greek: “anti” means against and “onyma” means name. In German it is therefore also called a **Gegenwort** (opposite word) or simply an opposite. Examples are big and small or up and down.

Antonyms are most often found among **adjectives**: hot and cold, loud and quiet, fast and slow. But nouns also have opposites, such as day and night or friend and enemy. Among verbs there are pairs such as open and close or come and go. Even small words such as up and down or before and after can be antonyms.

Sometimes the opposite depends on what you are talking about. When talking about people, the opposite of old is **young**. But for a bike or a book, the opposite of old is **new**. It is similar with “light”: a light suitcase is the opposite of a heavy one, and in German a “leichte” (easy) task is the opposite of a difficult one.

Some opposites have steps in between; for example, between hot and cold there is warm and lukewarm. Others are simply either one or the other, such as on and off or dead and alive. Many opposites are also formed with **prefixes** such as un-, for example honest and dishonest (in German “ehrlich” and “unehrlich”). For nouns the ending -less sometimes helps, as with hope and hopeless (in German “Hoffnung” and “hoffnungslos”).

With antonyms you can make differences clear and make texts more exciting. In fairy tales opposite characters often meet, for example poor and rich or good and evil. When learning a language, it helps to learn words together with their opposite. The counterpart of the antonym is the **synonym**, a word with the same or a similar meaning.

begriffe.erklaerung: A word with the opposite meaning.
A word with the same or a similar meaning.
A part added at the beginning of a word, such as un- in unfriendly.
Two words that together form an opposite.

gewusst: The opposite of “antonym” is “synonym”, so the two words are themselves antonyms.
Not every word has an opposite; for example, there is none for “table” or “banana”.
Some words can mean their own opposite, such as the German “umfahren”, which can mean both to drive around something and to knock it over.

teile.einleitung: A compost heap is a place where new soil is made from plant remains. Small creatures eat the waste and over time turn it into fertile humus.
wichtigste: Plant remains such as peel, leaves and grass cuttings belong in the compost.
Worms, fungi and tiny bacteria break down the waste.
Compost turns into dark soil rich in nutrients.
Many municipalities collect green waste with a separate collection.
Biogas can also be produced from green waste in special plants.
Plastic, glass and metal never belong in the compost.

abschnitte.text: **Plant remains** go into the compost: banana skins, apple cores, vegetable peelings, coffee grounds, leaves, grass and small twigs. Wilted flowers belong there too. Plastic, glass, metal, ash from the barbecue, cat litter and diseased plants do not belong in it. In the garden people usually leave out meat and cooked food, because they can attract rats.

Many creatures work in the compost. **Earthworms** and **compost worms** eat the waste and leave behind valuable crumbs. Woodlice, millipedes and beetles break the remains into smaller pieces. Invisibly small **bacteria** and **fungi** do most of the work. This can make it really warm inside the compost heap.

After a few months the waste has turned into dark, crumbly soil. It smells like the forest floor and is called **humus**. Gardeners mix it into flower beds and pots. In this way the plants get back the **nutrients** that were in the remains. This completes a natural cycle.

Not everyone has a garden. That is why many Swiss municipalities collect **green waste** in their own containers. Each municipality decides exactly what may go in. The green waste goes to large **composting plants** or **fermentation plants**. In fermentation plants **biogas** is produced, which can be used to generate electricity and heat or to power vehicles.

gewusst: A handful of good compost contains more tiny living things than there are people on Earth.
Inside, a compost heap can get so warm that it steams on cold days.

teile.einleitung: Anyone in Switzerland who passes their driving test first gets their driving licence only on probation. This probationary period lasts three years and is meant to guide young drivers towards driving safely.
wichtigste: After passing the test you get a probationary driving licence.
The probationary period lasts 3 years.
During this time you must attend a further training course.
New drivers have an alcohol limit of 0.1 per mille, so practically no alcohol.
If the licence is withdrawn because of an offence, the probationary period is extended.
In a second serious case the licence is cancelled.

abschnitte.text: After the practical test you receive a **probationary driving licence**. It is valid for **three years**. Only when you have got through this time without any major problems and have attended the course do you receive the **full driving licence**. The probationary period is meant to show that you can drive safely without a driving instructor.

During the probationary period you must attend a **further training course**. There you learn, for example, to recognise dangers early and to judge your own abilities well. Young drivers have accidents more often because they lack **experience**. Anyone who does not take the course in time loses their probationary licence.

Anyone who commits an offence during the probationary period and has to hand in their licence gets an **extension** of the probationary period by one year. If a second such case happens, the licence is **cancelled**. Then you must later start again from the beginning, with a learner’s licence and a new test. Before that you first need an **assessment** by experts.

The word **probationary period** also exists at work. In Switzerland, with a new job, the first month counts as the probationary period; it can be extended to up to **three months**. During this time both sides can end the contract with a short **notice period** of seven days. This lets employers and employees check whether they are a good fit.

gewusst: The probationary driving licence has existed in Switzerland since 2005.
Young new drivers are involved in accidents more often, relative to their numbers, than experienced drivers; this was one reason for introducing the probationary period.

teile.einleitung: A defibrillator, AED for short, is a device that can save lives when someone’s heart stops. It is designed so that even people without training can use it.
wichtigste: AED stands for automated external defibrillator.
It is needed when the heart has stopped (cardiac arrest).
The AED gives the heart an electric shock so that it beats properly again.
The device explains step by step with a voice what you have to do.
It only gives a shock if one is needed.
First you call 144 and start chest compressions.

abschnitte.text: In **cardiac arrest**, the heart no longer pumps blood through the body. Often the heart muscle only quivers irregularly; this is called **ventricular fibrillation**. The person collapses, does not respond and no longer breathes normally. Without help the brain gets no oxygen. That is why every minute counts.

An **AED** measures the heart rhythm through two sticky electrodes on the chest. If it detects ventricular fibrillation, it gives a short **electric shock**. This can bring the heart back into a normal rhythm. The device decides by itself whether a shock is needed. That is why you cannot use it wrongly: without ventricular fibrillation there is no shock.

First you call the ambulance service on **144**. Then you start **chest compressions**: pressing hard and fast in the middle of the chest. A second person fetches the AED. When you switch the device on, it **explains with a voice** what to do. You stick on the electrodes and follow the instructions. While the shock is given, nobody touches the person.

AEDs hang in many public places, for example at **stations**, in sports halls, schools, shopping centres and municipal buildings. You can recognise them by a **green sign** with a white heart and a lightning bolt. In Switzerland there are apps and maps that show where the nearest AED is. It is worth looking out for them on your next walk.

gewusst: In cardiac arrest, the chance of survival falls sharply with every minute without help. That is why acting quickly is so important.
In a first aid course you learn how chest compressions and the AED work. In Switzerland you need this course for your driving licence.

teile.einleitung: Articles are small words that come in front of a noun, for example the German words for “the”. They tell us whether a German noun is masculine, feminine or neuter. That is why they are also called companions.
wichtigste: Words such as “der” and “die” are called **articles** or companions (Begleiter).
“der”, “die” and “das” are **definite articles** (the).
“ein” and “eine” are **indefinite articles** (a, an).
In German it is “die Tasche” (the bag) and “der Mond” (the moon).
In Switzerland people say “das Velo” (the bike).
In the plural the German definite article is always “die”.

abschnitte.text: An **article** almost always comes in front of a noun. It accompanies it like a good friend. That is why articles are also called **companions** (Begleiter) in German. For example: “der Käse” (the cheese), “die Gabel” (the fork). When you learn a new German noun, it is best to learn the article with it straight away.

In German every noun has a **gender**. Experts call this **genus**. Masculine nouns have the article “der”, for example “der Mond” (the moon). Feminine nouns have “die”, for example “die Tasche” (the bag). Neuter nouns have “das”, for example “Velo” (bike). The gender of a word often has nothing to do with the thing itself: “Mädchen” (girl) is neuter.

The German words for “the” are **definite articles**. You use them when you mean something known: “Der Hund schläft” (The dog is sleeping). The words “ein” and “eine” are **indefinite articles**. You use them when something is new or not exactly known: “Ein Hund bellt” (A dog is barking). A story often begins with the indefinite article and then continues with the definite one.

German articles do not always stay the same. In the plural it is always “die”: “die Monde” (the moons), “die Bücher” (the books). In a sentence the article also changes depending on the **case**: “der Hund”, “des Hundes”, “dem Hund”, “den Hund” (all forms of “the dog”). In this way the article shows what role the noun plays in the sentence.

Some nouns have a different article in Switzerland from in Germany. In Switzerland, for example, people say “das Tram” (the tram), while in Germany it is usually “die Tram”. Both forms are correct in their own country. Other languages have fewer articles: in English the only definite article is “the”.

gewusst: The word “article” comes from the Latin “articulus”, which means “small joint”.
French has only two genders, German has three.

teile.einleitung: Singular and plural show whether we are talking about one thing or several. One house is in the singular, many houses are in the plural. German has various endings for this, and sometimes the word even gets an umlaut.
wichtigste: In German the singular is also called Einzahl and the plural Mehrzahl.
The plural of Haus (house) is Häuser, and the plural of Kind (child) is Kinder.
The singular of Bäume (trees) is Baum.
Many words get an umlaut in the plural, such as Maus and Mäuse (mouse, mice).
With some words you simply add an s, as with Auto and Autos (car, cars).
In the plural the article is always “die” (the).
Some words exist only in the singular or only in the plural.

abschnitte.text: You use the **singular** when talking about a single thing: ein Apfel (an apple), ein Buch (a book), ein Kind (a child). The **plural** shows that there are several: Äpfel, Bücher, Kinder. This change mainly affects nouns, but articles, adjectives and verbs adapt too. You say “Das Kind spielt” (The child plays), but “Die Kinder spielen” (The children play).

German has several ways of forming the plural. Some words get the ending -er, like Kind and **Kinder** (children). Others get -e, like Tisch and Tische (tables), or -en, like Frau and Frauen (women). With many foreign words and short words you add an -s, for example Auto and **Autos** (cars) or Velo and Velos (bikes). And some words stay the same, like der Lehrer and die Lehrer (the teacher, the teachers).

Often the vowel in the word also changes in the plural. A becomes ä, o becomes ö, u becomes ü and au becomes äu. So Maus becomes **Mäuse** (mice), Haus becomes Häuser (houses), Apfel becomes **Äpfel** (apples) and Buch becomes Bücher (books). This change is called an **umlaut**, and it also helps with spelling: Bäume (trees) is written with äu because it comes from Baum.

In the plural the article is always “die”, whether the word has der, die or das in the singular. So: der Baum, die Bäume (tree, trees); das Buch, die Bücher (book, books). This makes it easy to recognise words like Bücher, Häuser or Kinder as plurals. If you are looking for the singular, ask yourself: what is it called when there is only one? That way you get from Bäume back to **Baum**.

Some words exist almost only in the singular, for example Milch (milk), Glück (luck) or Gold (gold). Others exist only in the plural, such as **Ferien** (holidays), Leute (people) or Eltern (parents). Some words have different plural forms depending on their meaning: Bank meaning a bench becomes Bänke, while Bank meaning a financial institution becomes Banken. By the way, in Switzerland people say ein Velo, zwei Velos (one bike, two bikes) instead of Fahrrad and Fahrräder.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical term for one (Einzahl).
The technical term for more than one (Mehrzahl).
The letters ä, ö and ü.
A word such as der, die or das in front of a noun.

gewusst: The German word “Ferien” (holidays) exists only in the plural, so you cannot talk about one “Ferie”.
Some words, such as “Wort” (word), have two plural forms: Wörter for individual words and Worte for connected statements.
With foreign words such as “Museum”, the plural is formed in a special way, namely Museen.

teile.einleitung: The **narrative perspective** describes from whose point of view a story is told. Whether an “I” is speaking or an all-knowing narrator makes a big difference to how we experience a story.
wichtigste: The **first-person narrator** is a character and tells the story using “I”.
The **authorial narrator** knows everything and comments on what happens.
With the **figural** point of view you experience everything through one character, in the third person.
The **neutral narrator** only describes what can be seen from the outside, like a camera.
The narrator is not the same as the author.
In 1955, **Franz K. Stanzel** described the typical narrative situations.

abschnitte.text: With a **first-person narrator**, the storytelling voice is itself a character in the story: “I ran to the station.” You only find out what this “I” knows and feels. A well-known example is the series “Diary of a Wimpy Kid” by Jeff Kinney, in which Greg Heffley tells the story himself. There is a difference between the **narrating I**, who looks back from a distance, and the **experiencing I**, who is right in the middle of events.

The **authorial narrator** stands above the events. He knows the thoughts of all the characters, makes comments and hints at what is to come. In the **figural** narrative situation the narrator steps back, and you experience everything through one character, but with “he” or “she”. The **neutral narrator** only reports what you could see and hear, like a camera.

In 1955 the Austrian literary scholar **Franz K. Stanzel** distinguished three typical narrative situations: **authorial**, **figural** and the **first-person** narrative situation. His model is often used in German lessons. It helps you describe texts more precisely. In many books, however, the perspective changes.

Sometimes you hear a character’s thoughts directly, without “he thought”: “I hope nobody notices.” This is called an **interior monologue**. With a **flashback** the story jumps into the past to show what happened before. It is always important to remember: the narrator is an invented voice. A grown-up author can, for example, let a child tell the story.

gewusst: The same story can feel completely different when it is told from the point of view of another character.
A first-person narrator can be wrong or keep something quiet. So you should not believe everything they say.

teile.einleitung: Companies and authorities store a lot of data about people. The right of access allows you to ask what data someone holds about you.
wichtigste: Everyone has the right to find out what personal data about them is being processed.
This is set out in the Swiss Data Protection Act.
The information is usually free of charge.
The company normally has to reply within 30 days.
It is best to make the request in writing and prove who you are.
If data is wrong, you can ask for it to be corrected.

abschnitte.text: **Personal data** means any information that belongs to a particular person. This includes name, address, date of birth and phone number, but also photos, purchases or what someone does in an app. Many companies collect such data, for example online shops, insurance companies or apps. The **Data Protection Act** sets out what they are allowed to do with it.

Under the Data Protection Act, everyone may ask a company or a federal authority to find out **what data** it holds about them. The company must also say what it uses the data for, where it comes from and how long it is kept. This **right of access** applies to everyone, including children and young people. For children, the parents usually help with the request.

It is best to write a short letter or email to the company. You ask for **information** about your own data and include proof of who you are, for example a copy of your identity card. This prevents strangers from getting other people’s data. The company usually has to reply **within 30 days**. The information is normally **free of charge**.

Once you have received the information, you can use further rights. If data is wrong, you can ask for it to be **corrected**. In certain circumstances you can also ask for it to be **deleted**. If a company does not reply, you can contact the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner or take legal action.

gewusst: Switzerland’s revised Data Protection Act came into force on 1 September 2023.
For cantonal authorities, the cantons’ data protection laws apply, and they also include a right of access.

teile.einleitung: The General Abonnement, GA for short, is a travel pass for public transport in Switzerland. Anyone with a GA can travel almost everywhere by train, bus, tram and on many boats, as often as they like.
wichtigste: GA is the abbreviation for General Abonnement.
The GA is valid on almost all trains, buses, trams and many boats in Switzerland.
You can travel with it as often as you like without buying tickets.
There is a GA for 1st class and for 2nd class.
There are cheaper versions for children, young people and senior citizens.
The GA is stored on the SwissPass.

abschnitte.text: With the **General Abonnement** you can travel on almost the whole **public transport** network of Switzerland. This includes the trains of SBB and many other railways, buses, **PostBuses**, the trams in the towns and many boats on the lakes. You no longer have to buy tickets and can simply get on. The GA is valid for a year or as a monthly pass.

Today the GA is stored on the **SwissPass**, a red card. When tickets are checked, you hold out the card and the device shows whether the GA is valid. The SwissPass is also available in an app on your mobile phone. Other offers can be stored on the same card, for example a ski pass or a Mobility car-sharing subscription.

There is a GA for **1st class** and for **2nd class**. There are also cheaper versions for children, young people, students, senior citizens and people with disabilities. Families can also buy reduced-price GAs. The prices change from time to time, so it is best to look up the current ones.

The GA is valid **almost** everywhere, but not quite. On many **mountain railways**, such as cable cars and some cogwheel railways, the GA only gives a discount. Some tourist trains and boats also need a supplement. For journeys abroad, the GA is only valid as far as the border. Even so, it is very handy for people who travel a lot.

gewusst: The first General Abonnement already existed in Switzerland in the 19th century.
Many people in Switzerland own a GA and so leave the car at home more often.

teile.einleitung: A good story is like a path with a beginning, a middle and an end. At school these are called the introduction, the main part and the ending. Anyone who knows this structure can write exciting stories themselves.
wichtigste: A story consists of an **introduction, a main part and an ending**.
The introduction tells you who is in it and where and when it happens.
In the main part the tension rises to the **climax**.
In the ending the problem is solved.
“One day” works well at the beginning, and “Suddenly” makes the main part exciting.
A good title makes you curious but does not give everything away.

abschnitte.text: The **introduction** opens the door to the story. It introduces the characters and says where and when everything takes place. The readers should quickly know what it is about. Good beginnings are, for example, “One day” or “It was a cold winter morning”. The introduction is short, because the most important part comes afterwards.

In the **main part** the real action happens. Often there is a problem, an adventure or a surprise. The tension rises step by step, like a path up a mountain. The most exciting point is called the **climax**. Words such as “Suddenly” or “All at once” show that something unexpected is happening. Direct speech and the characters’ feelings also make the main part come alive.

In the **ending** the problem is solved. The tension falls again, and the story comes to an end. Sometimes a character thinks about what has happened at the end. The ending should be short and should not simply stop in the middle of a sentence. A good ending leaves the readers satisfied.

In a **picture story** you are given several pictures in the right order. Each picture shows part of the action. You tell what happens one after the other. Here too the structure with introduction, main part and ending applies. You are welcome to tell more than you can see in the pictures, for example what the characters are thinking.

At the very top is the **title**. It should be short and make people want to read. But it must not give everything away yet, or the tension is gone. “The secret in the cellar” makes you more curious than “How we found the lost key”. Many people only write the title at the end, when the story is finished.

gewusst: The way the tension develops in a story is called the **narrative arc**.
Stories are usually told in the past tense, for example “Suddenly I heard a noise”.

teile.einleitung: Direct speech reports exactly what someone said, word for word. You can recognise it by the quotation marks that frame what was said. In Switzerland people usually use guillemets for this, the angle-shaped quotation marks.
wichtigste: Direct speech reports a person's words exactly.
It is placed in quotation marks.
In Switzerland people usually use guillemets, angle-shaped quotation marks.
The reporting clause says who is speaking, for example “sagte Mama” (said Mum).
When the reporting clause comes first, it is followed by a colon.
When the reporting clause comes after, the full stop at the end of the spoken words is left out.
Indirect speech reports what was said using the subjunctive.

abschnitte.text: **Direct speech**, also called quoted speech, reports exactly what a person says. The spoken words are put in **quotation marks**. There is usually also a **reporting clause** that tells you who is speaking and how, for example “rief Mama” (called Mum) or “flüsterte Tim” (whispered Tim). Direct speech brings stories to life, because you hear the characters speaking for themselves.

In German, if the reporting clause comes at the beginning, it is followed by a **colon**. Then come the quotation marks and the spoken words, which begin with a capital letter. An example: Mama sagte: “Das Essen ist fertig.” (Mum said: “Dinner is ready.”) Here the full stop goes inside the quotation marks.

abschnitte.titel: Reporting clause at the end or in the middle
abschnitte.text: In German, if the reporting clause comes after the spoken words, a **comma** is placed after the closing quotation mark. A full stop at the end of the spoken words is dropped, but exclamation marks and question marks stay. So this is correct: “Komm her!”, rief Mama. (“Come here!” called Mum.) A reporting clause in the middle is separated off by commas on both sides: “Morgen”, sagte Lea, “gehen wir baden.” (“Tomorrow,” said Lea, “we are going swimming.”)

In Switzerland people usually use **guillemets**, quotation marks shaped like small double arrows, with the points facing outwards. In Germany people mostly use one mark low down at the start and one high up at the end. If there is another quotation inside the direct speech, single guillemets, shaped like small single arrows, are used. For example: Lena sagte: “Auf dem Schild stand ‘Bitte nicht füttern’.” (Lena said: “The sign said ‘Please do not feed’.”)

You can also report what was said in **indirect speech**. Then the quotation marks are left out, and the verb is usually in the subjunctive. “Ich bin müde”, sagt sie (“I am tired,” she says) becomes: Sie sagt, sie sei müde (she says she is tired). Here “sei” is the subjunctive form of “sein” (to be). Newspapers and reports often use indirect speech to show neutrally what someone said.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the sentence that says who is speaking.
Marks that frame direct speech.
Quotation marks in the shape of small arrows, used in Switzerland.
Reporting what was said without quotation marks, in German usually in the subjunctive.

gewusst: The word guillemets comes from French and probably goes back to a printer called Guillaume.
In comics the speech bubble replaces the quotation marks of direct speech.
In France the points of the guillemets face outwards, while in Germany they are often set the other way round, pointing inwards.

teile.einleitung: **Expressionism** was a movement in literature and art from about 1910 to 1925. The artists did not want to copy reality, but to express feelings and deep inner turmoil.
wichtigste: Literary Expressionism flourished from about **1910 to 1925**.
It was a reaction to the **big city**, technology, war and the collapse of old values.
In 1911 Jakob van Hoddis launched Expressionist poetry with the poem **“End of the World”**.
In 1914 Georg Trakl wrote the anti-war poem **“Grodek”**.
Kurt Pinthus published the collection **“Twilight of Humanity”** in 1919.
Important magazines were **“Der Sturm”** (The Storm) and **“Die Aktion”** (Action).

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “expressio”, which means expression. Shortly before the **First World War** the world was changing fast: cities grew, and machines and noise shaped everyday life. Many young poets felt threatened by this world and like strangers in it. They wanted to shake people up with strong images and fierce language.

In 1911 **“End of the World”** by **Jakob van Hoddis** was published. It begins with “From the citizen’s pointed head the hat flies off” and lines up one image of disaster after another. In “The God of the City”, **Georg Heym** showed the big city as a threatening idol. **Gottfried Benn**, a doctor by profession, published the collection “Morgue” in 1912. In 1914 **Georg Trakl** experienced the Battle of Grodek as a medic and wrote the poem “Grodek” about it.

From 1910, **Herwarth Walden** published the magazine **“Der Sturm”** in Berlin, which supported literature and art. Alongside it, **“Die Aktion”** was especially important. In 1919 **Kurt Pinthus** brought many poems together in the collection **“Twilight of Humanity”**. The title means both decline and a new beginning. **Franz Kafka** is also often placed in this period: in “The Metamorphosis” (1915), Gregor Samsa wakes up as a monstrous insect.

Painters also worked in an Expressionist way, with strong, often unnatural colours. Well-known groups were **“Die Brücke”** (The Bridge) and **“Der Blaue Reiter”** (The Blue Rider), to which Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc belonged. The painter **Paul Klee**, born near Bern, exhibited with the Blue Rider in 1912. **Dadaism** also grew out of Expressionism in Zurich in 1916.

gewusst: Franz Marc painted blue horses because colour mattered more to him than reality.
Many young Expressionists were killed in the First World War; Georg Trakl also died in 1914.

teile.einleitung: An **Elfchen** is a short poem made of exactly eleven words. The name is German and comes from “elf”, the German word for eleven. It is very popular in schools because you can write one quickly and you do not need any rhymes.
wichtigste: An Elfchen is made of **11 words**.
The words are spread over **5 lines**.
The lines have 1, 2, 3, 4 and 1 word.
An Elfchen does **not have to rhyme**.

abschnitte.text: An Elfchen has five lines with a fixed number of words: the first line has **1 word**, the second **2**, the third **3**, the fourth **4** and the last one **1 word** again. Together that makes 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 11. That is where the name comes from.

There is often a simple guide. The first line names a colour, a quality or a topic. The second says what or who is like that. The third tells where or how it is. The fourth line often begins with “Ich” (I) and says something about yourself. The last word is an ending, a kind of conclusion.

An Elfchen about summer could look like this: “Blau” (blue) in the first line, “Der See” (the lake) in the second, “Er glitzert hell” (it sparkles brightly) in the third, “Ich springe jubelnd hinein” (I jump in, cheering) in the fourth and “Sommer” (summer) in the fifth. Count them: there are exactly eleven German words. With just a few words, a little picture appears in your mind.

gewusst: Because every word counts, writing an Elfchen teaches you to choose just the right words.

teile.einleitung: The alcohol limit says how much alcohol someone may have in their blood at most when driving a vehicle. Alcohol makes you slower and less careful, which is why there are strict rules on the road.
wichtigste: Per mille means “per thousand”.
0.5 per mille means half a part of alcohol per thousand parts of blood.
For most drivers in Switzerland the limit is 0.5 per mille.
New drivers with a probationary licence and learner drivers have a limit of 0.1 per mille.
The 0.5 per mille limit also applies when cycling.
The body breaks down alcohol only slowly; coffee or sleep hardly make it faster.

abschnitte.text: **Per mille** means a thousandth, so much smaller than one per cent. The figure shows how much **alcohol is in the blood**. Even a little alcohol changes your vision, your **reaction time** and your sense of danger. You often feel safer than you actually are.

For most drivers the limit is **0.5 per mille**. From 0.8 per mille, driving counts as a serious offence and is punished severely. For **new drivers**, learner drivers, driving instructors and professional drivers the limit is **0.1 per mille**. That is practically a **ban on alcohol**, because even one glass can be too much.

The **police** can ask for a breath test at any time. Anyone with too much alcohol can expect a **fine** and often the **withdrawal of their driving licence**. For new drivers the probationary period is also extended. Anyone who causes an accident under the influence of alcohol must also expect consequences with their insurance.

The limit of **0.5 per mille** does not only apply in a car but also on a **bike** and an e-bike. Anyone who has been drinking is best off leaving the vehicle where it is. Good alternatives are **public transport**, a taxi or someone who stays sober and drives.

gewusst: The body only breaks down about 0.1 to 0.15 per mille of alcohol per hour.
On the morning after a party you can still have too much alcohol in your blood, even if you feel fine again.

teile.einleitung: The Trottoir is the Swiss word for the pavement, the path for pedestrians next to the road. It is usually a little raised and separated from the carriageway by a kerb. There pedestrians are protected from cars.
wichtigste: The word Trottoir comes from French.
In Germany people say Gehweg or Bürgersteig.
Pedestrians walk on the pavement if there is one.
Since 2021 children up to the age of 12 may cycle on the pavement if there is no cycle path.
They must show consideration for pedestrians when doing so.
Cars may only park on the pavement where it is allowed.

abschnitte.text: The **pavement** lies at the edge of the road and is meant for **pedestrians**. A **kerb** separates it from the carriageway. If there is a pavement, pedestrians must use it. If there is none, they walk at the edge of the road; outside built-up areas it is best on the left-hand side, so that they face the oncoming cars.

The word **Trottoir** comes from the French “trotter”, which means something like to trot or to walk. In Switzerland and Austria it is completely normal. In Germany people tend to say **Gehweg** or Bürgersteig instead. Words like this show how the languages in Switzerland influence each other.

Since **2021**, **children up to the age of 12** in Switzerland have been allowed to cycle on the pavement if there is no cycle path or cycle lane. But they must ride **slowly** and show consideration for pedestrians. Pedestrians always have **right of way**. Older children and adults ride on the road.

You may ride on the pavement with a **kick scooter**, skateboard or inline skates. These are called vehicle-like devices. Here too the rule is: **pedestrians first**, and you do not go too fast. Electric scooters, on the other hand, count as vehicles and belong on the cycle path or the road.

gewusst: In French the pavement is still called “trottoir” today.
Lowered kerbs help people in wheelchairs and with pushchairs to get onto the pavement.

teile.einleitung: The word anaphora has two meanings. In rhetoric it is a figure of speech in which several sentences or lines begin with the same word. In linguistics it means a reference back to something that has already been mentioned.
wichtigste: In anaphora, several sentences or lines begin with the same word.
An example is “Who is coming? Who is helping? Who is staying?”.
Anaphora is popular in political speeches because it is memorable.
Its counterpart is epiphora, in which a word is repeated at the end.
In linguistics an anaphor is a reference back, usually through a pronoun.
The Greek word means roughly “carrying back”.

abschnitte.text: In **rhetoric**, the art of speaking, **anaphora** is repetition at the **beginning**. Several sentences, parts of sentences or lines begin with the same word or group of words, for example **“Who is coming? Who is helping? Who is staying?”**. The repetition strengthens the message and gives the text a clear **rhythm**.

Anaphora is very popular in **political speeches**. An example: **“We want peace. We want freedom. We want justice.”** The repeated “We want” makes the message stick in your head. Anaphora also often appears in **poems** and songs, because it sounds good and is easy to remember.

In **epiphora** the repetition is not at the beginning but at the **end** of sentences that follow each other. An example is “He wants power, she wants power, everyone wants power”. It has a similarly powerful effect to anaphora. Both belong to the **figures of repetition**.

In **linguistics**, anaphor means something different: it is an expression that refers back to something **mentioned earlier**. Usually it is a **pronoun**. In the sentence “The dog is barking because it is hungry”, **“it”** refers back to “the dog”. The Greek word anaphora means roughly **“carrying back”**. Such references back link sentences into a connected text.

gewusst: Without pronouns to refer back, you would have to keep repeating names, and texts would sound very clumsy.
A famous speech using anaphora is “I have a dream” by Martin Luther King, in which this sentence appears again and again at the beginning.

teile.einleitung: The recovery position is an important first aid measure. It is used to put an unconscious person who is breathing normally into a position in which their airways stay clear.
wichtigste: The recovery position is for people who are unconscious but breathing normally.
In this position saliva or vomit can run out of the mouth.
This keeps the airways clear so that the person does not choke.
Afterwards you call the ambulance service on 144.
You keep checking whether the person is still breathing.
If they are not breathing, chest compressions are needed.

abschnitte.text: If someone is lying on the ground, you first check whether it is **safe** for you. Then you speak to the person loudly and touch them on the shoulder. If they do not respond, they are **unconscious**. Now you check whether they are **breathing normally**: is the chest rising and falling?

If an unconscious person is lying on their back, the **tongue** can fall back and block the throat. **Saliva** or vomit can also get into the windpipe. In the **recovery position** the mouth is the lowest point, so everything runs out. The head is tilted slightly back so that air can flow freely.

You kneel next to the person and place the arm nearest to you bent upwards. You lay the other arm across their chest, with the hand against their cheek. Then you pull up the far leg by the knee and roll the person towards you onto their **side**. Finally you tilt the **head** slightly back and open the mouth a little.

Call **144** if this has not already been done. Stay with the person, cover them and keep checking their **breathing**. If they stop breathing, you roll them onto their back again and start **chest compressions**. If there is a **defibrillator** nearby, have someone fetch it.

gewusst: Anyone in Switzerland who wants a learner’s licence must first take a first aid course.
Defibrillators often hang at stations, in sports halls and shopping centres and explain how to use them with a voice.

teile.einleitung: Anyone out on foot or by bike must be easy to see in the dark. Light-coloured clothes, reflective bands and lights help drivers to spot you early. This can prevent accidents.
wichtigste: At night a driver only sees dark clothes very late.
Light colours stand out much earlier in the headlights.
Reflectors throw back the light of cars and shine brightly.
Fluorescent colours work especially well at dusk and in fog.
At night bikes need a white light at the front and a red light at the back.
Being easy to see is especially important in winter, because it gets dark early.

abschnitte.text: At night a driver only sees what their **headlights** light up. Dark clothes blend in with the road. That is why they often only notice a person in dark clothes when it is too late to **brake**. **Rain** and fog also make it harder to see.

**Reflectors** are small surfaces that throw light back exactly where it comes from. When the light of a car hits them, they light up brightly. They come as **reflective bands** for your arm, as tags on your school bag or as strips on jackets and shoes. They work best where you move, for example on your arms and legs.

**Fluorescent colours** such as neon yellow or orange stand out especially at **dusk** and in dull weather. In complete darkness they help less; then reflectors are more important. A **high-visibility vest** combines both. That is why many children wear a vest or a reflective triangle on the way to school.

Anyone riding a bike must switch on their **lights** at night and when visibility is poor: white at the front, red at the back. In addition there are **reflectors** at the back and on the pedals. Spoke reflectors make the bike visible from the side too. A bike without lights is almost invisible at night.

gewusst: Accident prevention experts estimate that with reflectors you can be seen several times further away than with dark clothes.
Many pedestrians think drivers can see them because they themselves can see the headlights well. That is a dangerous mistake.

teile.einleitung: The **colon** is a punctuation mark made of two dots, one above the other. It announces that something is still to come, such as a list, an explanation or direct speech.
wichtigste: The colon **announces something**.
It is often followed by a **list**, an **explanation** or **direct speech**.
In German, if a **complete sentence** follows, you continue with a capital letter.
Otherwise you continue with a small letter, except for nouns.
In scores such as 3:1 the colon is read as “to” (in German “zu”).

abschnitte.text: The colon tells the reader: pay attention, something is coming now. It comes, for example, before a **list**: “Ich brauche drei Dinge: Mehl, Eier und Zucker.” (I need three things: flour, eggs and sugar.) It can also introduce an **explanation**: “Sie hatte nur einen Wunsch: ein eigenes Velo.” (She had only one wish: a bike of her own.) The second part then explains more precisely what was announced in the first part.

Very often the colon comes before **direct speech**. First comes the reporting clause, then the colon and then the speech in quotation marks. An example: Mia rief: “Komm schnell!” (Mia called: “Come quickly!”) If the reporting clause only comes after the speech, no colon is needed, but a comma.

In German you continue with a **capital letter** after a colon if a complete sentence follows: “Eines ist sicher: Morgen regnet es” (One thing is certain: it will rain tomorrow). If only part of a sentence or a list follows, you continue with a **small letter**: “Sie hatte nur einen Wunsch: ein eigenes Velo” (She had only one wish: a bike of her own). Nouns, of course, always have a capital letter in German. Direct speech also begins with a capital letter.

In scores the colon goes between the numbers: a match ends **3:1**, read in German as “drei zu eins” (three to one). Ratios are also written like this, for example the **scale** of a map, such as 1:25,000. In maths lessons the colon is also a sign for dividing: 12 : 3 = 4.

gewusst: The technical term for the colon is **kolon**, a word from Greek.
On a map with a scale of 1:25,000, 1 centimetre corresponds to 250 metres in reality.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who causes damage on a bike has to take responsibility for it. In Switzerland such damage is usually covered by private liability insurance. The former bike vignette has no longer existed since 2012.
wichtigste: Being liable means paying for damage you have caused.
Until 2011 every bike needed a bike vignette.
Since 2012 private liability insurance has paid for damage caused with a bike.
Children are often insured through their parents’ family insurance.
Private liability insurance is not compulsory but is very common.
Fast e-bikes need a number plate with their own insurance.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who causes someone **damage** has to pay for it. This is called **liability**. If, for example, you scratch a parked car with your bike, the repair can be expensive. **Liability insurance** covers such costs so that you do not have to pay everything yourself.

In the past every bike in Switzerland needed a **bike vignette**. This was a small sticker that had to be bought new every year. It included liability insurance. Since **2012** the vignette has no longer existed, because almost all households already have **private liability insurance**.

**Private liability insurance** usually covers the whole **family** living in the same household. So children are protected by their parents’ insurance. Anyone without such insurance has to **pay for damage themselves**. Private liability insurance does not cost much and protects you from very high bills.

For **slow e-bikes** up to 25 kilometres per hour, the same applies as for bikes. **Fast e-bikes** up to 45 kilometres per hour, on the other hand, need a yellow **number plate**. This requires separate liability insurance, as for a Mofa. A helmet is also compulsory for these fast e-bikes.

gewusst: Anyone who causes damage on purpose or very recklessly may get less money from the insurer.
Liability insurance does not pay for your own bike, only for damage to other people.

teile.einleitung: Old electrical appliances such as hairdryers, toasters or mobile phones contain valuable raw materials and also harmful substances. In Switzerland you can return them free of charge so that they are recycled properly.
wichtigste: Electronic waste does not belong in the general rubbish.
Shops must take back old electrical appliances free of charge.
This applies to the kinds of appliances the shop itself sells, even if you do not buy anything new.
Recycling is already paid for in the purchase price, as an advance recycling fee.
Old appliances contain metals such as copper, gold and silver.
If possible, you take out rechargeable batteries and batteries first.

abschnitte.text: **Electronic waste** means old or broken appliances that work with electricity or batteries. These include hairdryers, kettles, games consoles, mobile phones, computers, fridges and much more. These appliances are made of many different materials. That is why they must not be thrown into the **rubbish bag**.

abschnitte.titel: Back to the shop for free
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland **shops are obliged** to take back old electrical appliances **free of charge**. This applies to all appliances of the kind they sell themselves, even if you do not buy anything new. So you can take an old **hairdryer** to any shop that sells hairdryers. There are also official collection points. Large appliances are often taken away when a new one is delivered.

When you buy a new appliance, you pay a small **advance recycling fee**. It is included in the price. This money later pays for the recycling. This is organised by industry organisations such as **SENS** and **Swico**. That is why returning appliances costs nothing.

In the recycling plants the appliances are taken apart and shredded. Metals such as **copper**, iron, aluminium and small amounts of **gold** and **silver** are separated from each other. These raw materials can be used again. At the same time, **harmful substances** are disposed of safely, for example from fridges or lamps. Rechargeable batteries and batteries are removed first, because they can start fires.

gewusst: A tonne of old mobile phones contains more gold than a tonne of gold ore from a mine.
Switzerland was one of the first countries to set up a nationwide system for recycling electrical appliances.

teile.einleitung: A description explains exactly what something looks like or how something works. Others should be able to imagine what is described or copy it. There are descriptions of people, objects, pictures, routes and processes.
wichtigste: Descriptions are written in the **present tense**.
**Adjectives** help to give features precisely.
A description of a person names outward features such as height, hair colour and clothing.
A **process description** explains a sequence step by step, for example a recipe.
In German instructions people often use “man” (one) or the imperative.
You describe a picture from the overall impression to the details.

abschnitte.text: You need a **description of a person**, for example, for a missing person report. So that others can recognise the person, you name outward features. These include **height, hair colour, clothing** and special features such as glasses. You describe in an orderly way, for example from top to bottom. Opinions such as “looks nice” do not help here.

If you have lost your rucksack, you write a **lost property report**. The most important things are precise features such as **colour, size**, brand or a special keyring. **Adjectives** such as “round”, “striped” or “light blue” help here. The more precise the details, the easier it is for the finder to recognise the object. Descriptions are written in the **present tense**, because they apply now: “The rucksack has two side pockets.”

A **process description** explains how to do something step by step. Examples are a recipe, instructions for making something or an experiment. The steps are in the right order. German instructions often use “man” (one) or the **imperative**: “Man schneidet das Brot” (One cuts the bread) or “Schneide das Brot” (Cut the bread). At the beginning you usually list what you need.

In **directions**, words giving the direction are especially important. Words such as **left, right, straight on** show where to go. You also name landmarks, for example: “Turn left at the church.” Distances help too, for example “after about 100 metres”. This way even someone who does not know the area can find the way.

In a **picture description** you first say what the picture shows in general. Then you describe the details in an orderly way. You can go from left to right or from the **foreground** to the **background**. Only at the end do you say what effect the picture has or how you like it. This keeps the description clear.

gewusst: In German, adjectives are also called Eigenschaftswörter (property words), because they describe properties.
Good instructions often manage with pictures and very few words, as with a lot of self-assembly furniture.

teile.einleitung: A Billett is the ticket for the train, bus, tram or boat. In Switzerland you usually buy it before getting on.
wichtigste: Billett is the Swiss word for a ticket.
On almost all trains, trams and buses you must have your ticket before the journey.
Tickets are available from machines, at the counter or in an app.
Anyone travelling without a valid ticket pays a surcharge.
Children aged 6 and over need a ticket; under 6 they travel free with an adult.
The Half Fare travelcard and the GA make travelling cheaper.

abschnitte.text: The word **Billett** comes from French and in Switzerland means a ticket. With a ticket you may travel a certain route on **public transport**. There are single tickets, day passes and season tickets. In towns there are often zones: you buy a ticket for the zones you travel through.

In Switzerland **self-checking** usually applies: you must already have your ticket **before getting on**. Ticket inspectors check it during the journey. Anyone caught without a valid ticket has to pay a **surcharge**. Only in a few cases, for example on some buses in the countryside, can you buy a ticket from the driver.

Tickets are available from **machines** at stations and stops, at **counters** and in **apps** on your mobile phone. In an app you can often simply check in and check out at the end. Then the cheapest price is worked out automatically. It is important that your phone has enough battery, because you must be able to show the ticket when it is checked.

Children under 6 travel free with an adult. Children from 6 to 16 pay a lower price. With the **Junior Card** they even travel free with a parent. Adults save with the **Half Fare travelcard**, which halves the price of many tickets. Anyone who travels very often buys a **GA**, a General Abonnement or travelcard for the whole network.

gewusst: Season tickets such as the Half Fare travelcard and the GA are stored on the SwissPass, a red card.
The Swiss rail network is very dense, and trains, buses and boats are coordinated with each other by a common timetable.

teile.einleitung: A child ticket is a cheaper ticket for children on public transport. In Switzerland small children even travel free if an adult is with them.
wichtigste: Children under 6 travel free when accompanied.
From the age of 6 a child needs their own ticket.
From 6 to 16, children usually pay a reduced price.
From 16 you pay the normal price or use a pass.
With family cards, children travel especially cheaply with their parents or grandparents.
When tickets are checked, every child must have a valid ticket.

abschnitte.text: Small children up to their 6th birthday need **no ticket** on Swiss public transport if they are travelling with someone who is at least 12 years old. They simply travel along. When it is very busy, though, people show consideration about seats: when it is full, small children often sit on someone’s lap.

From their 6th birthday a child needs their **own ticket**. Up to their 16th birthday a reduced **child price** usually applies, which costs about as much as a ticket with the Half Fare travelcard. This applies on trains, buses, trams and many boats. From 16 you pay the adult price.

There are special offers for families. With the **Junior Card**, children aged 6 to 16 travel free when they are out with their mother or father. There is a similar card for travelling with grandparents or other companions. The cards cost something once a year and are often worth it after just a few outings.

On the train the **ticket inspectors** sometimes come round. Then everyone shows their ticket or pass. Anyone without a valid ticket has to pay a **surcharge**. That is why you buy your ticket before the journey at the machine, at the counter or in the app. Children travelling alone should keep their ticket safely with them.

gewusst: In Switzerland the age limits of 6 and 16 for child tickets are the same almost everywhere, whichever railway you take.
Many children in Switzerland travel alone by bus and train to school or training from an early age.

teile.einleitung: A fat fire starts when oil or fat in the pan gets too hot and catches fire. Then you must never pour water on it. With the right method the fire can be smothered.
wichtigste: You must never pour water on burning oil.
The water turns to steam instantly and throws burning fat around.
You smother the fire with a lid or a fire blanket.
You switch off the cooker.
You do not carry the burning pan away.
If the fire gets too big, you leave the room and call the fire brigade on 118.

abschnitte.text: Oil and fat get very hot when frying. If you leave a pan on the cooker for too long, the oil can get so hot that it **catches fire by itself**. First it starts to smoke heavily. Then flames shoot out of the pan. That is why you never leave hot oil alone on the cooker.

Water is heavier than oil and sinks straight to the bottom of the hot pan. There it **turns to steam** in an instant. A little water makes a great deal of steam. This steam carries the burning fat with it and hurls it through the kitchen as a huge **jet of flame**. This is called a **fat explosion**. It can cause serious burns and set the kitchen on fire.

A fire needs **oxygen**. If you take away its air, it goes out. That is why you put a suitable **lid** on the pan or cover it with a **fire blanket**. Then you switch off the cooker and leave the lid on for a long time until everything has cooled down. You do not carry the pan away, because you could burn yourself or spill oil. There are also special **fire extinguishers** for fat fires.

In a fat fire children immediately fetch an **adult**. If the fire spreads, you leave the kitchen, close the door and call the **fire brigade** on **118**. A **fire blanket** in the kitchen is a good precaution. It hangs within easy reach on the wall and can be pulled out of its case with one tug.

gewusst: When one litre of water turns to steam, it makes well over a thousand litres of steam.
Fire extinguishers for fat fires carry fire class F.

teile.einleitung: A **double consonant** is a consonant written twice, as in the German words “Teller” (plate), “Suppe” (soup) or “Bett” (bed). When reading, it shows that the vowel before it is pronounced short.
wichtigste: A double consonant is a **consonant written twice**, for example ll, mm, pp or tt.
It often comes after a **short vowel**: Sonne (sun), Himmel (sky), Affe (monkey).
Instead of kk you write **ck**, and instead of zz you write **tz**.
After a long vowel there is usually only one consonant, as in “Tal” (valley).
If two different consonants already follow, nothing is doubled, as in “Hand” (hand).

abschnitte.text: The letters a, e, i, o, u and the umlauts ä, ö, ü are **vowels**. All the others are **consonants**, such as l, m, p or t. A vowel can sound long, as in “Tal” (valley), or short, as in “Ball” (ball). It is exactly this difference that often decides whether there is a double consonant.

If the vowel sounds **short** and only one consonant follows, that consonant is usually written twice. That is why the German words are spelt “Teller” (plate), “Suppe” (soup), “Bett” (bed), “Ball”, “Himmel” (sky), “Affe” (monkey) and “Treppe” (stairs). If you say them slowly in syllables, you can hear it well: “Tel-ler”, “Sup-pe”. So “Hamer” would be wrong; the correct spelling is “Hammer”.

Two consonants are written differently: instead of kk you write **ck**, as in “Zucker” (sugar), and instead of zz you write **tz**, as in “Katze” (cat). If you already hear two different consonants after a short vowel, nothing is doubled, for example in “Hand” (hand), “Wurst” (sausage) or “Kind” (child). Small words such as “in” (in), “mit” (with) or “ab” (off) also have only one consonant.

If you are unsure, make the word longer: “Bett” (bed) becomes “Betten” (beds), and then you can hear the break between syllables. Look for related words: “kennen” (to know) helps with “Kenntnis” (knowledge). Read words aloud and clap out the syllables. In addition, you simply have to practise many words with double consonants until you know them for certain.

gewusst: Double vowels, as in “Meer” (sea) or “Boot” (boat), show exactly the opposite: a long sound.
When a word is split at the end of a line, one consonant goes on each line: “Tel-ler”, “Him-mel”.

teile.einleitung: A ball rolling onto the road is a typical dangerous situation. Anyone who runs after it can easily forget about the cars. So the rule is: stop and get help.
wichtigste: If your ball rolls onto the road, you do not run after it.
You stay at the edge of the road and fetch an adult.
Cars cannot stop immediately; they need a stopping distance.
Drivers can easily fail to see children.
The best place to play ball is the playground or sports ground.
Before crossing, the rule is: wait, look, listen, walk.

abschnitte.text: When you are playing, you only think about the **ball**. If it rolls onto the road, you want to fetch it back quickly. At exactly that moment you forget to look out for cars. That is why such accidents keep happening. The most important rule is simple: **Stop!** A ball is never as important as you are.

A car cannot stop on the spot. First the driver has to see the danger and react. Then the car rolls on a bit further until it stops. This distance is called the **stopping distance**. The faster a car is going, the longer it is. Because children are small, they are often only seen very late between parked cars.

Stay at the **edge of the road** and fetch an **adult**. They can get the ball back safely when the road is clear. If you ever have to cross the road yourself, the Swiss rule **“warte, luege, lose, laufe”** applies: stop, look left and right, listen for engines, and only go when everything is clear.

The safest place to play is where no cars drive: in the **playground**, in the school playground or on a field. Some neighbourhoods also have **shared zones**. There cars may drive at no more than 20 km/h, and pedestrians have priority. Even there, though, the rule is: keep your eyes open.

gewusst: Some warning signs for drivers show a child with a ball, so they know that children might be playing here.
In Switzerland police road safety instructors visit many school classes to practise such rules.

teile.einleitung: Words can be arranged according to the alphabet. This is called alphabetical sorting or putting things in ABC order. This lets you find words in the dictionary or names on a list quickly.
wichtigste: When sorting, you look first at the first letter.
If the first letters are the same, the second one decides.
The alphabet has 26 letters, from A to Z.
Words beginning with Z come right at the end.
In the dictionary all words are arranged in ABC order.
Names can also be put in ABC order.

abschnitte.text: When putting things in ABC order, you look first at the **first letter**. With the German words Ziege, Kuh, Pferd and Schaf (goat, cow, horse, sheep) you compare Z, K, P and S. **K** comes first in the alphabet, so **“Kuh”** comes first. **Z** is the last letter, which is why “Zebra” usually comes right at the end of a list.

abschnitte.titel: When the first letter is the same
abschnitte.text: If two words begin with the same letter, you look at the **second** one. “Ball” and “Bein” (ball and leg) both begin with B. Then the rule is: a comes before e, so **“Ball”** comes first. With “Maus”, “Mond” and “Mehl” (mouse, moon, flour), a comes before e and o, so **“Maus”** is the first word. If the second letters are also the same, you take the third.

In the **dictionary** all words are arranged in ABC order. At the top of each page there are often the first and last words on that page. This lets you leaf through quickly. Anyone who knows the ABC well finds a word much faster. A phone book, an encyclopedia or the index in a non-fiction book are also sorted in ABC order.

You can also put **names** in order, for example for a class list. With Mia, Noah, Paul and Tim, **M** comes before N, P and T. That is why Mia comes first. In German dictionaries, umlauts such as Ä, Ö and Ü are usually treated like A, O and U. So “Äpfel” (apples) is found among the words beginning with A.

gewusst: The word alphabet comes from the first two letters of the Greek alphabet: alpha and beta.
Computers sort words into ABC order in fractions of a second.

teile.einleitung: Many accounts on the internet are only protected by a password. **Two-factor authentication** asks for a second proof as well when you log in. This protects an account much better, even if someone knows the password.
wichtigste: Two-factor authentication is 2FA for short.
As well as the password, a second proof is needed, for example a code.
The code often comes by app or text message and is only valid for a short time.
A thief with only the password cannot get into the account this way.
Banks in Switzerland almost always ask for a second factor for e-banking.
You never pass codes on to other people.

abschnitte.text: A **factor** is proof that you really are you. There are three kinds: something you **know** (password, PIN), something you **have** (mobile phone, card, key) and something you **are** (fingerprint, face). Two-factor authentication combines two different kinds. So two passwords one after the other do not count as two factors.
